issues.title: A stacked round trip does not say which leg is outbound and which is the return
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #240 and deliberately left out of that slice.

## What was observed

At phone width a booking is stacked into a card. A round trip renders both legs
one after the other, each as FLIGHT / ROUTE / DEPARTURE, with no wording saying
which is the outbound and which is the return:

```
FLIGHT     Mona Airways MA102
ROUTE      Detroit, USA → Seattle, USA
DEPARTURE  Aug 17, 2026
FLIGHT     Mona Airways MA404
ROUTE      Seattle, USA → Detroit, USA
DEPARTURE  Aug 24, 2026
PRICE      $620
STATUS     MA404 cancelled by airline
```

The captions FLIGHT / ROUTE / DEPARTURE simply repeat. On a one-way card they
earn their place — the values are heterogeneous and unlabelled strings would be
guesswork — but on a round trip the second set adds nothing and the reader has
to infer direction from the route.

`#240` fixed the ordering defect underneath this (the legs used to be split by
the price, status and action cells) and added a rule between legs so they read
as two groups. What is missing is naming them.

## What would fix it

`lib/bookingItinerary.ts` already exports `legDirectionLabel`, and
`ProfileClient.tsx` already imports it for the seat modal. The stacked layout
could use it in place of the repeated FLIGHT caption — "Outbound" and "Return"
rather than FLIGHT twice.

The reason it was not done in #240: the caption is a single element shared by
both layouts, so changing it changes the desktop table's Flight column too.
That is arguably an improvement, but it is a different change with its own
review, and #240 was already carrying a layout rewrite.

Read from the rendered application at 390px; the `legDirectionLabel` route is a
reading of the source and has not been tried.
issues.display_title: A stacked round trip does not say which leg is outbound and which is the return

issues.title: Stacked bookings read in a different order than they display
issues.body:
Introduced by #240 and knowingly accepted there; filed rather than widening that
slice. Found by the `verifier` via a CDP accessibility-tree dump.

## What was observed

Below 767px the bookings table stacks into cards. The visual order is produced
by CSS `order:` on the Price, Status and Actions cells, which does not move the
DOM:

```
DOM order    : Flight Route Departure Price Status Actions Flight Route Departure
Visual order : Flight Route Departure Flight Route Departure Price Status Actions
```

A screen reader in browse mode therefore hears the status and the Cancel button
*before* the second leg of a round trip; a sighted user sees them after. That is
WCAG 1.3.2 (Meaningful Sequence) territory.

## Why it was accepted

The alternative was worse. `rowSpan` stops meaning anything once rows are
blocks, so without the reorder the booking-level cells land mid-card: a round
trip printed "MA404 cancelled by airline" above a block naming its *outbound*,
with the cancelled leg trailing below the buttons. That was a blocking
`ui-review` finding and the reorder fixed it.

Mitigating it: the status names its flight number explicitly ("MA404 cancelled
by airline"), so the announcement is not ambiguous even heard early, and table
navigation is intact — the row and cell roles survive `display: contents` in
Chromium, measured.

## What would fix it

DOM order matching visual order, which means the booking-level cells rendering
after the leg rows. A table needs them in the first row for `rowSpan`, so this
wants either a genuinely separate card tree (rejected in #240 — two DOM copies
is what caused the locator bug in #243) or dropping `rowSpan` and accepting
empty cells on continuation rows at desktop.

Measured in Chromium only; the Playwright project here is chromium-only, so
other engines are unobserved.
issues.display_title: Stacked bookings read in a different order than they display

issues.title: Checkout seat map scrolls horizontally at 390px
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #74 slice 1; pre-existing and outside that slice.

## What was observed

At 390x844 on the seat step of `/checkout`:

```
document.scrollWidth  419
document.clientWidth  390
```

29px of horizontal page scroll, present both before and after the seat-hold
error. The fuselage container and the F column are clipped at the right edge.
The Review step at the same width is clean, so it is the seat map specifically.

## Why it matters

A page that scrolls sideways at phone width hides content with no affordance —
the same class of defect as #240, where the fix was to stop the layout
overflowing rather than to make the scroll discoverable. Here the F column is
part of choosing a seat, so a customer on a phone cannot see one sixth of the
cabin without discovering a scroll that has no visible indication.

Related: #193 (checkout scrolls horizontally at 390px) may be the same
underlying container; check before fixing separately.

Measured in Chromium at 390x844 against the running application.

## Summary

Begin roadmap P0.5 by making email identity canonical, adding durable abuse
protection to registration and credential login, and keeping immediate signup
outcomes generic. This closes the most direct duplicate-account, enumeration,
and brute-force paths before verification and recovery are introduced in the
next P0.5 slice.

## Changes

- normalize email addresses in the application and database, including a
  database constraint and case-insensitive uniqueness migration
- add atomic PostgreSQL-backed registration and login rate limits with HMAC
  identifiers, bounded expiry pruning, and fail-closed trusted-proxy handling
- return the same immediate registration response for new and existing users
- make authentication pages responsive and improve pending, error, focus, and
  autocomplete accessibility states
- route the recommended Compose deployment only through a non-root nginx proxy
  that overwrites incoming `X-Forwarded-For` values
- add focused unit, component, migration, container, and Playwright abuse tests
- update the P0.5 roadmap progress entry and security/deployment guidance

explicit hop count is configured; per-email login attempts never lock out a
valid password; and limiter identifiers are keyed digests rather than raw

issues.body:
## Summary

- encrypt passport numbers and dates of birth with versioned AES-256-GCM envelopes and authenticated passenger/field context
- restrict customer and staff passenger projections to non-sensitive manifest fields
- add 30-day post-departure retention deletion, immediate erasure support, and bounded active-key rotation
- migrate away from plaintext columns and enforce protected-or-deleted passenger state in PostgreSQL
- document the passenger-data policy and require the key ring in local, CI, and container environments
- add database, security, component, responsive, and real-passenger browser regression coverage

## Why

This completes the passenger-data protection subitem of roadmap item P0.5. Passport numbers and birth dates previously lived in plaintext and routine profile/admin queries loaded them even when the UI did not need them.

Existing pre-production demo identity values are deliberately purged by the migration instead of being copied through migration tooling without the runtime encryption key. Booking and seat history remain intact.

## Validation

- Jest: 45 suites, 333 tests passed
- Playwright: 14 Chromium journeys passed without retries
- TypeScript and Prisma validation/generation passed
- all 14 migrations applied both to the live development database and a fresh temporary database
- production Next.js build passed
- ESLint passed with 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- Docker image built; 17 layers passed the secret scan
- final UI review and code review approved with no findings

issues.body:
## Summary

A session-signing `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` reached this public repository in `ff161ca`
(2026-06-26), inlined in the verify subagent's Playwright command. #55 removed
it, but nothing in the suite would have caught it, and nothing would catch the
next one.

Existing coverage did not apply. The container checks inspect image contents,
and `.dockerignore` excludes `.agents`, `.claude`, `.codex`, and `.github`, so
the value never entered an image — no test looked at repository sources.

## Exposure assessment

Recorded here so the risk is not overstated or understated:

- The exposed value is **29 characters**. `lib/env.ts` has required ≥32 since
  #34 (2026-07-11), so it **cannot boot the application today** — a deployment
  still using it would crash in `validateServerEnvironment`.
- The window was 2026-06-26 to 2026-07-11, and only for an environment that
  actually used it. Consumers are NextAuth JWT signing and
  `createAuthRateLimitKey`, so a forged session was the theoretical risk.
- The local `.env` uses a different value.

Per the decision recorded below, history is **not** rewritten.

## What the scan does

Flags assignments of `NEXTAUTH_SECRET`, `PASSENGER_DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`,
`STAFF_MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`, and `AUTH_EMAIL_API_TOKEN` to **quoted literals**
across every tracked text file, including the escaped quoting that hid the
original value inside a JSON string.

Unquoted values are runtime references, not literals, so these correctly pass:

- Compose interpolation — `NEXTAUTH_SECRET: ${NEXTAUTH_SECRET:?...}`
- TypeScript — `const NEXTAUTH_SECRET = requireValue(...)`
- Empty template entries — `NEXTAUTH_SECRET=`

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `__tests__/` are allowlisted: those values are
disposable and never reach a running service. Unit tests pin both the detection
and the accepted-reference behavior, so the allowlist cannot silently rot.

## Verification

- **Catches the real bug.** Restoring the pre-fix `agent.json` fails the scan:
  ```
  ✕ never assigns NEXTAUTH_SECRET to a literal in a tracked file
    + ".agents/agents/verify/agent.json: supersecretjwtpassphrase12345"
  ✕ keeps agent instructions free of the value exposed in ff161ca
  ```
- **No false positives.** Full suite green: 54 suites, 411 tests.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. `npm run lint` reports 0 errors (8 pre-existing
  warnings in untouched components; the script scopes to `app components lib`
  and does not lint `__tests__`).
- **Rendered UI review: not applicable** — no component, style, or route touched.

## Roadmap

Closest to Phase 0 secret handling, but this adds regression coverage rather
than completing a roadmap item, so no progress row is added.

## Follow-up for the maintainer

If that value ever ran in a reachable environment before 2026-07-11, rotate it
and invalidate active sessions per `SECURITY.md`. Nothing in this PR can
determine that.

flake on `main`**, reported separately rather than fixed here:

`__tests__/lib/passengerDataProtection.test.ts` › *rejects tampered ciphertext*
fails roughly 1 run in 16. The test tampers by rewriting the final base64url

character has two unused low bits. `'A'` and `'B'` differ only in that unused

to identical bytes, GCM authenticates it, and the expected throw never happens.

issues.title: chore(hooks): let the review hooks read git history
issues.body:
## Summary

The `PreToolUse` agent hooks on `git push` and `gh pr create` instruct their
reviewer to run `git diff` against the push range. `.claude/settings.json` had
no `permissions.allow` list, so under don't-ask mode the reviewer had Bash
denied. It could not obtain the diff and failed closed — blocking the command
it was meant to review, without having reviewed anything.

Observed during this session, on a read-only `grep`:

> Could not complete the review: Bash is denied in this environment ("don't ask
> mode"), so I was unable to run `git diff @{u}..HEAD` [...] This is a
> review-not-performed result, NOT a finding of blocking issues.

## Change

Adds the read-only git commands the reviewers need:

```json
"allow": [
  "Bash(git diff:*)", "Bash(git log:*)", "Bash(git rev-parse:*)",
  "Bash(git status:*)", "Bash(git show:*)", "Bash(git merge-base:*)"
]
```

These live in tracked project settings beside the hooks, because the hooks are
shared with the team and do not work without them. Nothing else changed: all
six hook events, both `if` conditions, and the existing `deny` entry are
preserved (verified with `jq`).

## Scope note

`permissions.allow` is not hook-scoped — these commands become allowed for the
main session too. All six are read-only and cannot mutate the repository, so
this is a deliberate and narrow widening. Write operations (`git commit`,
`git push`, `git checkout`) are **not** included and still prompt.

## Verification limits — please read

`jq` confirms the merge is correct and nothing was lost. What I **cannot**
confirm is that the hook now succeeds end to end: a push that is not blocked
looks identical whether the reviewer ran and passed or never fired at all.
Proving it needs a push where the reviewer demonstrably produces a verdict.

## Known separate issue, not fixed here

The same hook **misfired on a command that was not a push** — a read-only
`grep` over Markdown files matched `"if": "Bash(git push:*)"` and triggered a
blocking review. Whatever the cause, the `if` predicate is matching too
broadly. Tightening it changes hook semantics, so it is left for a decision
rather than bundled in.

issues.title: fix(test): tamper ciphertext in a way that always mutates it
issues.body:
## Summary

`passengerDataProtection.test.ts` › *rejects tampered ciphertext* fails about
one run in fifteen. It is not a new problem, but it **blocked CI on #56**, an
unrelated pull request, so it is now on the critical path.

The test tampered by rewriting the final base64url character:

```js
parts[3] = `${parts[3].slice(0, -1)}${parts[3].endsWith('A') ? 'B' : 'A'}`;
```

An 8-byte ciphertext encodes to 11 base64url characters. Those carry 66 bits
for 64 bits of data, so the final character holds **two unused low bits**:

```
'A' = 000000
'B' = 000001   differ only in an unused bit
```

Whenever the ciphertext already ended in `'A'`, the "tampered" envelope decoded
to byte-identical ciphertext, GCM authenticated it, decryption succeeded, and
the expected throw never happened.

This matters beyond flakiness. In those runs the test asserted that tampering
is detected **while tampering with nothing** — a security assertion that
silently verified nothing roughly 7% of the time.

## Fix

Decode, flip every bit of the first byte, re-encode. The mutation always lands
on authenticated bytes regardless of encoding alignment.

## Verification

| Measure | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| Mutation was a no-op (50,000 samples) | 6.67% | **0** |
| Failures in 40 consecutive test runs | ~2–3 expected | **0** |

Full suite green: 53 suites, 403 tests.

- **Rendered UI review: not applicable** — test-only change, no component,
  style, or route touched.

## Roadmap

Closest to Phase 0 passenger-data protection, but this repairs existing
coverage rather than completing an item, so no progress row is added.

## Merge order

This should merge **first**. #56, #57, and #58 are all exposed to the same
flake on every CI run until it lands.

## Summary

#57 made `CLAUDE.md` a symlink (git mode `120000`). That tradeoff was flagged
at the time and is now being paid down: Windows checks symlinks out as **plain
text files containing the target path** unless `core.symlinks` is enabled. A
Windows contributor's agent would read the literal string `AGENTS.md` and load
no project context at all — silently, with no error.

`CLAUDE.md` becomes a regular file that points at `AGENTS.md` and imports it,
so both names work with no dependence on symlink support.

## The drift problem, and the guard

A pointer file invites the failure it was meant to prevent: the `#` shortcut
appends to `CLAUDE.md`, and anything landing there would never reach
`AGENTS.md` — two files with content again, which is what #57 set out to fix.

`__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts` pins:

1. **File mode is `100644`, and the path is not a symlink** — stops the symlink
   from creeping back and breaking Windows checkouts again.
2. **Exact contents of `CLAUDE.md`** — any appended note fails the build, and
   the assertion diff names the lines to move.
3. **`AGENTS.md` still carries its sections** (Commands, Environment,
   Architecture, Gotchas, Code Style, Development Workflow, Testing
   Expectations, Roadmap Tracking) — the pointer cannot end up aimed at a
   hollowed-out target.

`CLAUDE.md` itself states the rule, so whoever trips the guard has already been
told where the content belongs.

**Failed against the symlink for the right reasons:**

issues.title: fix(hooks): stop the review hooks blocking when they cannot review
issues.body:
## Summary

Both `PreToolUse` agent hooks conflated **"I could not review"** with
**"block"**. When the reviewer failed to obtain a diff it returned a not-met
condition, refusing the command without any defect having been found. Its own
words, from the incident that surfaced this:

> This is a review-not-performed result, NOT a finding of blocking issues in
> the commits.

#58 fixed the immediate cause of the failure (git was denied). This fixes the
behaviour that turned that failure into a block.

## Why the `if` filters are unchanged

The obvious move — tighten `"if": "Bash(git push:*)"` — is the wrong one.

A filter is a cheap way to avoid spawning an agent on every Bash call. It is
not a correctness boundary. Two commands were refused despite containing
neither `git push` nor `gh pr create`:

```
for f in AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md .github/copilot-instructions.md; do grep …
for pr in 56 57 58; do gh pr view $pr --json … ; done
```

while real pushes such as `git push -u origin <branch> 2>&1 | tail -5` went
through untouched. Two explanations fit — the matcher cannot decompose
multi-statement commands and fires conservatively, or it fires far more often
than observed and the reviewer was simply inconsistent about blocking when it
could not read the diff. Neither can be confirmed from inside this repository:
the hook runs before the command, so in-shell timing cannot see it, and a
sentinel hook needs a settings reload to take effect.

Tightening a pattern against matching semantics we cannot observe is guesswork,
and it would not have prevented the block. So: leave the filter, make
over-firing harmless.

## Change

Both prompts gain two rules:

1. **Relevance pre-check** — confirm the command really is a push, or really
   creates a pull request, and PASS immediately when it is not.
2. **Fail open, loudly** — inability to obtain the diff is an explicit PASS
   that states review was not performed and why. *"Being unable to review is
   not a finding."*

## Tradeoff, stated plainly

A reviewer denied git access no longer stops the command, so the gate can be
bypassed by breaking its access. That is the right way round here: this is an
advisory review that already blocks only on high-confidence findings, and CI
plus the merge gates are the actual enforcement. A fail-closed gate that cannot
read the diff does not fail safe — it eventually blocks everything.

## Verification

Configuration only; no application code, and no test covers hook prompts.

- `jq` confirms valid JSON, that **both** hooks carry **both** new rules, and
  that the six hook events, both `if` predicates, and the `permissions` block
  are unchanged.
- Full behavioural verification needs a settings reload plus a real push, so it
  cannot be completed in the session that wrote it.
- **Rendered UI review: not applicable** — no component, style, or route.

## Roadmap

No roadmap item applies — developer tooling configuration.

|---|---|

| Configured repository secrets | none |
| Committed value length | 29 chars, against a 32 minimum since #34 |
| Present in any image | no — `.dockerignore` excludes the agent directories |

exposure window was 2026-06-26 to 2026-07-11, and the theoretical risk (a

## Summary

`REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md` duplicated what an issue tracker already does, and its
progress log had to be hand-updated in the same pull request as the work it
described. Migrated to GitHub issues and deleted (520 lines).

## What was created

**28 issues, #63-#90**, all labelled `roadmap`:

| Milestone | Issues | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 0 | #63-#67 | 5 closed — delivered |
| Phase 1 | #68-#72 | 5 open |
| Phase 2 | #73-#77 | 5 open |
| Phase 3 | #78-#82 | 5 open |
| Phase 4 | #83-#86 | 4 open |
| Phase 5 | #87-#90 | 4 open |

Each issue carries its tasks as checkboxes and its acceptance criteria verbatim
from the roadmap. Milestones preserve the priority ordering the phases encoded.

**Delivered work is not lost.** The five Phase 0 items were created and
immediately closed, each carrying its progress-log rows and PR numbers, so the
delivery record stays visible and linkable instead of surviving only in the
history of a deleted file.

**Partial items are explicit.** #68 (P1.1) and #71 (P1.4) separate what remains
from what shipped, with PR numbers against the delivered lines — the roadmap
expressed this only as a mix of ticked and unticked boxes.

- `AGENTS.md`: `## Roadmap Tracking` becomes `## Issue Tracking`, restated for
  issues — reference the number, let the PR close it, and **comment rather than

  rule no longer says "roadmap item".
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: points at the label and milestones.
- `docs/STAFF_ACCOUNT_POLICY.md`: its dangling "P4.3 roadmap item" reference now
  links #85.

  case-insensitive sweep for "roadmap" found the stale `STAFF_ACCOUNT_POLICY.md`
  reference, which is why it is included here.
- Milestone counts confirmed against the API: Phase 0 at 5/5 closed, 23 open
  across Phases 1-5, all 28 carrying the label.
- Full suite green: 55 suites, 414 tests. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
  `npm run lint` 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched components).

This is the last change that can cite a roadmap item ID. Future pull requests

issues.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #91. The `## Issue Tracking` section carried four bullets; two
were not earning their place. `AGENTS.md` loads into every agent's context on
every task, so filler competes directly with the gotchas that prevent real
mistakes.

## Removed

- **`GitHub CI is the source of truth for build, lint, …`** — vestigial. It came
  across from the roadmap's own "Sources of truth" section, where it meant *do
  not hand-copy test counts into this markdown file*. With the file gone there
  is no competing record, and `## Testing Expectations` plus workflow step 7
  already cover CI. I carried it over in #91 without re-earning it.
- **`Tick a task box only after verification passes`** — restates workflow step
  7, which already gates everything on the verifier.

## Kept

The two facts that cannot be derived from the repository:

- **Where the work is tracked** — that issues exist, that the `roadmap` label
  filters them, and that milestones carry *priority order* rather than mere
  grouping. Nothing in the tree says this since the roadmap file was deleted.
- **The partial-delivery convention** — comment rather than close. The default
  instinct is to close an issue on touching it; P1.1 took six pull requests, and
  closing it at #45 would have lost the remaining scope.

The issue-reference convention is folded into the second bullet: near-universal
practice, worth one clause, not three lines.

Net: 14 lines to 7.

## Verification

- `__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts` passes — the `## Issue Tracking`
  heading it asserts is unchanged.
- 53 suites, 411 tests pass. The two `*.database.test.ts` suites were skipped
  locally rather than starting Postgres for a Markdown-only edit; CI runs them.
- **Rendered UI review: not applicable** — one Markdown section.

## Issue

None. Documentation hygiene on the file that describes the tracker.

issues.title: fix(checkout): review every leg, with each seat under its own flight
issues.body:
Fixes the defect #143 recorded as the most-reported finding of the roadmap
investigation — raised independently by 8 of 12 areas, never reproduced until now.

## The defect

Step 3 of checkout read `flights[activeLegIndex]`, whichever leg the seat map was
last showing, so a round trip showed **one flight card** on the last screen before
payment. The return leg was not on it. Seats compounded it: a traveller's seats were
joined into `Seats: 11A, 12C` with nothing saying which seat belonged to which
flight.

The confirmation step was fixed for exactly this during the round-trip work and
carries the reasoning in a comment; review was the half that was missed.

## The fix

One card per leg in itinerary order, each carrying that leg's flight details and each
traveller's seat **on that leg**.

Moving seats into the leg cards left the fare rows repeating a name already given
once per leg — and for a lone traveller, a "breakdown" of one row identical to the
total directly beneath it. That case now states the cabin and stops.

## From the `ui-review` pass

It exercised one-way, round-trip, 2-, 3- and 9-passenger bookings at 390/768/1440,
plus the submitting state and a real concurrent seat conflict. Two blocking defects
in the new markup, both fixed:

- **A long name pushed the seat outside the card and the page into horizontal
  scroll** at 390px — measured, the seat landed 93px past the card edge, so the one
  traveller with a long name saw no seat at all. `lib/validation.ts` allows
  100-character names, so this was reachable input, not a contrived fixture.
- **A hyphenated name broke the name↔seat pairing**: the seat wrapped to two lines
  and ended up adjacent to the *next* traveller's name — the same class of confusion
  this change exists to remove.

Also applied: `role="list"` on both lists and an accessible name on the per-leg list
(WebKit strips list semantics from `list-style: none`), an "Itinerary" heading so
heading navigation no longer skips the legs, and a contrast lift on the direction
eyebrow, which was the dimmest text on the card despite being the discriminator that
matters.

It confirmed the fix reports the seat actually held rather than the seat clicked —
the group auto-allocator had reassigned one, and review followed the assignment.

## The e2e assertion that never could have caught this

`e2e/booking.spec.ts` asserted `text=Seats: 11A, 12C` on the review step and passed
throughout the defect's life: a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats
are paired with the right legs. Both it and `e2e/multi-passenger.spec.ts` now assert
seat against traveller, row by row.

The verifier caught that both legs of that spec were picking `11A` — identical empty
layouts, `.first()` on each — which would have made the new assertions
near-tautologies. The inbound leg now takes a different seat so the check
discriminates.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (555 passing, twice), the three changed
e2e specs, and `npm run build` — all clean. The verifier also ran the new tests
against the **pre-change** component in a detached worktree: all eight touched tests
fail there, each for its intended reason, so none of them pass vacuously.

## Filed rather than fixed here

- #158 — the boarding pass still says `GEMINI AIRWAYS`, and `productIdentity.test.ts`
  misses it because its regex is case-sensitive
- #159 — a seat-conflict rejection is invisible on phone, drops focus to `<body>`,
  and leaves the refused seat showing in success green
- #160 — `ProfileClient` keeps a third copy of the direction label and will disagree
  with checkout about a middle leg once #131 lands

Also noted the review step as a call site on #84, which owns timezone-aware
departure display — the leg cards show a date but no time.

Migrated from `REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md`. P1.1's two remaining tasks depend on the airport timezone reference introduced here.

## Tasks

- [ ] Store schedule intent using airport-local time and IANA timezone.
- [ ] Store flight-instance timestamps as unambiguous instants.
- [ ] Maintain an airport reference (IATA code plus IANA timezone) as the single source for every local conversion.

- [ ] Show booking, ticket-issuance, and account-activity times in the customer's timezone, labeled — never in the viewer's incidental browser timezone.
- [ ] Keep comparisons and rules (already-departed, sorting, booking windows, fare time limits) on the UTC instant, using local time only for display and date pickers.
- [ ] Separate upcoming, departed, arrived, delayed, and cancelled flights.
- [ ] Replace the unqualified real-time claim unless a live data source exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- Daylight-saving transitions and cross-date international legs have tests.
- Customers can tell which timezone every displayed time uses.
- No flight time renders in the viewer's browser timezone: flight times use the relevant airport timezone and account times use the customer's timezone.

issues.title: Reward flight search and redemption
issues.body:
Split out of #70, where the task was "implement reward search and redemption, or remove the control until the loyalty model supports it". The control is removed; this tracks the feature.

## Why it could not be wired up

The search form had a "Search reward flights" checkbox that was uncontrolled — no state, no handler, no effect. Wiring it up was not an option, because there is nothing behind it:

- `PointsActivityService` records status points **earned** and reversed on cancellation
- there is no spendable balance, no award chart, no redemption ledger, and no notion of a fare priced in points
- `Flight.price` is a single cash price

So this is not a control fix. It is a pricing and loyalty model.

## What it would need

- A points balance distinct from status points, with its own ledger and expiry rules
- Award availability per flight and cabin — typically a separate inventory bucket from cash fares, not a conversion of one
- Award pricing (fixed chart, dynamic, or both) and the rules for taxes and carrier charges still payable in cash
- Redemption at checkout, including partial pay-with-points if that is wanted
- Refund and cancellation behaviour for redeemed bookings, which must return points rather than money (#76 covers the cash side)

## Scope note

This is Phase 2 scale and overlaps #76 (cancellation and refund rules). It should not be started before the payment work in #75, since redemption is a payment method.
issues.display_title: Reward flight search and redemption

issues.title: Multicity itineraries
issues.body:
Split out of #70, where the task was "implement multicity itineraries, or remove the dead link until the itinerary model supports them". The link is removed; this tracks the feature.

## The booking side is closer than it looks

The itinerary work for round trips (#109, #118, #119) generalised more than round trips needed:

- `Booking` is a sequence of `ItineraryLeg` rows, ordered by `sequence` — not a pair
- `FlightBookingService.bookFlight` takes `flightIds: number[]` and locks them in ascending id
- `BookingCheckoutWizard` renders `flights[]` with a tab per leg and a seat per leg
- `calculateItineraryTotal` sums each leg at its own fare
- the profile renders one row per leg with the seat held on each

None of that assumes two.

## What actually blocks it

- `MAX_ITINERARY_LEGS = 2` in `lib/validation.ts`, and `bookingRequestSchema` requires `seatNumbers.length === flightIds.length`
- **Search** is the real gap: `searchFlightsAction` takes one origin, one destination, and up to two dates. A multicity search is N independent leg searches with their own routes and dates
- The search form is built around outbound/return radio buttons and a single from/to pair
- `/checkout?outbound=X&inbound=Y` addresses exactly two legs
- Connections are a different concept from multicity stops and should not be conflated — a customer choosing to stop in a city is not the same as an itinerary routed through one

## Suggested slices

1. Raise the leg cap and generalise the checkout URL to an ordered list of flight ids
2. A multicity search form producing N leg searches, each with its own route and date
3. Reinstate the navigation entry

Worth deciding first whether "multicity" here means customer-chosen stopovers or connecting itineraries; they need different search behaviour.

issues.title: Roadmap investigation: findings and execution plan
issues.body:
A 14-agent investigation read every remaining roadmap issue against the code at `110cf2d` and produced an ordered plan. Recording it so the analysis is not lost.

## Scale

Roughly **130 pull requests** across Phases 2–5. Phase 3 alone (#78–#82) is ~40. This is not a backlog that closes in a sitting.

## Migration ownership — decide before anyone writes SQL

Six schema changes were independently proposed by two or more areas. Each needs a single owner or they will collide:

| Change | Owner | Consumers |
|---|---|---|
| `Booking.status` typing + status history | #76 | #73, #75 |
| `Flight.scheduleId` + schedule flight-number unique | #83 | #73 |
| `Booking.reference` | #77 | #86 |
| Flight duration / arrival instant / schedule timezone | #84 | #131, #73 |
| `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK | #73 | #84, #78 |
| Seat release (`releasedAt` + partial unique) | #76 | #74, #75 |

Four call sites (`FlightBookingService.ts:192`, `actions.ts:335`, `actions.ts:573`, `FlightSeatLayoutService.ts:41`) get rewritten independently by #74, #75 **and** #76. Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines in four files into one function.

## Recommended order

1. **Contract steps** (#135, #137) — six PRs. Both are declared blockers by four separate areas, and they remove two-sources-of-truth hazards that every later change otherwise has to double-write around.
2. **Cheap correctness fixes** — six PRs, one day each, blocking nothing. Includes #142 and the round-trip defect below.
3. #73 remainder → #76 → #74 → #75 → #77.

#76 before #74 and #75 because it owns booking status typing and seat release, which both build on. #74 before #75 because without holds, a checkout dying between commit and capture strands a seat — #75's own analysis proposes a throwaway sweeper to compensate, which landing #74 first deletes.

## The most-reported defect

**Round-trip review and e-ticket show one leg and the wrong seat** — found independently by 8 of 12 areas. Not yet verified by hand. Worth fixing before #81 splits the checkout wizard into modules, or it gets baked into two files instead of one.

Other unverified findings worth checking: `/flights` issues an unbounded query (~1,459 rows into an RSC payload); `getOccupiedSeatsAction` has no session check despite being a server action; itineraries whose legs are out of order or do not connect are accepted.

## Decisions needed before the relevant slices

- **#76**: the cancellation policy table — refundable cabins, cut-off before departure, fee flat vs percent, and whether post-departure cancellation is refused or zero-refund
- **#76**: does a staff CANCELLED flight auto-cancel bookings, or move them to DISRUPTED and let the customer choose?
- **#74**: hold TTL, and whether a hold is taken on leaving the Seats step or on first seat click
- **#75**: authorize-then-book vs book-PENDING-then-capture
- **#73**: must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?
- **#77**: what "confirm document details" means — an attestation checkbox is the only option that does not require amending `docs/PASSENGER_DATA_POLICY.md`

## Already answered

Stripe sandbox, mocked (#75). Travel guide redesigned rather than repaired (#78, delivered in #141). Multicity means connecting itineraries (#131) — note that area reports the route network has no connections to find until #84 lands arrival times.

Full per-agent output: `subagents/workflows/wf_f62a28db-761/journal.jsonl`.

issues.title: Two directions of place-to-airport mapping read different sources
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2a (`refactor/read-flight-airports`), and **verified against running code** by editing one row.

## Where

- `lib/flightRoute.ts:60` — `flightRouteWhere` turns the requested place into a code via `airportCodeFor` (`lib/airports.ts:58`), which reads the compiled `lib/data/AirportData`.
- Every route render now takes its words from the `Airport` row (`fromAirport.label` / `toAirport.label`).
- The origin/destination dropdown is a third source again: `FlightSchedule.from`/`to` prose, via `getFlightRoutesAction` (`app/actions.ts:264-281`).

So a search resolves label → code through a compiled file, and the results resolve code → label through the database.

## What was observed

With `Airport.label` for `DTW` edited to `Detroit Metro, USA` and nothing else changed, on `/?from=Seattle, USA&to=Detroit, USA&depart=2026-08-10&trip=one-way`:

- the `#to` select still read `Detroit, USA`
- the result card read `Seattle, USA ------> Detroit Metro, USA`

The form and the results named different places. The row was restored immediately.

## Why it matters

No code path in the application can create this drift today — only the seed writes `Airport`, and `scheduleSchema` rejects a place `airportCodeFor` does not know (`app/actions.ts:706-714`). That is why it was not fixed inside 2a. But the guard is "nobody edits that table", not a constraint, and the whole direction of #73 is that the `Airport` row is the truth. Any future admin screen for airports, or any data fix applied straight to the table, makes it real.

It closes when one source feeds both directions — related to #105, which proposes sourcing the codes from a dataset rather than by hand. The `FlightSchedule` prose is a separate strand of the same problem: that model has no airport references at all.

Recorded in a comment on `flightRouteWhere` in the meantime.

issues.title: An unrecognised shared search URL falls back to defaults without saying so
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2a. **Pre-existing**, not introduced by that change — verified by rendering the same URL against pre-change `HEAD`.

## Where

`lib/flightSearchUrl.ts:74-77`. `parseFlightSearchParams` rejects a `from`/`to` pair that is not in `routes`, returning `undefined`.

## What was observed

`/?from=Atlantis` renders the default form (Chicago -> Paris) with no results and no indication that the link was not understood. Verified at 390x844, 768x1024 and 1440x900. No error, no crash, no `undefined` in the output.

## Why it matters

Silently substituting a different route is worse than an empty result: someone following a link sees a plausible search they did not ask for, and nothing tells them the origin they wanted was dropped. The same fallback fires for a route that was valid and has since been withdrawn, which is the case most likely to happen for real.

The fix is a message on the form saying the link's route is not one the airline flies, and defaulting only after saying so.

issues.title: The e-ticket truncates the route at the first comma
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2a. **Pre-existing**, but the change moves what it truncates.

## Where

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1434` renders `legFlight.from.split(',')[0]`.

## What was observed

The e-ticket says `ROUTE London to New York` where every other surface in the application says `London, UK -> New York, USA`.

## Why it matters

Two problems. The ticket drops the country, which is the part that disambiguates cities sharing a name, and it does so only on the document someone carries to the airport. And the truncation assumes the label has a `City, Country` shape — after #73 step 2a that string comes from `Airport.label` rather than `Flight.from`, so it is now one more place quietly depending on how that column is written.

The fix is either to render the label whole, or to give `Airport` a separate short name and read that, rather than splitting prose at a comma.

`app/globals.css:416-423` applies `width: 100%` to every `button`, so the manifest close button at `app/admin/flights/AdminFlightsTable.tsx:243-250` measures 494px on desktop.

```
Review Air UIR900 | Miami, USA → Chicago, USA | 8/8/2026, 2:15:00 AM
```

wraps mid-label — `…→ Chicago,` / `USA | …`. Three lines at phone.

## Why it matters

issues.title: E-ticket caption text fails AA contrast
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2c. **Pre-existing**, sampled from rendered pixels at desktop.

## Where

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1433` renders the `ROUTE` caption — and its siblings `PASSENGER`, `FLIGHT`, `SEAT`, `DATE` — at `rgba(255,255,255,0.3)` and `0.65rem`.

## What was observed

**2.69:1**, against the 4.5:1 required at that size. The values beneath the captions measure 18.2:1 and are fine.

## Why it matters

The captions are what say which value is which on the document someone carries to the airport. At 0.65rem and 2.69:1 they are the least legible part of the boarding pass, and the failure is on the label rather than the data — so someone who cannot read them sees five unlabelled strings. Belongs with #80 (P3.3 accessibility pass); filed separately as a concrete measurement. Related to #194, which is about the same e-ticket truncating the route.

issues.title: Admin tables at phone width squeeze the route column to 89px
issues.body:

## What was observed

On `/admin/flights` at 390px the ROUTE cells are 89px wide and 111px tall. `San Francisco, USA → Tokyo, Japan` wraps to five lines, splitting `San Francisco,` from `USA`, and the price column is visually clipped (`$1,20C`).

The content is recoverable — the wrapper is `overflow-x: auto`, client width 324 against scroll width 867 — but there is **no visible affordance that it scrolls**. Same pattern at tablet, where the table is 916px in a 768px viewport.

## Why it matters

Containment inside `overflow-x: auto` is the right structure, and it is what keeps this off the page-level horizontal-scroll list. But a staff member on a phone sees a clipped price and a five-line route with nothing indicating there is more to the right. The fix is an affordance (a fade, a shadow, or a scroll hint), or a stacked layout at that width rather than a table. Belongs to #79 (P3.2 responsive layouts).

issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2c. Pre-existing accessibility gap, verified against running code.

## Where

`components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx:962-982`.

## What was observed

The accessible reading of a search result card is:

```
8/10/2026  Seattle, USA  Detroit, USA
```

The `------>` separator is correctly `aria-hidden="true"`, but nothing then carries the from/to relationship — the two places are distinguished only by the order they appear in the document.

## Why it matters

Choosing a flight is exactly the moment the direction matters, and a screen-reader user gets two place names with no stated relationship between them. The status board already solves this properly with `From`/`To` column headers; the search card is the surface that does not. issues.body:

## Where

`#from`, `#to`, `#class`, `#sortBy`, `#depart`, `#returnDate` on the home search form.

## What was observed

issues.body:

## What was observed

`#returnDate` renders `08/17/202` at 1440 and 768, and `08/17/20` at 390 — the year is cut off. Box width is 114.8px (110 at phone).

`scrollWidth` does not report the overflow because a date input clips inside its shadow DOM, which is why no horizontal-scroll check catches it.

issues.title: The notification drawer says "You're all caught up!" when loading has failed
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for the test-infrastructure cleanup. **Pre-existing**, reproduced by blocking every poll from first paint.

## What was observed

With 5 unread rows in the database and every notifications poll failing, `/profile` renders:

```
badge:  (none)
drawer: "Notifications / You're all caught up!"
```

## Why it matters

The empty state at `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:299-308` is an affirmative claim rendered from the initial `useState<Notification[]>([])` at line 44. "We have never successfully loaded" and "there is nothing to show" are indistinguishable, so a failure is reported to the user as good news.

The component has no error state and no way to render one. This became more pressing with the change that silences aborted polls: for that class of error there is now no signal anywhere. Distinguishing "not loaded yet" from "loaded, empty" is the fix.

issues.title: Notification bell: unread count invisible to assistive tech, drawer not keyboard operable
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for the test-infrastructure cleanup. All **pre-existing**, all measured against running code in `components/ui/titlebar.tsx`.

Grouped because they are one control and one fix pass.

- **The unread count is announced to nobody.** The accessibility tree for the bell is `{role: "button", name: "Toggle notifications"}` — the `aria-label` at `:165` overrides the `{unreadCount}` text node at `:195`, so "5 unread" is conveyed by a red circle alone.
- **No `aria-expanded`, no `aria-haspopup`, and no role or label on the panel.** Measured `ariaExpanded: null, ariaHasPopup: null`; the drawer div at `:202` has neither `role` nor `aria-label`. Nothing signals that the button opens anything, or whether it is open.
- **No visible focus indicator on the bell.** `:175` sets `outline: 'none'`; computed `outlineStyle: "none"` when focused.
- **Individual notifications are not keyboard operable.** Rows are `<div onClick>` (`:259-273`) with no `tabindex` and no role. Tabbing an open drawer reaches only "Mark all read". Mark-one-as-read is mouse-only.
- **Escape does not close the drawer**, and focus is never moved into it or restored. Only an outside `mousedown` closes it (`:88-101`).
- **Three contrast failures** against the drawer background: the timestamp (`:282`) and the empty-state text (`:303`) both measure **3.78:1**, and the unread badge (`:185-186`) **3.76:1** — all below 4.5:1 at those sizes. The badge failure compounds the first point: the count is colour-only *and* low contrast.

Belongs to #80 (P3.3 accessibility pass).

issues.title: next-auth's own session poll logs CLIENT_FETCH_ERROR on hard navigation
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for the test-infrastructure cleanup, while confirming #195's fix.

## What was observed

Rapid hard navigation (`page.goto` cycling `/` → `/flights` → `/profile` → `/admin` → back) while signed in produces, repeatedly:

```
[next-auth][error][CLIENT_FETCH_ERROR] ... /api/auth/session, message: Failed to fetch
```

This is `next-auth/react`'s own session poll being torn down mid-flight — the same class of non-failure #195 was about, from a different source. Under client-side navigation (Link clicks) the console is completely empty, so it is specific to hard navigation.

## Why it matters

#195 is fixed for the notification poll, but a spec asserting a clean console still cannot rely on one after a hard navigation. It also trains anyone reading the console to ignore `CLIENT_FETCH_ERROR`, which is the same erosion #195 described.

The library logs this itself, so the fix is either a `next-auth` logger override that drops aborted session fetches, or accepting it and scoping any console assertion to application errors.
issues.display_title: next-auth's own session poll logs CLIENT_FETCH_ERROR on hard navigation

issues.title: A direct departure edit still shows a stale return date for one render
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` while checking #181's fix. **Pre-existing and unchanged** by it — the same class of defect, on a different path.

## What was observed

Typing a new departure date into `#depart` (`components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx:736-739`) commits:

```
2026-08-01 | 2026-07-22     <- new departure, previous return
2026-08-01 | 2026-08-08     <- settled
```

The return date is still derived by a separate effect keyed on `departureDate`, so the intermediate render is the same mismatched pair #181 removed from the route-change path.

There is a second window of the same kind: after changing origin, `To` shows the new destination while both dates still hold the previous route's values, which is what `e2e/search.spec.ts:34` unblocks on.

## Why it matters

#181 fixed the route-change path in the component precisely because the intermediate state is visible to a customer, not only to a test. The invariant the new test asserts — a return date is either absent or exactly a week after the departure beside it — is currently route-change-only rather than global.

Making it global means deriving the return wherever the departure is set, rather than reacting to it afterwards. The `defaultReturnDate` helper added in #181 is already the shared rule; the direct-edit handler is the remaining caller that does not use it.

Related: #181, and #206 which means a phone user cannot read either date's year in any case.

issues.title: Rebook a disrupted itinerary instead of refunding it
issues.body:
Split out of #76, which delivered the refund half of "offer rebooking, refund, or credit
for disrupted itineraries" across five slices. Rebooking was deliberately left out rather
than half-built.

## Where things stand

A flight cancelled by staff moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED` (#232). The seat stays
held, the customer sees the state on their profile, and their only offered action is to
cancel for a full refund with no fee (#231). Reinstating the flight puts them back.

So a customer who wants to travel anyway has no path: they must take the refund and book
again from scratch, losing their seat and paying whatever the fare is by then.

## What rebooking needs

- A flight search constrained to the same route and a comparable date, offered from the
  disrupted booking rather than from the search page.
- Seat reselection on the new flight — the held seat does not transfer, and the new
  aircraft may have a different layout (`lib/seatLayout.ts`).
- A fare difference to resolve. The original `totalPriceCents` was charged; the
  replacement may cost more or less, and #75 owns whether anything moves.
- A decision about the original booking's history: is a rebooking a new `Booking` with
  the old one cancelled, or the same booking repointed at a different flight? The second
  keeps the reference and the passenger records but makes `ItineraryLeg` mutable, which
  nothing else in the schema currently allows.
- What it does to `releasedAt` on the old leg, and to the status history — `#231` added
  `BookingStatusChange.refundCents` and a monotonic `sequence`, so there is somewhere to
  record it.

That last question is the one to settle first; the rest follows from it.

## Credit

Also unbuilt, and further out: there is no credit balance anywhere in the schema, and
whether it is wanted at all probably depends on what #75 does with payments.

## Related

- #76 — the parent, and the decision record for the cancellation policy
- #75 — real payments, which owns any money actually moving
issues.display_title: Rebook a disrupted itinerary instead of refunding it

issues.title: Admin flight board still windows on UTC midnight
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` during #84's first slice, which fixed the same mistake in
customer search but left this one.

## What was observed

`app/admin/flights/page.tsx:21-29` builds its "Active occurrences (Next 7 Days)" window
from UTC midnight to UTC midnight plus seven days. Since #84 made `Flight.departureDate`
a true instant, those edges no longer line up with any airport's day: the board silently
gains or loses a few hours of flights at each end, by the origin's offset.

Concretely, a Tokyo departure early on the eighth local day is already inside the UTC
window and appears; a late Miami departure on the first local day is outside it and does
not.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

The customer search fix bounds a day at *the origin the customer named*
(`airportDayBounds` in `lib/flightTime.ts`). This board has no single origin — it lists
every flight across every route — so "the local day" is not defined for it, and the right
answer is a product decision:

- keep a UTC window and label it as such, or
- window per row against each flight's own origin, or
- treat it as "the next seven days" from now as an instant, which is probably what staff
  actually mean and needs no local day at all.

Low severity: the board is operational, the window is coarse, and nothing downstream
depends on its edges. Verified by reading the source against the migrated column, not by
observing a wrong row.

## Two smaller notes from the same review

- `zoneOffsetMs` in `lib/flightTime.ts` and `zoneOffsetMilliseconds` in `lib/dates.ts` are
  near-duplicates that differ in whether they subtract milliseconds. Harmless today
  because every instant either sees has `ms = 0`, but two copies of one function
  differing subtly is what bites later.
- Flight dates now render as `Aug 16, 2026` via hard-coded `en-US`, where they previously
  followed the viewer's locale. That was a deliberate part of removing the hydration
  mismatch, but a non-US viewer who saw `16/08/2026` now sees US ordering. If that
  matters, the fix is a locale the *customer* chose, not the browser's — which is the
  same shape as #84's outstanding "show account times in the customer's timezone" task.

issues.title: A schedule's duration or fare never reaches occurrences already generated
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` during #84's second slice. The pattern is pre-existing; the
consequence is newly larger.

## What was observed

`saveFlightScheduleAction` (`app/actions.ts`) pre-generates occurrences and skips any
that already exist, so editing a schedule reaches only future generations. That has
always been true of `priceCents`. It is now also true of `durationMinutes`, which
decides the arrival time printed on every one of those flights.

Verified against running code: a corrected duration leaves existing `Flight` rows on the
old value.

## Why it matters more now

At 157 occurrences per route across the 365-day booking horizon, a duration typed wrong
once puts a wrong arrival time on all 157 — and there is no way to notice:

- the admin schedule list (`app/admin/flights/page.tsx`) has no Duration column;
- nothing mounts `FlightScheduleForm` with `initialSchedule`, so there is no edit form at
  all — the list offers Delete only;
- the form's duration input is not cleared between creates, so a second schedule on a
  different route silently inherits the first one's block time unless the admin
  overwrites it. (That last one is fixed in the slice; the other two are not.)

## Worth deciding

Three separate things, in rough order of value:

1. **Show the duration in the admin schedule list.** Cheapest, and makes a wrong value
   visible at all.
2. **An edit path.** The form already accepts `initialSchedule` and prefills from it;
   nothing routes to it.
3. **What editing a schedule should do to occurrences already generated.** Updating them
   is not obviously right — a flight somebody has booked has a departure and an arrival
   they were told — so this is a product decision, not just a missing update. It is the
   same question #234 raises for rebooking.

## Related

- #84 — where the duration came from
- #235 — the other admin-board item from the same review

issues.title: Notification rows cannot be marked read from the keyboard
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` while re-checking the drawer for #208. Pre-existing.

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx` renders each notification as

```tsx
<div onClick={...} className="notification-item">
```

with no `role`, no `tabIndex` and no key handler. Clicking one marks it read; there is no
keyboard equivalent, so a keyboard or switch user can only use "Mark all read" — losing
the ability to read one and keep the rest unread.

It also means an empty drawer has **zero** focusable children, which is why tabbing
forward out of the drawer lands at the top of the document rather than after the bell.

## Related, from the same review

Two smaller things in the same component, both pre-existing:

- Tab order after the drawer is the document order of the portal, i.e. the end of
  `<body>`, so tabbing forward from the drawer goes to the top of the page. Escape now
  closes it from anywhere and returns focus to the bell (#208's fix), so there is a way
  back, but a focus trap while open would be the conventional answer for a `role="dialog"`.
- `setAnchor` runs on every capture-phase scroll event while the drawer is open,
  allocating a new object and re-rendering the titlebar each frame. Correct, just
  wasteful; bailing out when the position is unchanged would stop it.

Belongs with #210, which already records the unread count being invisible to assistive
technology and the drawer not being keyboard operable — this is the specific mechanism.

issues.title: Cancel renders in the same gradient as every other button, and its label fails AA
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #240, measured against the rendered application at
390px and 1280px. Pre-existing, not introduced by that change.

## What was observed

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx` sets `backgroundColor: '#ef4444'` on the
Cancel button and `#8b5cf6` on Change Seats. **Neither is ever painted.** The
global rule at `app/globals.css:416-417` sets

```css
background: linear-gradient(135deg, #6366f1, #8b5cf6, #d946ef);
```

A background-*image* paints over an inline background-*color*, so both buttons
render the identical indigo-to-magenta gradient. The destructive action is
visually indistinguishable from the benign one sitting next to it.

White 12px/700 text over what is actually painted:

| gradient position | colour | ratio vs white |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | `#6366f1` | 4.47:1 |
| 50% | `#8b5cf6` | 4.23:1 |
| 100% | `#d946ef` | **3.46:1** |

12px bold is not "large text" under WCAG (that needs 18.66px bold), so the
threshold is 4.5:1 and every point along the gradient fails. The worst is the
magenta end at 3.46:1.

## Why it matters

Two reasons beyond the raw contrast number.

A customer confirming a cancellation is doing something irreversible, and the
only thing distinguishing it from "Change Seats" is the word. The inline
`#ef4444` shows the intent was for it to read as destructive; it simply never
took effect, so nobody noticed it was not working.

And #240 has just made both buttons taller — `min-height: 44px` for touch — so
each one now spans more of the gradient, including more of the failing end.

## Where

- `app/globals.css:416-417` — the gradient that overrides
- `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx` — the two `backgroundColor` values that do
  nothing, in the booking actions

The same override presumably reaches every other button in the application, so
this is worth checking more widely than the profile before fixing.

Verified against running code at 390px and 1280px, not read from source.

issues.title: A stacked round trip does not say which leg is outbound and which is the return
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #240 and deliberately left out of that slice.

## What was observed

At phone width a booking is stacked into a card. A round trip renders both legs
one after the other, each as FLIGHT / ROUTE / DEPARTURE, with no wording saying
which is the outbound and which is the return:

```
FLIGHT     Mona Airways MA102
ROUTE      Detroit, USA → Seattle, USA
DEPARTURE  Aug 17, 2026
FLIGHT     Mona Airways MA404
ROUTE      Seattle, USA → Detroit, USA
DEPARTURE  Aug 24, 2026
PRICE      $620
STATUS     MA404 cancelled by airline
```

The captions FLIGHT / ROUTE / DEPARTURE simply repeat. On a one-way card they
earn their place — the values are heterogeneous and unlabelled strings would be
guesswork — but on a round trip the second set adds nothing and the reader has
to infer direction from the route.

`#240` fixed the ordering defect underneath this (the legs used to be split by
the price, status and action cells) and added a rule between legs so they read
as two groups. What is missing is naming them.

## What would fix it

`lib/bookingItinerary.ts` already exports `legDirectionLabel`, and
`ProfileClient.tsx` already imports it for the seat modal. The stacked layout
could use it in place of the repeated FLIGHT caption — "Outbound" and "Return"
rather than FLIGHT twice.

The reason it was not done in #240: the caption is a single element shared by
both layouts, so changing it changes the desktop table's Flight column too.
That is arguably an improvement, but it is a different change with its own
review, and #240 was already carrying a layout rewrite.

Read from the rendered application at 390px; the `legDirectionLabel` route is a
reading of the source and has not been tried.

issues.title: Stacked bookings read in a different order than they display
issues.body:
Introduced by #240 and knowingly accepted there; filed rather than widening that
slice. Found by the `verifier` via a CDP accessibility-tree dump.

## What was observed

Below 767px the bookings table stacks into cards. The visual order is produced
by CSS `order:` on the Price, Status and Actions cells, which does not move the
DOM:

```
DOM order    : Flight Route Departure Price Status Actions Flight Route Departure
Visual order : Flight Route Departure Flight Route Departure Price Status Actions
```

A screen reader in browse mode therefore hears the status and the Cancel button
*before* the second leg of a round trip; a sighted user sees them after. That is
WCAG 1.3.2 (Meaningful Sequence) territory.

## Why it was accepted

The alternative was worse. `rowSpan` stops meaning anything once rows are
blocks, so without the reorder the booking-level cells land mid-card: a round
trip printed "MA404 cancelled by airline" above a block naming its *outbound*,
with the cancelled leg trailing below the buttons. That was a blocking
`ui-review` finding and the reorder fixed it.

Mitigating it: the status names its flight number explicitly ("MA404 cancelled
by airline"), so the announcement is not ambiguous even heard early, and table
navigation is intact — the row and cell roles survive `display: contents` in
Chromium, measured.

## What would fix it

DOM order matching visual order, which means the booking-level cells rendering
after the leg rows. A table needs them in the first row for `rowSpan`, so this
wants either a genuinely separate card tree (rejected in #240 — two DOM copies
is what caused the locator bug in #243) or dropping `rowSpan` and accepting
empty cells on continuation rows at desktop.

Measured in Chromium only; the Playwright project here is chromium-only, so
other engines are unobserved.

issues.title: Checkout seat map scrolls horizontally at 390px
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #74 slice 1; pre-existing and outside that slice.

## What was observed

At 390x844 on the seat step of `/checkout`:

```
document.scrollWidth  419
document.clientWidth  390
```

29px of horizontal page scroll, present both before and after the seat-hold
error. The fuselage container and the F column are clipped at the right edge.
The Review step at the same width is clean, so it is the seat map specifically.

## Why it matters

A page that scrolls sideways at phone width hides content with no affordance —
the same class of defect as #240, where the fix was to stop the layout
overflowing rather than to make the scroll discoverable. Here the F column is
part of choosing a seat, so a customer on a phone cannot see one sixth of the
cabin without discovering a scroll that has no visible indication.

Related: #193 (checkout scrolls horizontally at 390px) may be the same
underlying container; check before fixing separately.

Measured in Chromium at 390x844 against the running application.

issue.title: P2.2 Add inventory holds
issue.body:
Migrated from `REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md`.

## Tasks

- [ ] Create expiring seat/fare holds during checkout.
- [ ] Release abandoned holds automatically.
- [ ] Convert holds atomically when booking completes.
- [ ] Display expiry and recovery behavior to the customer.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two customers cannot purchase the same seat.
- Abandoned checkout does not permanently reduce inventory.
- Hold expiry and conversion are covered by concurrency tests.

content.text: Action completed.

comments.body:
Slice 1 delivered in #257 (`8f8e4e8`). Left open — two of the four tasks remain.

**Done**

- [x] Create expiring seat/fare holds during checkout. `SeatHold`, claimed when
  the customer leaves the seat map, expiring after 10 minutes.
- [x] Release abandoned holds automatically. By expiry rather than by a sweeper,
  which is what makes "abandoned checkout does not permanently reduce inventory"
  true without depending on a job that could fail. `releaseHoldsExcept` also
  drops a seat the customer swaps away from, and a completed booking releases
  what it bought.

**Remaining**

- [ ] **Convert holds atomically when booking completes.** Today the release
  happens *after* `bookFlight` returns, deliberately — a hold is an optimisation
  and failing to tidy one up must never undo a purchase. But it is not a
  conversion: between the assignment being written and the hold being deleted
  there is a window where both exist, and if the release fails the seat stays
  "held" by its own buyer until it expires. Doing it inside the booking
  transaction is the real acceptance criterion and needs the deadlock question
  below answered first.
- [ ] **Display expiry and recovery behaviour to the customer.** Nothing tells
  them a seat is being held at all, and nothing shows the countdown. A customer
  can sit on the review step past ten minutes and have the confirmation succeed
  or fail on a race they were never told about.

**Two things the review turned up that the next slice has to answer**

`holderKey` is the user id, not a checkout session. Two tabs on the same flight
therefore stomp each other: advancing in the second releases the first tab's
seat, and another customer can take it. Verified. A per-checkout key fixes it
and is a prerequisite for guests booking at all.

`holdSeat` returns `false` for "someone else has it" only at READ COMMITTED,
which is what every call uses today because each is autocommit. Wrapping the
claim loop in a transaction — the obvious way to make conversion atomic — makes
the loser raise `40001` instead, and introduces an ordering-dependent deadlock
between two customers claiming the same pair of seats in opposite order. Both
are noted in `lib/seatHolds.ts`; neither is a problem until the next slice
starts.

Filed while working on this: #255 (seat buttons announce as just "A"), #256
(seat map scrolls horizontally at 390px).

issue.title: Roadmap investigation: findings and execution plan
issue.body:
A 14-agent investigation read every remaining roadmap issue against the code at `110cf2d` and produced an ordered plan. Recording it so the analysis is not lost.

## Scale

Roughly **130 pull requests** across Phases 2–5. Phase 3 alone (#78–#82) is ~40. This is not a backlog that closes in a sitting.

## Migration ownership — decide before anyone writes SQL

Six schema changes were independently proposed by two or more areas. Each needs a single owner or they will collide:

| Change | Owner | Consumers |
|---|---|---|
| `Booking.status` typing + status history | #76 | #73, #75 |
| `Flight.scheduleId` + schedule flight-number unique | #83 | #73 |
| `Booking.reference` | #77 | #86 |
| Flight duration / arrival instant / schedule timezone | #84 | #131, #73 |
| `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK | #73 | #84, #78 |
| Seat release (`releasedAt` + partial unique) | #76 | #74, #75 |

Four call sites (`FlightBookingService.ts:192`, `actions.ts:335`, `actions.ts:573`, `FlightSeatLayoutService.ts:41`) get rewritten independently by #74, #75 **and** #76. Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines in four files into one function.

## Recommended order

1. **Contract steps** (#135, #137) — six PRs. Both are declared blockers by four separate areas, and they remove two-sources-of-truth hazards that every later change otherwise has to double-write around.
2. **Cheap correctness fixes** — six PRs, one day each, blocking nothing. Includes #142 and the round-trip defect below.
3. #73 remainder → #76 → #74 → #75 → #77.

#76 before #74 and #75 because it owns booking status typing and seat release, which both build on. #74 before #75 because without holds, a checkout dying between commit and capture strands a seat — #75's own analysis proposes a throwaway sweeper to compensate, which landing #74 first deletes.

## The most-reported defect

**Round-trip review and e-ticket show one leg and the wrong seat** — found independently by 8 of 12 areas. Not yet verified by hand. Worth fixing before #81 splits the checkout wizard into modules, or it gets baked into two files instead of one.

Other unverified findings worth checking: `/flights` issues an unbounded query (~1,459 rows into an RSC payload); `getOccupiedSeatsAction` has no session check despite being a server action; itineraries whose legs are out of order or do not connect are accepted.

## Decisions needed before the relevant slices

- **#76**: the cancellation policy table — refundable cabins, cut-off before departure, fee flat vs percent, and whether post-departure cancellation is refused or zero-refund
- **#76**: does a staff CANCELLED flight auto-cancel bookings, or move them to DISRUPTED and let the customer choose?
- **#74**: hold TTL, and whether a hold is taken on leaving the Seats step or on first seat click
- **#75**: authorize-then-book vs book-PENDING-then-capture
- **#73**: must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?
- **#77**: what "confirm document details" means — an attestation checkbox is the only option that does not require amending `docs/PASSENGER_DATA_POLICY.md`

## Already answered

Stripe sandbox, mocked (#75). Travel guide redesigned rather than repaired (#78, delivered in #141). Multicity means connecting itineraries (#131) — note that area reports the route network has no connections to find until #84 lands arrival times.

Full per-agent output: `subagents/workflows/wf_f62a28db-761/journal.jsonl`.

issues.title: feat(checkout): hold a seat while the customer is choosing it
issues.body:
First slice of #74. Converting the hold at booking and showing the customer a
countdown are later slices; this one stops two customers being invited to buy
the same seat.

## The problem

A seat only became unavailable once a booking existed. Between picking 12A and
paying for it, the seat stayed on every other customer's map. The partial unique
index on `SeatAssignment` already made it impossible for two people to *own*
12A — but nothing stopped them both being invited to try, and the loser found
out at the payment step.

## Three decisions worth review

**A hold is not an assignment.** An assignment is a seat somebody owns and part
of a booking's history; a hold is a claim with a deadline belonging to nobody's
itinerary. Putting unpaid rows in `SeatAssignment` would make all four queries
behind `heldSeats()` learn the difference.

**The unique index is unconditional** — the opposite of the partial one chosen
for `SeatAssignment` in `20260810050000`. An expired hold is *taken over in
place* by `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, never deleted, so a second row for a seat
should never exist, dead or alive. Claiming is one statement for the same
reason: read-then-write loses to the interleaving where both customers read
first, while a conflict is decided inside the row's own lock.

The verifier attacked this directly rather than trusting the `Promise.all`
test — two genuinely overlapping transactions, B's statement issued while A was
open and confirmed blocked for 400ms:

| isolation | case | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| READ COMMITTED | empty seat | one winner, one row, loser gets `false` |
| READ COMMITTED | expired row | one winner, one row |
| SERIALIZABLE | either | loser gets `40001` |

Every call is autocommit, so READ COMMITTED is what runs. Deadlock is not
possible as written: no transaction ever holds two seat locks at once. Both
properties are now stated in the docstring, because making the loop
transactional would buy an ordering-dependent deadlock.

**Every timestamp is the database's**, in `TIMESTAMPTZ`. `now()` decides the
expiry and the liveness test, so no clock skew can make a hold read live to one
party and dead to another. The zone-aware column matters for the same reason:
the verifier measured one hold, written under UTC, reading as *430 minutes
remaining* in Los Angeles and *530 minutes expired* in Tokyo. `Flight.departureDate`
is `TIMESTAMPTZ` from #84 for exactly this.

**Nothing sweeps expired rows**, which is what satisfies "abandoned checkout
does not permanently reduce inventory" — no cleanup job whose failure could
quietly lose seats.

## What review caught

`ui-review` found four blocking defects and the `verifier` a fifth. All fixed:

- **The refusal blamed the wrong leg.** A round trip carries 16A twice, so the
  client marked whichever leg it found first — telling a customer the outbound
  seat they had just been *granted* was gone, drawn red and disabled, while the
  leg that really failed sat on a tab they weren't looking at.
- **The error rendered off-screen** — 598px above the viewport at 390, 207px at
  1280. Announced to screen readers, so the only people who learned the request
  failed were the ones not looking at the button.
- **The refused seat stayed selected**, so the passenger list said it was theirs
  while the map drew it occupied, and pressing the button re-failed forever.
- **A thrown action was silent** — an expired session gave an unhandled
  rejection and a dead button.
- **Nothing released a hold on the success path.** A bought seat stayed held for
  ten more minutes and outlived the account that took it, since `holderKey` is
  not a foreign key. That failed two Playwright specs *deterministically*, and
  the #213 leak detector missed it because it did not track `SeatHold`. It does
  now, and the full suite leaves zero holds behind.

## Mutation testing

Two mutants survived and drove changes:

- Deleting the read-side integration entirely — another customer's hold no
  longer greying out the seat — was **green across the whole suite**. The hold
  would have decided races invisibly. Two database tests now kill it.
- Asserting the claims payload on a *single-leg* flight is equivalent to the bug:
  `flights[0].id` is the right answer by accident. Only a round trip
  distinguishes "the leg this seat belongs to" from "the first leg".

One reported count was wrong: I claimed "advancing no longer holds seats → 2
red" when the current source gives 4, because I ran it before two round-trip
tests existed. The verifier caught that the number wasn't auditable.

## Verification

794 unit, 111 database, **38/38 Playwright**, build, tsc, lint 0 errors.
Migration applied to a fresh *and* a populated database with no drift; the
`expiresAt > createdAt` check exercised in both directions including the exact
boundary, plus the unique index and the foreign key.

Filed rather than fixed: #255 (seat buttons announce as just "A", so the group
that hears the error can't locate the seat), #256 (seat map scrolls horizontally
at 390px).

Note on #252: it did not reproduce in this run — all 38 passed — so that
failure is less deterministic than reported, and the stranded holds may have
been contributing to it.

I was about to recommend "typed statuses" as the next slice under #73. That would have walked into exactly the collision this plan exists to prevent — the table above assigns **`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**, with #73 and #75 as consumers.

So the split is:

- **#73 owns** `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK. That one needs the decision below.
- **Nobody owns** `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` or `Flight.status` typing. Those are free to take now, and `cabinClass` has the evidence behind it.

Six are listed here, belonging to four different slices. Deciding all of them now means committing months ahead of the code, and this plan's own premises have already drifted in a fortnight. Only one is needed to start #73:

> must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?

The cancellation policy table and staff-cancel behaviour belong to #76, hold TTL and timing to #74, authorize-vs-capture to #75, and document attestation to #77. Each is better answered by whoever opens that slice.

Phase 3 alone is ~40 PRs. Every one pays that tax, and every red run for an unrelated reason erodes the signal that tells you a real regression happened. Worth clearing before the volume rather than during.

## Filed along the way

Not part of any phase, all found by verification rather than by looking for them: #156, #159, #162, #163, #165, #167, #171, #173, #175, #177, #178.

test(suite): keep tests to product code and the run harness (#266)

Six suites had the repository as their subject rather than the product: they
asserted on package.json, .dockerignore, the set of git-tracked files, where
test files may live, and the Jest and CI harnesses. A test like that pins a
property nobody asked the product for, and goes red on a refactor that broke
nothing.

Remove five, and write the rule down so the next one is not written:

- __tests__/docs/databaseTestHygiene.test.ts
- __tests__/security/committedSecrets.test.ts
- __tests__/security/containerSecrets.test.ts
- __tests__/security/dependencyPolicy.test.ts
- __tests__/security/scanImageLayers.test.ts

The rule is in AGENTS.md under Testing Expectations: tests are written against
code or assets that ship, or that produce what ships. Subject decides it, not
technique — a recursive scan of app/components/lib qualifies, reading
package.json does not, however it is written.

One exception, because a rule without it deletes the wrong things: the harness
deciding whether a Jest or Playwright run can be believed. e2e/global-setup.ts,
the leak snapshotter and jest.database-setup.js ship nothing, but a silent
failure in any of them invalidates every other test rather than failing
honestly — which is how three specs leaked data for months (#213), how a
parallel database run counted another file's fixtures (#155, #215), and how a
stale server made a healthy branch look broken (#196). A CI check sits outside
it: a green CI job is not a test result.

Two files move rather than go. databaseSerialisation.test.ts and
productIdentity.test.ts are restored byte-identical under __tests__/harness/
and __tests__/app/ — the first is covered by the exception, the second was
never in scope, its subject being app/globals.css, app/layout.tsx,
lib/data/FlightData.ts and the shipped assets. __tests__/docs/ is gone; it was
the wrong home for both.

Removing a guard silently is how the property gets lost, so each one is filed
before it goes: #263 for the CI gates, the layer scanner and $disconnect()
hygiene, #265 for the dependency pins and the committed-secret scan. SECURITY.md
no longer claims a recurrence control that no longer exists.

Verified: lint 0 errors/8 warnings, tsc clean, unit 720/720, database 111/111,
the parallel-run guard still aborting. Baseline on main was 773 unit tests; the
drop of 53 is the five deletions exactly, both restorations contributing zero.
