pull_requests.body:
Slice 1 of 5 for #76. The [decision record](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235526479) on the issue has the policy and the plan.

## Why this first

`Booking.status` was `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CONFIRMED'` with no enum and no check
constraint — and unlike `Flight.status`, not even a Zod schema at the boundary. The
whole definition of the domain was a string literal in `lib/seatOccupancy.ts`, whose
own comment said so. That literal is what `heldSeats()` filters on, so a status written
any other way sells a seat somebody is sitting in, or holds one nobody paid for.

#74 and #75 are both waiting on this typing, which is why it leads.

## `DISRUPTED` exists before anything writes it

The decision record settled it: a staff-cancelled flight moves its bookings to
`DISRUPTED` rather than cancelling them, so the customer keeps the choice between a
refund and a rebooking. This migration is where the domain is defined, and Postgres
will not let a value added later by `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` be used in the same
transaction that adds it — Prisma applies each migration in one, so deferring costs two
migrations rather than none.

`heldSeats()` deliberately does not treat `DISRUPTED` as released: that booking keeps
its seat until the customer chooses.

## The history writes itself

The first version had the application insert the row nested in the same statement as
the change, so the two could not come apart. **The next test fixture I wrote created a
booking without it and got a booking with no history** — which is the whole objection.
"Every status change is recorded" was true only while every caller remembered, and the
callers include a repair script and a psql session.

So a trigger is the only writer, and there is no way to change a booking's status
without a row appearing. The two things a trigger cannot know — why, and who — are read
from transaction-local settings:

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_reason', 'Flight cancelled', true);
SELECT set_config('app.booking_status_actor', '<user id>', true);
UPDATE "Booking" SET "status" = 'DISRUPTED' WHERE "id" = 1;
COMMIT;
```

Transaction-local matters: a session-scoped setting would survive the commit and
attribute the next booking on that pooled connection to whoever set it last. There is a
test for exactly that.

## Append-only, with one deliberate hole

A history that can be rewritten is not one, so the rule is a trigger rather than a
convention. One update is allowed: `actorUserId` may go from a user to null, because
that is what `ON DELETE SET NULL` does and refusing it would make **any user who ever
acted undeletable** — which the e2e harness and account deletion both need.

The carve-out compares the whole row with that one field cleared, rather than listing
the columns that must not change. A list would go stale silently the day somebody adds
a column. Its limit is documented: row equality needs an equality operator, which
`json`, `xml` and `point` lack — `jsonb` is the answer for an audit payload.

## What review caught

The `verifier` found **the documented reversal was wrong and left the database
unusable**. Run verbatim it fails at the third statement — Postgres refuses to retype a
column a trigger mentions — and with no `BEGIN`, the first two have already committed,
leaving `status` as the enum with no default. Every booking insert then violates NOT
NULL, and since the `_prisma_migrations` row is never reached, `migrate deploy` reports
nothing pending and will not heal it. The header now drops the triggers first and wraps
the whole thing in a transaction, and that form was run end-to-end: reversal → old
schema works → re-applied with the backfill.

It also found the carve-out's central claim untested — a naive `if the actor went to
null, allow it` passed the entire suite while permitting
`SET actorUserId=NULL, to='CONFIRMED', reason='tidying up'`. There is a test for that
now, and it kills the naive version. Same for the GUC channel and the no-op
suppression, neither of which had any coverage.

Two findings are [recorded on the issue](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235702982)
for later slices rather than fixed here: changes made in one transaction share a
timestamp with no tiebreaker (slices 3 and 5 will want a monotonic column), and the
backfill is only exercised by a database that predates the migration, which is not one
CI or a developer ever has.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 682 unit + 72 database, `npm run build`,
Playwright 30/30, and `prisma migrate diff` reports no drift.

The verifier additionally applied the migration to a **pre-migration database holding
bookings**, which is the only way the guard and the backfill run: the guard rejected
`'REFUNDED' (2 rows), 'pending' (1 rows)` and rolled back whole, and after fixing the
rows the backfill wrote exactly one row per booking with `from` null and the booking's
own `createdAt`.

Mutations that now die: dropping either trigger, widening the carve-out either way,
omitting `DISRUPTED`, and removing the backfill (against a populated database).

pull_requests.body:
Closes the last test-infrastructure issue before Phase 3's ~40 pull requests.

## What #213 filed, and what was actually there

The issue named one spec. Counting the database found three:

| Rows in the development database | Source |
|---|---|
| 25 users, 25 reviews, 25 favorites (`guidetest-*`) | `travelguide.spec.ts` — no cleanup at all |
| 42 users (`test-*`, `login-test-*`) | `auth.spec.ts` — no cleanup at all |
| 20 `VerificationToken` rows (`verify-email:case-*`) | `auth-abuse.spec.ts` — deletes the user and the rate limits, not the token registration issues for it |

Every run passed throughout. That is the part worth fixing: the leak was invisible, so
it grew, and #213 itself caught one of three by eye.

## The slice

Each spec now deletes what it created, which is what its neighbours already did. The
review and the favorite cascade from the account, so `travelguide` needs one delete;
the token has no foreign key to the user, so `auth-abuse` needs its own.

Then the part that keeps it true. `global-setup` snapshots the tables nothing else
clears; `global-teardown` fails the run when rows created during it survive it.

**Compared rather than matched by prefix.** `global-setup` deliberately does not delete
accounts because it cannot tell a run's account from a developer's — that is why 67 of
them were still there. Two snapshots can: whatever is absent at the start and present
at the end appeared while the run had the database to itself.

**Reported rather than deleted.** Tidying up in teardown would keep the database clean
and leave the specs wrong, and the next spec to leak would be just as invisible.

Rows are named by their owning account, because a leaked `Review` is a cuid and a cuid
says nothing:

```
Error: This run left rows behind in a database that nothing else clears:
  User (1): cmsmmld7y0000ejk1yq4kt7ed (guidetest-1786329719258@example.com)
  Review (1): cmsmmlkam000111n2uk2g0nnw (guidetest-1786329719258@example.com)
  UserFavorite (1): cmsmmlkue000311n2vo826610 (guidetest-1786329719258@example.com)
```

## Verified by reproduction

- **Red first.** With the guard in and the specs untouched, the three specs passed 6/6
  and the run failed in teardown naming 3 users, 1 token, 1 review and 1 favorite.
- **Independent of the guard.** Counted the four tables in Postgres either side of a
  run: 74/26/26/18 before, 74/26/26/18 after.
- After a full 30-test run the database sits at **seed state** — 0 users, 0 reviews,
  0 favorites, 0 tokens, 0 notifications, 1412 flights, 9 schedules.

## What review caught

The `verifier` found the guard **silently removable**: deleting `recordRunBaseline`
from `global-setup` left teardown warning and skipping, so a run leaked with every test
green and exit 0. An absent baseline is not a clean run, it is an unchecked one, and
that difference was invisible. It now fails. The wiring test also passed on a
*commented-out* call, since a text search finds the call either way — it strips comments
before matching now.

It also found `Flight` and `FlightSchedule` untracked while meeting the comment's own
criterion for inclusion. `admin.spec.ts` and `booking-authority.spec.ts` create them
and clean up today, but a leaked `E2E606` is not inert — it turns up in search results.
Both are tracked now.

Two more: a `toEqual({})` assertion that passed under any mutation making the
comparison return nothing, replaced by one that creates two accounts, deletes one, and
names the survivor; and the baseline snapshot running *before* the
`DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE` check, so a misaimed checkout listed every account before
being refused. The check goes first now.

Every mutation the verifier tried is dead: comparison always empty, missing baseline
read as clean, throw replaced by a warn, throw moved above the rate-limit cleanup, each
of the three `afterAll` blocks removed, and `Flight` dropped from the tracked set.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 681 unit + 59 database, `npm run build`,
and two full Playwright runs at 30/30.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#225** — `npm run lint` is `eslint app components lib`, so neither `e2e/**` nor
  `__tests__/**` has ever been linted. Verified: a file under `e2e/` with an unused
  variable leaves `npm run lint` at 0 errors while `npx eslint` on that same file
  reports it.

## One behaviour change worth knowing

A run that leaks now exits 1. A failing or interrupted test can trip it too, since its
`afterAll` never finished — the message says so, and so does the new `AGENTS.md`
bullet. Fix the failure rather than the report.

Removes the Codex code review portion of the workflow, as requested.

## What went

**Step 11** in full — eleven lines of protocol for a reviewer the merge no longer turns
on: which reaction means reading and which means satisfied, where the reactions live,
how to page GraphQL `reviewThreads` because the REST comments endpoint carries neither
`isResolved` nor the thread id, and how to tell a 👍 that arrived after your push from
the one that was already sitting there.

**Step 12's Codex clause** — the merge gate now reads "no review thread is left
unresolved" rather than naming an approver.

**Step 8's pointer** to step 11 as the thing that reviews every pull request.

## What replaces it

Nothing new. What was already there: the `PreToolUse` hooks in `.claude/settings.json`,
which review the diff and block on `git push` and `gh pr create`. Step 8 now says
plainly that this pass *is* the review rather than a first draft of one, since nothing
looks at the pull request afterwards.

Step 11 keeps only what is true of any reviewer — answer the findings, re-run steps 6
to 9 for what changed, and say so when a finding is right about the problem and wrong
about the fix.

## Worth knowing

`grep -ri codex` over `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/`, `.github/` and `.claude/`
returns nothing after this. The two remaining hits in the repository are unrelated to
review: `.codex/hooks.json` is the Entire CLI's hook wiring for the Codex *CLI agent*,
and `.dockerignore` plus `__tests__/security/containerSecrets.test.ts` name that
directory as one that must not reach an image layer. I left all three alone.

The bot is a GitHub App installed on the repository. This stops the workflow waiting on
it — it does not uninstall it, so it may still comment until you remove it in the
repository settings.

## Verification

`npm run test:unit` (669 passed), including `__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts`,
which is what pins CLAUDE.md to a pointer and AGENTS.md as the file agents read.
Documentation-only change: no source, test or configuration file is touched.

pull_requests.body:
#215. The database test files share one Postgres and several assert against whole
tables, so beside each other they count one another's fixtures — the interference
#155 was filed for. Splitting them into their own Jest project is what *allows*
serialisation; `--runInBand` in `npm run test:database` is what *performs* it.

That left the guarantee resting on which command someone typed, and the dangerous
one is shorter. `npx jest --selectProjects database` looks equivalent, runs the
files in parallel, and reproduces the interference exactly:

```
● the route a page renders › comes from the airports on the admin dashboard
  Expected substring: "RTE-66f9eabc"
```

It cost me an afternoon during #73, because each failure looked like a real
regression in the code under review rather than in how I had invoked the tests.

## The fix

Jest has no per-project `maxWorkers`, so this cannot be configured away. But a
project's `globalSetup` is handed the resolved global config, which is enough to
refuse:

```
Error: Jest: Got error running globalSetup … reason: The database test project must
run one file at a time, and this run has maxWorkers=23. These files share one
database and several assert against whole tables, so in parallel they count each
other's fixtures and fail on work that is not their own (#155).

Use `npm run test:database`, which passes --runInBand, or add --runInBand yourself.
```

The message carries the worker count and the remedy, because whoever hits it is
mid-run and needs to know what to type, not which issue to read.

## Every invocation, checked

| command | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `npm run test:database` | 51 passed | 51 passed |
| `npm run test:unit` | 662 passed | 662 passed |
| `npx jest --selectProjects unit` | 662 passed | 662 passed |
| `npm test` | both projects | both projects |
| `npx jest --selectProjects database` | **ran in parallel** | refused |
| `npx jest` (no flags) | ran the database project in parallel | refused |

The last row is the deliberate cost: a bare `npx jest` now stops rather than running
the unit project and quietly mis-running the database one. `npm test` is the
documented entry point and is unaffected.

## Coverage

`__tests__/docs/databaseSerialisation.test.ts` pins both halves — that the guard
refuses, and that the config still points at it and only at the database project. A
guard the config has stopped calling is worth nothing, and one wired into the unit
project would refuse every parallel run in the repository.

Mutation-tested: neutering the check, removing the `globalSetup` line, and treating
an absent `maxWorkers` as many each fail it. The "absent is not many" case matters —
defaulting the other way would refuse runs that are perfectly safe.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 662 unit + 51 database. `AGENTS.md`
now describes the guard rather than the trap.

The last of the test-infrastructure cleanup: #178 and #165. One of the three items
turned out not to reproduce, and I have left it alone rather than fixing a symptom
nobody can produce.

## #178 — the round trip's budget

One test carries a two-leg checkout, a confirmation, a profile load and a seat
change inside a fixed 30s budget, against a dev server that compiles each route the
first time it is asked for.

Measured before changing anything: **21.6s on a cold run**, so roughly 8s of
headroom — tighter than the ~12s the issue recorded, because #196 means every run
now starts its own server and is therefore cold.

`test.slow()` triples the budget. Verified rather than assumed: a 33s delay inside
the test **passes with it** (56.5s) and **fails without it**.

The issue notes that splitting the test would be better, since one case covers four
outcomes and a timeout tells you nothing about which. That is true and still worth
doing; it is a different change from giving the existing test room, and it belongs
with whoever restructures that journey.

## #165 — one half fixed, one half not reproducible

**Fixed:** `authTokens.database.test.ts` and `passengerDataProtection.database.test.ts`
never called `prisma.$disconnect()`. That mattered less when every file ran in its
own worker; the database project shares one process now, so they held connections
for the rest of the run.

Since nothing noticed for as long as it was wrong, the convention is now a test:
`__tests__/docs/databaseTestHygiene.test.ts` scans every `*.database.test.ts` and
asserts each disconnects. Mutation-tested, and guarded against a vacuous scan.

**Not reproducible:** the haste module naming collision. With
`.next/standalone/package.json` present and its `name` genuinely colliding
(`travel-app` both sides), four invocations produced zero `haste` lines — the two
npm scripts, a filtered `jest` run, and `--listTests`. The resolved config shows
`modulePathIgnorePatterns` empty and `throwOnModuleCollision: false`, so nothing is
suppressing it.

I drafted the suggested `modulePathIgnorePatterns: ['<rootDir>/.next/']` and then
removed it: it changes module resolution for everything under `.next/` in exchange
for silencing a warning that no longer appears. The repro conditions and the
one-line fix are recorded on #165 in case a Jest upgrade brings it back.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 662 unit + 51 database, and the full
Playwright suite 30/30.

#181. Choosing a new origin or destination set the departure date in one effect and
let a *second* effect derive the return from it, so a render committed in between
showing the new route's departure beside the **previous** route's return:

```
NY | London | 2026-07-15 | 2026-07-22
NY | London | 2026-07-18 | 2026-07-22   <- mismatched pair, on screen
NY | London | 2026-07-18 | 2026-07-25
```

It was found because an e2e spec reading both inputs in that gap captured the stale
value, but a customer could see it too — which is why it is fixed in the component
rather than in the test. Both dates now move together, and the rule they share lives
in one `defaultReturnDate` helper instead of three copies of the same arithmetic.

## What review changed

**`ui-review`** drove all seven paths at three viewports, capturing every rendered
frame rather than the settled state, and found no mismatched pair. It also caught
that my new code clamped against `latestBookingDateRef`, which a *later* effect
refreshes — so on a route change across timezones it used the previous origin's last
bookable date, and claiming the derive effect's guard meant nothing corrected it
afterwards. It now computes the window for the new origin directly. It also spotted
that `handleNearbyDateSearch` was a third, un-deduplicated copy of the rule the
helper exists to unify.

**The `verifier` then found the headline claim was wrong.** The component fix alone
did *not* close the e2e flake: the spec read the two inputs in two separate CDP
round trips, so the commit could land between them and compose a pair the form never
held — an 8-day gap. Reproduced **2 in 50**. The spec now reads both in one
`page.evaluate`; that was 0 in 50.

It also found three mutants alive, all now caught:

- the stale-ref clamp — reachable only when the destination is *unchanged*, so the
  route effect runs in the same flush as the origin change, which is why the first
  test could not see it
- switching to one-way no longer clearing the return
- a nearby-date search ignoring one-way — invisible in the end state, because a
  later effect corrects it, so the test inspects every commit

And that my first test could pass while the route effect did nothing at all: the
initial pair is consistent, so the invariant alone is satisfied. It now asserts the
dates actually moved.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 645 unit + 51 database, `npm run
build`, `e2e/search.spec.ts` three times, and the full Playwright suite 30/30.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#218** — a direct edit of the departure date still shows a stale return for one
  render. Same class, different path; the invariant this PR asserts is
  route-change-only rather than global.
- **#206** — updated with the measured cause: at 390px both date inputs truncate
  (`08/10/20`, `08/17/2`), so a phone user cannot read the year of either — and
  therefore cannot see the coherence this change guarantees.

A read-through of `AGENTS.md` against the repository, checking each claim rather
than reading for sense. Three things were wrong and two were imprecise.

## Wrong

**The Codex loop was in the wrong step.** It sat inside step 8, *"Review the code
before every commit"*, while its own opening line said it belonged after step 10.
An agent following the steps in order would reach a loop it could not run, because
no pull request existed yet. It is now step 11, between opening the pull request and
merging it; merge becomes 12. Numbering is contiguous and the one cross-reference
("re-run steps 6 to 9") still points at ui-review, verifier, review and commit.

**`/code-review` was described as built-in.** It ships in
`code-review@claude-plugins-official`, and this repository does not enable it — it
exists only where someone has installed it themselves. An agent told to use it may
find nothing there. The text now says so and points at step 11 as the thing that
actually reviews every pull request.

**Step 10's bullets were mis-nested.** Three spaces under a four-character marker
(`10. `) ends the ordered list rather than nesting under it. Step 11's continuation
lines already used four; step 10's bullets did not.

## Imprecise

- *"The test suites delete every booking"* — only a Playwright run and the database
  Jest project do. `npm run test:unit` does not, and does not need the marker.
- The Gotchas explained the two-project split but not that `--runInBand` in the
  `test:database` script is what serialises it. `npx jest --selectProjects database`
  looks equivalent and runs the files in parallel, reproducing exactly the
  interference the split removed. That is #215, and it cost me several confusing
  failures in one session.

## Verified rather than assumed

- `npm run lint` really is `eslint app components lib` (line 13).
- `lib/env.ts` really has eight `requireValue` calls, so "all eight required
  variables" is right.
- `playwright.config.ts` really sets `workers: 1` and `fullyParallel: false`.
- `/code-review`'s plugin and enablement state, from the plugin cache and both
  settings files.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, and the 14 documentation tests
including the `AGENTS.md` guard. Rendered UI review is not applicable: one markdown
file, no component, route or style.

pull_requests.body:
Codex reviews every pull request in this repository and nothing in the workflow
said so. An agent that opened a PR and merged it on a green check would skip a
gate that is already running — which is what would have happened on #214, where
Codex found a P1 that no other check did.

Written from driving the loop on #214 rather than from the bot's own
description. That description is incomplete in the way that matters most: it
says reviews are triggered by opening a pull request, marking a draft ready, or
commenting `@codex review`, and does not mention that **every push
re-triggers it** — which is what makes the loop a loop.

## What it records

- **Reactions are on the pull request**, not on a comment: 👀 while reading,
  removed and replaced with 👍 when clean.
- **Findings are inline review threads**, invisible to
  `gh pr view --json comments`. They need `pulls/<pr>/comments`, or GraphQL
  `reviewThreads` for the IDs to resolve them.
- **Reply before resolving, and say what you actually did.** A resolved thread
  with no reply cannot be told from one dismissed unread.
- **Do not confuse your own replies with a new review.** Replying creates
  review objects under your name, so "the review count went up" fires on your
  own replies. Only a review by the bot on the current head SHA is a verdict.
  I got this wrong on the first attempt.

Step 11 now makes 👍 with no unresolved threads a merge condition alongside the
checks.

## Why "worth arguing with" is in there

Three rounds on #214, each rejecting the previous fix for a concrete reason,
each correct:

1. `booking.deleteMany()` was unguarded — a misaimed `DATABASE_URL` wipes every
   booking.
2. A hostname allowlist still passed `postgresql://…@localhost:5432/production`.
3. Host **and** name still passed, because `db/travel_app` is exactly what
   `docker-compose.yml` gives the *application* — no address can separate a
   developer's database from a deployment.

That ended at an environment marker, which is a different design from where it
started. Recording it so the next agent treats a P1 as an argument to engage
with rather than a box to tick.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, and the 14 documentation tests
including the `AGENTS.md` guard. Rendered UI review is not applicable: one
markdown file, no component, route or style.

This PR is also the first test of the workflow it documents.

pull_requests.body:
First of three slices clearing the test-infrastructure tax before Phase 3's ~40 PRs.
Four issues, all of them ways a run could lie about the code under test.

## What each one was

**#196 — a reused dev server.** `reuseExistingServer` borrowed whatever was on the
port. That made a healthy branch fail three runs of three, and the bisect that
followed was worthless: with `webServer: npm run dev`, rebuilding between steps
changes nothing, so every "fix" was really just a server restart. The mirror case is
worse — a stale server can report a pass for code that is not under test. Playwright
now starts its own.

**#173 — seat 11A, held forever.** The suite booked it and nothing released it, so
the seat map rendered it taken and three specs failed on that database from the
first run onwards. CI never saw it because CI seeds a fresh database each time.
Global setup now clears what a previous run booked.

**#182 — navigating before the write landed.** `selectOption` returns on the change
event, not on the server action committing, and `/flights` is `force-dynamic`. The
spec now waits for the change to settle on the page that made it.

**#195 — an aborted poll reported as a failure.** The notification bell polls every
3s; a navigation tears that down. It was the only console error the suite ever
produced.

## Verified by reproduction, not by reading

- Planted the exact leftover #173 describes — 11A held on a seeded flight by a stale
  booking — and the three named specs **failed without the cleanup and passed with
  it**.
- #182 failed 3/3 before the wait and passed 3/3 after. I checked it against
  unmodified `main` first, because I had changed how the server starts and needed to
  rule myself out: it fails there too.
- Two consecutive full green runs, 30/30 each.

## What review caught

`ui-review` found a real defect in my #195 fix. The original matched by regex, and
`/aborted/i` as a substring silenced PostgreSQL's *"current transaction is aborted,
commands ignored until end of transaction block"* and Prisma's *"Transaction
aborted."* — in development Next forwards a server error's message to the client
verbatim, so exactly the failures a developer most needs arrive at that `catch` as
written. It now matches whole messages against a closed set of what browsers
actually say. Whole-message equality is what makes it safe.

The `verifier` then found the new test **green against code that does not do the
job**: it inlined `booking.deleteMany()` rather than calling the function, so
deleting the call from `global-setup.ts` left it passing. Its "seeded inventory
survives" assertions were vacuous too — `flight.count() > 0` is guaranteed by the
fixture the test creates itself. It now imports the real function, counts before and
after, and asserts to the row. Both mutants die.

It also caught that the config assertion pinned source text, so reintroducing reuse
*conditionally* slipped past. It reads the loaded config now.

I removed one of my own tests outright: it asserted a property of whatever the
database happened to hold, and failed when a Playwright run was in progress — a
flake, in a PR about removing flakes.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 643 unit + 51 database, `npm run
build`, and Playwright 30/30 twice.

## One behaviour change worth knowing

A dev server already on port 3000 now **stops** the suite instead of being borrowed:

```
Error: http://localhost:3000 is already used, make sure that nothing is running
on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.
```

It exits in ~2.9s rather than hanging. `AGENTS.md` is updated, since it still said
Playwright auto-starts the server. Note the message advises the setting the config
now forbids — the reason is in the comment beside it.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#212** — the #195 fix means a *dead* dev server now fails silently too. The
  message cannot carry the signal; an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup can.
  Recorded rather than widened into this slice.
- **#213** — `travelguide.spec.ts` leaks a user, review and favorite per run; 37
  accounts had accumulated. Same class as #173, not covered by it.
- **#208, #209, #210, #211** — pre-existing notification-bell findings from
  `ui-review`: the drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone, the empty state
  claims "You're all caught up!" when loading failed, the unread count is invisible
  to assistive tech, and `next-auth`'s own session poll still logs on hard
  navigation.

## Still to come

#181 (search e2e reads a stale return date) and #178 (round-trip e2e headroom) are
the next slice; #165 is housekeeping after that.

The last of the route work #73 owns, after the references landed (#189), the reads
moved onto them (#197) and the columns went (#203). The search URL was the one
place left naming a place in prose: `?from=Seattle%2C+USA`.

A label is editable text; a code is what a link should outlive. Only the URL
changes — the form, the dropdowns and the results still work in words, and the
translation happens at the boundary. `buildFlightSearchUrl` writes codes,
`parseFlightSearchParams` reads them back as labels.

**No compatibility shim**, per the call that nothing has launched. An old-format
link is refused rather than accepted, so two spellings of the same link cannot both
survive.

## Refusing quietly was the harder half

`ui-review` blocked on this, and it was right: a rejected link fell back to the
default search in complete silence. The address bar said Seattle → Detroit, one-way,
20 Aug; the page showed Chicago → Paris, round trip, 10 Aug, with nothing to
distinguish it from a first visit. The no-shim decision *creates* that population —
old links are the expected path, not an edge case.

So the page now says the link was not used. Three things fell out of that, each
found by review rather than by me:

- **The notice never cleared.** Reading it straight from the prop meant it survived
  the traveller's own successful search, because the search rewrites the URL with
  `replaceState` and never re-renders the server component — a red banner sitting
  above results that contradict it, the mirror image of the bug being fixed.
- **A refused link still moved the booking window.** The origin is resolved before
  parsing, because the window is what parsing validates dates against; when parsing
  then refused the link, the selectable dates stayed in Tokyo while the form showed
  Chicago. It now comes back to the origin actually on screen.
- **Links refused for their date or cabin fell back silently**, because the check
  gated on `from`/`to` alone.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 634 unit + 49 database, `npm run
build`, Playwright 30/30. No new `act()` warnings — the two that appear are
pre-existing, in `TravelGuideClient` and `ProfileClient`.

`ui-review` drove all seven journeys at three viewports, including browser
back/forward across several searches and reload mid-search. It confirmed the
booking-window timezone resolves identically from a code as it did from a label for
all ten origins — measured at 23:56 UTC, when zones straddle the date boundary and
the check is at its most discriminating.

The `verifier` then found **four mutations that survived the whole suite**: the
`?? ''` fallback reinstating the label format, `airportLabelFor` becoming tolerant
of case and whitespace (a shim by the back door), and two ways the refusal notice
could be wrong. The root cause was that `app/page.tsx` had no test, so the predicate
is now an exported function with direct coverage. All four are caught.

It also caught two decayed assertions in my own new e2e: one comparing against
`encodeURIComponent`, which writes `%20` where a query string writes `+`, so it
could never match; and a hard-coded date that would have started passing for the
wrong reason in twelve days.

## Filed rather than fixed

#204 (no visible focus indicator on the search selects), #205 (shared-link arrival
drops focus past the whole form), #206 (return date clipped to `08/17/202`). All
pre-existing, all made more visible by this change, none caused by it.

## Why this does not close #73

It finishes the `Flight.from`/`to` work. The issue's typed-statuses task remains:
`Booking.currency` and `Notification.type` are still bare strings, and
`Booking.status` belongs to #76 per the ownership table in #143.

pull_requests.body:
The last structural piece of #73's route work, after #189 added the references and
#197 moved every read onto them. `Flight.from` and `Flight.to` have been write-only
since, and this removes them along with the four writers that filled them.

They were free text that was simultaneously the identity of a place and the words
shown to a customer, so editing the prose silently repointed a route and nothing
stopped a flight naming somewhere no airport exists.

## The migration

`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, a guard, then two `DROP COLUMN`s.

Dropping a column is the one change no later migration can undo from the data, so
the guard refuses to run while either column still says something the airports do
not. A disagreement means a label was edited after the flight was written, and an
operator has to decide which of the two is right — silently keeping the airport's
answer would discard the other one unrecorded.

Verified on scratch databases, by me and independently by the `verifier`:

- Two disagreeing rows and one agreeing: fails naming both bad ones and not the
  good one, columns survive, migration recorded failed, second deploy gives `P3009`
- `migrate resolve --rolled-back` → correct the rows → redeploy succeeds
- The reversal in the header reconstructs the labels exactly — 0 mismatches over 40
  rows
- From empty: `migrate deploy` + `db seed` gives 1412 flights, no orphan references,
  and `migrate diff` reports no difference
- Lock timeout applies: with a lock held from another session it aborts with `55P03`
  after ~3s and both columns survive, which also proves the file is one transaction
  and `SET LOCAL` is therefore not a silent no-op

The verifier found the guard's inner join let a flight referencing a **deleted**
airport slip past unchecked — and that row is precisely the one the reversal cannot
reconstruct, so it would fail on a `NOT NULL` it cannot satisfy. Reaching that state
needs `session_replication_role = replica`, since both FKs are validated and
`RESTRICT`, but the cost of being wrong is an unrecoverable reversal. It is a
`LEFT JOIN` with `IS DISTINCT FROM` now, and the message states the true total
rather than silently capping at 20.

## Removing the columns removed a cross-check

The whole-table invariant asserting the columns agreed with the airports is gone,
because the disagreement is now unstateable. That invariant was also what caught a
writer resolving a route to the *wrong* airports — and the verifier proved the gap
was real: reversing `airportCodesForRoute(from, to)` in `prisma/seed.ts` seeded 1412
flights onto backwards routes with all 608 unit and 48 database tests green.

The other three writers each fail a unit assertion on their create payload; the seed
was the only one without. It has one now, against the routes `FlightData` itself
names, covering 786 rows across both writers. Mutation-tested: the swap fails it.

## The two suites from #197 were rebuilt

Both were designed around a fixture whose columns contradicted its airports — the
only way to ask *which of two sources* a read used. That question is unaskable now,
so they assert the resolution itself: a page that forgets the relation gets
`undefined`, one that maps it wrongly gets the route backwards.

The fixture is Rio → Miami, because the seed flies Miami → Rio and not the reverse,
so no other row can satisfy the assertions on its behalf. The verifier confirmed
that against the seeded data (`GIG->MIA = 0`, `MIA->GIG = 157`) and re-ran the
mutation set: all 18 mutants killed, none that previously died now survives.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 49 database, `npm run
build`, Playwright 28/28 on a single cold run with no retries.

`ui-review` drove all eight journeys at three viewports, including creating a
schedule through the admin form — the path that writes new flights — and confirmed
the 30 generated occurrences render correctly, the unknown-place rejection is still
field-level and reports both fields at once, and no route renders `undefined`,
blank, or differently spaced.

## Filed rather than fixed

#198, #199, #200, #202, plus a comment on #193. And **#201**, which is not a
finding so much as a contradiction worth recording: `ui-review` measured focus
dropping to `<body>` after the schedule form rejects an unknown place, while the
jsdom test asserting that exact behaviour passes. Both can be true if a re-render
races the `requestAnimationFrame`. It needs a browser assertion to settle, and if
the browser is right then a test I added in #189 is asserting something
jsdom-specific.

## What remains of #73

The search URL still carries labels rather than IATA codes. That is the last piece,
it is independently shippable, and it needs no compatibility shim because the
product has not launched — so this PR does not close the issue.

pull_requests.body:
Step two of #73's route work, after #189 added the references. Every read of where
a flight goes now comes from the `Airport` rows it points at. The columns still
exist and hold the same words, so **this is intended to be invisible** — which is
the point: it is what makes dropping them a migration rather than a rewrite.

## What moved

`lib/flightRoute.ts` holds all of it, so no component learned about airports:

- `flightRouteInclude` — the relation a route-rendering query asks for. Spreads
  into a `select` as readily as an `include`.
- `withRouteLabels(flight)` / `withLegRouteLabels(leg)` — swap the columns for the
  airport labels, so every view keeps receiving a flight with `from` and `to`.
- `flightRouteWhere(from, to)` — narrows a query by the airports, not the prose.

Read sites migrated: search (both directions and the dateless branch), the
`/flights` status board, checkout, `/profile` history and points activity,
`/admin`, `/admin/flights`, and both notification paths.

## The filter mattered as much as the render

`where: { from, to }` made a search depend on two rows spelling a place
identically, and kept the columns load-bearing regardless of what was displayed.
Those now filter on `fromAirportCode`/`toAirportCode`.

`flightRouteWhere` returns `null` when no airport answers to a name and the caller
returns empty without querying — the same result the label match gave. `?from=` is
user-controlled, so an unknown place is reachable.

`FlightSchedule.from`/`to` are untouched: that model has no references, and giving
it them is separate work.

## Verification, and what it caught

Two database suites write a flight whose columns say `'Nowhere, Atlantis'` while
its references say Seattle→Detroit — the only way to tell which source a page read,
since on every real row the two agree. Each of the seven converted paths was
mutation-tested by reverting it.

Three `verifier` rounds ran, and the first two found real holes rather than
confirming the work:

- **Five of the seven paths were covered by nothing.** They reverted cleanly with
  the entire suite green. That is the whole value of this change, so the page-level
  suite exists to close it.
- **My first version of that suite was vacuous for three of four cases** — the
  fixture departed outside the window `/admin/flights` renders, so assertions were
  passing on other seeded flights that happen to name Seattle. Fixed, with a
  flight-number assertion in every case as the non-vacuity guard (#155 again).
- **Asserting the route as text was still too weak.** A seeded reversed flight
  satisfies it on the fixture's behalf, and `/admin/flights` ships `FlightSchedule`
  prose carrying the same keys — that case was outright vacuous. The suite now
  finds the fixture's own flight object by flight number and reads the route off
  it.
- **The element walk was blind to host-element props**, so a column leaking through
  `title` or `aria-label` would have passed. It walks them now.
- Two further mutants survived and are now caught: dropping the `include` from the
  dateless search (a `TypeError` on every dateless search, reachable from the
  form), and re-attaching the relation objects to `updateFlightStatusAction`'s
  return value.

Final: `npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, 608 unit + 48 database,
`npm run build`, and Playwright 28/28.

`ui-review` stood up a second server on the pre-change tree and diffed both:
text byte-identical across seven journeys at three viewports, 47 of 51 screenshot
pairs identical at 0.000% (the four are focus/hover timing).

One thing worth knowing: `admin.spec.ts` failed 3 runs of 3 and passed on `HEAD`,
which looked exactly like a regression. It was a stale dev server being reused —
filed as #196, because it can equally make a broken branch look healthy.

## Filed rather than fixed

#191 (the label→code and code→label mappings read different sources — the one
finding inside this slice's scope, and noted in `flightRouteWhere`), #192, #193,
#194, #195, #196, plus a note on #173.

## What remains of #73

Step three drops the columns. The search URL still carries labels; moving it to
IATA codes belongs there, and needs no compatibility shim because the product has
not launched.

pull_requests.body:
`npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` started failing **every** branch, including ones with no dependency changes. A new advisory landed for `nanoid <3.3.17` — [GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8), a custom generator looping indefinitely when asked for zero bytes.

It reaches this project transitively:

```
next@16.2.12 -> postcss@8.5.23 -> nanoid@3.3.16
```

Nothing here calls it, and no application code changes.

Fixed with an `overrides` entry rather than a direct dependency, which is how `postcss` and the other transitive pins in that block are already held. Resolves to `nanoid@3.3.18`; `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` reports **0 vulnerabilities**.

Split out from #189 deliberately — it is unrelated to that change and unblocks every branch, not just that one.

## Verification

`npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (597 unit + 33 database), `npm run build`. Rendered UI review is not applicable: no application code is touched.

Note for anyone reproducing locally — the database tests fail if your dev database still carries a migration from another branch. Resetting to this branch's migrations clears it; that is a branch/database mismatch rather than a defect.

pull_requests.body:
The last piece of #73 that #143's ownership table assigns to it. `Flight.from` and
`Flight.to` are free text that is simultaneously the identity of a place and the
words rendered to a customer — so editing the prose silently repointed a route, and
nothing stopped a flight naming somewhere no airport exists.

**Step one of two.** The references are here and filled; every read path still
renders `from`/`to`. Dropping the labels and moving the reads is step two. Splitting
it keeps each change reviewable and each rollback a single statement, which is the
shape #135 and #137 used.

Since the product has not launched there are **no shared search URLs to preserve**,
so the compatibility shim I had recommended is deliberately absent and the search URL
keeps using labels until step two.

## The migration

`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, add nullable, two backfill `UPDATE`s joining on
`Airport.label`, a guard naming unmatched places with flight counts, then NOT NULL,
two foreign keys (`ON DELETE RESTRICT`) and two indexes.

The verifier threw twelve adversarial rows at it — leading and trailing whitespace,
both case variants, a bare city, an IATA code in the label column, an empty string,
an unknown destination — and every one was named with counts:

```
ERROR: No airport matches these places named by flights: ' Seattle, USA' (1 flights),
'' (1 flights), 'Atlantis, Nowhere' (2 flights), 'JFK' (1 flights), 'SEA' (2 flights),
'SEATTLE, USA' (1 flights), 'Seattle' (1 flights), 'Seattle, USA ' (1 flights),
'Toronto, Canada' (1 flights), 'seattle, usa' (1 flights)
```

Duplicate labels are unreachable — `Airport_label_key` is unique, so the backfill
cannot match two rows and pick arbitrarily. Failure leaves no columns behind, and
recovery via `migrate resolve --rolled-back` then retry backfills correctly. It also
aborted in ~3s when a lock was held from another session, which proves both the
transaction and `SET LOCAL`.

## A required key means every writer learns about airports

All four resolve through one function that refuses an unknown place rather than
guessing one. **Three fixtures turned out to be using IATA codes (`'SEA'`, `'JFK'`)
or bare city names (`'New York'`) where a label belonged** — the resolver caught
them, which is the point.

## The regression this introduced, and how it is fixed

`ui-review` and the verifier both landed on this. `saveFlightScheduleAction` resolved
the codes *inside the occurrence loop*, which runs **after** the schedule is written.
A typo therefore left the write standing and threw — and Next masks server-action
messages in production, so an administrator saw a generic failure for a save that had
succeeded. `flightScheduleForm.tsx` renders origin as free text with a placeholder
naming a *different* city, so `New York` is a plausible thing to type.

Now it resolves before the write and returns a validation failure, the way every
other fixable input in that action does. Three further things `ui-review` measured:

- **The `fields` payload was dead data.** The form kept only the summary message, so
  nothing reached the input — `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid` were both null. I
  had claimed it was field-level; it was not. It is now, following the pattern
  `flightBookingForm.tsx` already uses.
- **The message rendered off-screen.** On phone the alert sat 232px above the
  viewport, so a rejected save looked like nothing happened. Focus now moves to the
  first field that needs changing, which fixes that and the next one together.
- **Focus was dropped to `<body>`** and Tab walked forward out of the form entirely.

Both ends are now reported at once — the short-circuit meant an unknown origin *and*
destination cost two round trips, with the second field left looking valid meanwhile.
That needed a multi-field `actionValidationFailures` helper, since the existing one
takes a single field.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (607 unit + 38 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + `db seed` on a fresh database, and the full Playwright
suite — 28/28 first try, no retries, so none of #173/#178/#181/#182 reproduced.

The verifier confirmed: no fifth writer (`scripts/generate-inventory.ts` routes
through the service already changed, and nothing anywhere updates `from`/`to` after
creation, so labels cannot drift from codes); `ON DELETE RESTRICT` refuses removing
a referenced airport and `ON UPDATE CASCADE` is inert; the whole-table
label-equals-code assertion catches one wrong row in 1400; and no assertion was
weakened by the fixture edits — including one regex edit that hit a *search*
assertion, which I reverted.

New tests are mutation-tested: the schedule guard fails against the pre-fix code, and
the form tests fail without the `fields` wiring.

## Known limits, recorded rather than papered over

The whole-table equality assertion is stronger than any constraint and covers data it
does not own: renaming a city in `AirportData` and re-seeding updates `Airport.label`
while existing `Flight.from` keeps the old prose, and the test then fails on hundreds
of rows though nothing is broken. `ON UPDATE CASCADE` gives the mirror case. Both are
inert today and both disappear in step two.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#188** — admin types origins and destinations as free text over a ten-value
  domain, while the customer-facing form already uses a `<select>` over the same
  domain. A select makes this class of rejection unreachable. Includes the related
  finding that the form's "Edit" branch has no route into it.

pull_requests.body:
Part of #73, and the same treatment #184 gave `SeatAssignment.cabinClass`.
`Flight.status` was `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ON_TIME'` with no enum and no check
constraint, so the three-status rule existed only in `flightStatusSchema` at the
request boundary.

A status written any other way would be filtered on by search, counted by the admin
board, and rendered to a customer checking whether their flight is running — where
the board's label lookup falls through to printing the raw value.

The three names are the ones already in use, so no row changes meaning.

## The difference from #184: this column has a default

Postgres will not retype a column whose default it cannot cast, so the migration is
**DROP DEFAULT → ALTER TYPE → SET DEFAULT**. Losing the last statement would leave
every flight created without an explicit status violating NOT NULL.

The verifier proved the whole file is one transaction by appending `SELECT 1/0;`
after the final statement: the column reverted to `text` with its original default
and no `FlightStatus` survived in `pg_type`. So a mid-file failure cannot leave the
column defaultless.

## `SET LOCAL`, not `SET`

A bare `SET lock_timeout` is session-scoped and commits with the migration, and
Prisma applies every migration in a deploy over one connection — so it silently
imposes itself on every migration written afterwards, which then fails for a reason
nothing in its own file explains. The verifier demonstrated this with a probe
migration that observed `lock_timeout = 3s` it never set.

`SET LOCAL` is safe here precisely because the file is one transaction. **#184
already shipped the leaking form**, and that migration cannot simply be edited —
Prisma checksums applied migrations — so that is **#185**.

## Verified against data, both directions

Independently by me and by the verifier, on separate scratch databases:

- `'DIVERTED'` ×2 and `'diverted'` ×1 present → migration fails naming both values
  with counts, `pg_type` has no orphan `FlightStatus`, column still `text`
- `migrate resolve --rolled-back` → fix the rows → `migrate deploy` applies, existing
  values preserved exactly
- default recast to `'ON_TIME'::"FlightStatus"`, and a **raw** insert omitting
  `status` gets `ON_TIME`
- lock timeout exercised: with an `ACCESS SHARE` lock held from another session the
  migration aborted after ~3s and rolled back cleanly

`prisma migrate diff` reports no difference between the migration chain and the
schema.

## The test that existed to protect the default did not protect it

The verifier deleted the third statement and my test still passed. Prisma
materialises `@default(ON_TIME)` client-side, so `flight.create()` sends the value
explicitly and never touches the column default — the assertion was testing
`schema.prisma`, not the migration.

It now asserts `information_schema.columns.column_default` directly **and** inserts
via raw SQL with the column omitted. Mutation-tested: dropping the default fails it,
restoring it passes.

## Also found

`satisfies Prisma.FlightCreateInput[]` on the seed fixtures is load-bearing, not
decoration — `prisma/seed.ts` passes them straight to `flight.create`, and without it
the literals widen to `string`, so a bad status would only fail when Postgres
rejected the insert. It also caught my own mistake: I put it on the wrong array first
(the file exports two), which type-checked `FlightScheduleData` against
`FlightCreateInput` and produced spurious errors. It is on `FlightData`;
`FlightScheduleData` is unconstrained.

The verifier confirmed nothing bypasses the boundary: every write is a Prisma call
with a literal, no raw SQL touches the column, reads are equality-only, and there is
**no `orderBy: { status }`** anywhere — which matters, because an enum sorts by
declaration order rather than alphabetically and that would have been a silent
behaviour change.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (597 unit + 33 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + `db seed` on a fresh database, and the full Playwright
suite — **28/28 first run, no retries**, including `admin.spec.ts:74` and
`search.spec.ts:30`, so none of #173/#178/#181/#182 reproduced.

Rendered UI review is not applicable: the three values and their labels are
unchanged, no prop type or rendering path changed, and the admin spec that flips a
live status and re-reads the board passes.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#185** — the leaking `SET lock_timeout` in #184's already-applied migration, with
  the checksum constraint that stops it being edited in place
- **#186** — three more hand-maintained copies of the statuses (an action parameter
  type, the admin selector's cast and options, the board's options), plus the render
  props still typed `string`. That last part is what keeps `getStatusLabel`'s
  `default` branch from being provably dead; typing the props is the fix, and
  deleting the branch while the prop is `string` would trade an ugly label for a
  crash.

pull_requests.body:
Part of #73. `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` was `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no enum and no
check constraint**, so the four-cabin rule existed only in the Zod schema at the
request boundary. That was established during #169 verification, not assumed.

Anything reaching the table another way — a repair script, the seed, a service added
later — could write nonsense, and the fare calculation, the seat map and the boarding
pass would each read it back and believe it.

The four names are the ones already in use, so no row changes meaning. This is a
constraint arriving late.

## Scope: deliberately not `Booking.status`

#73's remaining task names seven typed statuses, but #143's ownership table assigns
**`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**. Taking it here is precisely the
collision that plan exists to prevent. This takes the piece nobody owns and that has
evidence behind it.

## The migration

Hand-authored, per AGENTS.md. Three parts worth explaining:

**It says what is wrong before the cast does.** The bare `ALTER ... USING` reports
`invalid input value for enum "CabinClass": "STEERAGE"` — one value, chosen by scan
order, naming neither the table nor the column. The guard reports every offending
value with counts:

```
SeatAssignment.cabinClass holds values outside the four cabins:
'Premium Economy' (1 rows), 'STEERAGE' (2 rows), 'economy' (1 rows).
```

**It sets `lock_timeout`.** The verifier measured the rewrite at ~9.5s per million
rows and, more importantly, reproduced the lock queue: one open reader made the ALTER
wait 13s, and an ordinary `SELECT` arriving behind it blocked past its own timeout.
`docker-compose.yml` starts the one-shot `migrate` service *before* recreating `app`,
so on a redeploy the previous container is still serving seat maps from this table
while this runs. Failing fast and retryably beats freezing the table behind a lock
nobody chose to take.

**It documents its own reversal.** There are no down migrations in this repo, which
is consistent across all 28 — so the reversal is written into the header, along with
the fact that it needs no code/schema sequencing (the application only ever writes
the four names, so old code is fine against the enum and new code is fine against
TEXT).

## Verified against data, not just an empty database

Both directions, independently by me and by the verifier on separate scratch
databases:

- pre-change schema with `'STEERAGE'`, `'economy'` and `'Premium Economy'` rows →
  migration fails with the message above, and the failure **rolls back whole**: no
  orphan `CabinClass` type in `pg_type`, data untouched, retry clean
- clean data → applies, `udt_name` becomes `CabinClass`, existing rows preserved

`prisma migrate diff --from-migrations → --to-schema-datamodel --exit-code` reports
**no difference**, so the hand-authored SQL and `schema.prisma` agree exactly.

## What the verifier caught in my work

- **The enum stole the model's documentation.** I inserted it between
  `SeatAssignment`'s `///` block and the model with no blank line, so Prisma
  attributed the whole block to the enum and left the model — the one carrying the
  seat-uniqueness invariant — undocumented. Confirmed against the generated DMMF, not
  by eye. Moved.
- **One of my new assertions could not fail.** `cabinLabel` falls back to title-casing
  the enum, so "has a name, with no underscore" is satisfied by *any* enum-shaped
  input — deleting `FIRST: 'First Class'` would have printed "First" on the boarding
  pass and kept the test green. It now asserts the four words.
- **A bare `rejects.toThrow()`** would have gone green if a future constraint rejected
  that insert for an unrelated reason. Pinned to `/invalid input value for enum/`.
- **The database's own labels were unasserted** — the drift guard reads the generated
  client, i.e. `schema.prisma`. A second test reads `pg_enum` directly.
- **A cast in `FlightBookingService`** looked redundant and I removed it. The
  pre-push review pushed back, and although its premise was wrong — `tsc` exits 0
  because the binding there is the Zod-parsed request, not the DTO — its *suggestion*
  found something real: `PassengerInput.cabinClass` still declares `string`, as does a
  hand-written local type shadowing what Prisma now generates. Narrowing them produces
  15 errors across 4 files, almost all fixtures widening a literal. That is a type
  refactor across the test and e2e suites, so the cast is restored with a pointer and
  the work is **#183**. Folding it in would have made a schema change hard to review.

## Recovery, which #73 asks for

A failed migration leaves Prisma refusing everything else with `P3009` rather than
the original error, and needs `prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back` before
retrying. That was undocumented, and this is the **second** migration here using a
`RAISE EXCEPTION` guard, so it is a recurring path rather than a one-off. It is now
in AGENTS.md's Gotchas along with the no-down-migrations convention.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (594 unit + 29 database), `npm run
build`, `migrate deploy` + seed on a fresh database, and Playwright.

The verifier confirmed no other read or write of the column behaves differently:
three write sites, all through schemas that narrow to the four; no raw-SQL write
outside the tests; no `orderBy`/`contains`/`startsWith` on the column, so the change
in sort semantics (alphabetical → declaration order) is unobservable today. Worth
knowing before someone adds a sort.

## Filed rather than fixed

Two pre-existing e2e flakes, each diagnosed to a mechanism and neither being #173 or
#178:

- **#181** — `search.spec.ts:30` reads the return date between two effects and
  captures a value derived from the previous route. The arithmetic confirms it:
  `2026-08-17 = 2026-08-10 + 7`, the route that was selected before.
- **#182** — `admin.spec.ts:74` navigates before the status change settles. The write
  lands correctly; the board just renders first.

pull_requests.body:
#143 named this as the prerequisite before the Phase 2 chain:

> Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines
> in four files into one function.

Four queries each wrote out *a seat is held unless its booking was cancelled* —
booking a flight, reading a seat map, changing a seat, and editing a cabin layout.
Inventory holds (#74), payments (#75) and cancellation rules (#76) all rewrite those
same call sites, so each would have had to find all four and change them identically.

Nothing here needs a decision from anyone, which is why it goes first.

## A function, not an object to spread

I wrote it as an object first. The verifier found the hole: a caller's own `leg` key
written **before** the spread is a TypeScript error, but the same key written
**after** it compiles cleanly and removes the booking join from the generated SQL
entirely — no cancelled bookings filtered, and no inlined text for the grep guard to
find. Confirmed against real SQL:

```
WHERE ("j1"."bookingId" = $1 AND ("j1"."id" IS NOT NULL))
```

`heldSeats(scope)` applies the rule last, so it cannot be lost by accident — only by
editing this file. That is the whole point of the refactor, since three later issues
will be editing these call sites.

## The boundary

`searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled **flights** out of search results. It reads
almost identically and answers a different question — a cancelled flight is not a
released seat — so it is deliberately not folded in. My first pass at counting the
sites said five; it is four, and this is the one that isn't.

The verifier independently confirmed no fifth occupancy site, and that three other
`seatAssignment` reads are *deliberately* unfiltered: the admin manifest renders
cancelled bookings on purpose and labels their seats "Released", the profile shows a
customer their own cancelled bookings, and `FlightBookingService` has an
idempotency-replay read. Filtering any of them would be a regression.

## The site where it has teeth, which had no test

Everywhere else, dropping the predicate is invisible: a cancellation renames the seat
to a `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` placeholder that can never match a real seat id, so
seat-number comparisons are unaffected either way.

`FlightSeatLayoutService` is different — it feeds the stored seat number into
`assertSeatAvailableForCabin`, interpreting it rather than matching it. Without the
rule the placeholder reads back as an occupied seat and **every later layout change
on that flight is refused forever**. That case had no coverage, and
`seatLayoutGuard.database.test.ts` passed with the predicate neutered.

It now has a test that builds exactly the state `cancelBookingAction` leaves behind —
booking cancelled *and* seat renamed. Mutation-tested: neuter the predicate and it
fails with `Occupied seat CANCELLED-… is not available for ECONOMY in the requested
layout.`

That also corrected a sentence in my module doc. The rename is what frees the seat
for anything comparing seat numbers; the predicate's job is narrower — stopping the
placeholder row being *read back* as occupied.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (590 unit + 26 database), `npm run
build`, and the full Playwright suite (28/28, clean database, first run).

The verifier compared **generated SQL for all four sites**, inline versus extracted,
in one process against the same fixture: byte-identical query text, parameters and
rows. Including the two awkward ones — the nested `include` filter on the layout
edit, and the seat change where the rule sits beside a sibling `NOT: { leg: {
bookingId } }`. Those compose into separate joins (`j1`/`j2` for the rule, `j3` for
the exclusion) and still exclude only the caller's own booking.

It also proved the shared module-level object is never mutated, by wrapping it in a
recursive `Proxy` trapping writes and firing all four shapes concurrently. Worth
having checked: the spread is shallow, so every call site shares the same nested
`leg` object.

## Guard

`__tests__/lib/seatOccupancy.test.ts` fails if the rule is written out again, naming
the file and what to call instead. It is textual, with the limits that implies in
both directions — an equivalent re-inlining spelled `NOT: { status: … }` slips past,
and a future query legitimately filtering bookings by status would trip it. It
catches the copy-paste that actually happens; it is not a proof, and the test says so.

Rendered UI review is not applicable: no rendered output is touched, and the SQL
comparison above establishes the queries are unchanged.

pull_requests.body:
The boarding pass printed the raw cabin enum, so a customer's e-ticket read
`PREMIUM_ECONOMY` — underscore and capitals — on the artefact people keep and show
at a gate.

It was in **eight** places, not one:

- the seat step's `aria-label` and its visible "Class: X | Seat: Y"
- the review step's fare breakdown and its single-traveller line
- the boarding pass badge
- the staff passenger manifest
- the profile's seat-change modal, reading the cabin off the `SeatAssignment`
- the search picker — which was worse than raw

## The search picker was selling a different cabin by name

`flightBookingForm.tsx` kept its own map with `FIRST: 'First'`, while checkout, the
review and the ticket all said **First Class**. A customer picked one cabin by name
and was sold another. It now names cabins from the same helper, iterating
`SEARCH_CABINS` rather than four hardcoded `<option>`s.

## One helper

`cabinLabel()` lives in `lib/bookingItinerary.ts` beside `seatLabel` and
`legDirectionLabel`, since all three answer the same question: how a piece of an
itinerary reads to a customer. An unrecognised value is prettified rather than
passed through, so a cabin added to the schema before the map catches up still
cannot reach a ticket in snake case.

The picker keeps its surcharge, but derives it from `CABIN_FARE_PERCENT` instead of
writing it down — an option can no longer promise +50% while the fare charges
something else. Verified byte-identical to the strings it replaced, so that half is
a safety change with no visible effect.

## What the reviews caught

**I claimed a complete set twice and was wrong twice.** `ui-review` found the search
picker's competing map; the verifier then found that I had deleted the map feeding
the *unavailable note* but not the `<option>` elements the customer actually picks
from — so the disagreement had merely moved inside one component. It also found the
profile's seat modal, which reads the cabin off a `SeatAssignment` rather than a
`Passenger` and so escaped every grep I ran.

Both now have component tests. I also deleted a test of mine that the verifier showed
passes against the old code: it asserted a property of the helper, not of the search
form, while its comment claimed to cover the "First" vs "First Class" bug. A test
that cannot fail for the reason it names is worse than no test.

**The badge wrap was a real regression.** `ui-review` measured that "Premium
Economy" splits to two lines inside its pill at 390px — the enum was one unbreakable
token and never did. The badge is `nowrap` now; the carrier name takes the two lines
instead, which is a lockup rather than a broken word. Measured: badge 141px → 119px,
banner 67px → 63.4px.

**The `aria-label` I added was inert.** ARIA ignores `aria-label` on a bare `<span>`
— the role is `generic` — so it read as nothing. It is a visually-hidden "Cabin: "
in the reading order instead, which is what every other field on the pass has
visibly.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (586 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`, and the full Playwright suite on a freshly reset database.

The verifier ran the changed assertions against the previous code: 5 fail, including
the new boarding-pass test. It flagged that in two multi-assertion tests the first
changed assertion masks the second, so a couple of the updated strings are carried by
their siblings rather than demonstrated independently — worth knowing rather than
counting as coverage.

It also confirmed the fallback branch is unreachable through the app, and for a
reason worth recording: `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no
check constraint and no Postgres enum**, so the guard is entirely Zod at the booking
boundary. The fallback is not defended by the schema.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#177** — two seat-validation error strings still interpolate the enum, one of
  them customer-reachable. Left out because error copy wants rewording, not a
  mechanical substitution.
- **#178** — `booking.spec.ts:267` has ~12s of headroom and timed out once on a cold
  run against a clean database. Not #173; a suite-budget problem that wants
  `test.slow()` or a split.
- Two responsive measurements added to **#79**: the Travel Class select truncates
  below 390px (and `booking.spec.ts` drives checkout at 320px), and the seat-step
  card wraps mid-value. Neither is a regression — both strings are shorter than the
  enum they replaced.

pull_requests.body:
`getOccupiedSeatsAction` had no session check. Of 18 exported actions, 15 gate on a
session; the other two — `searchFlightsAction` and `getFlightRoutesAction` — are
open because the unauthenticated home page genuinely needs them. This one was open
with nothing public that needed it.

## The decision this issue was filed to ask about turned out not to exist

I filed #154 as a product call: gating it means an unauthenticated visitor cannot see
a seat map before signing in. **That was wrong.** Both callers already require a
session:

- `app/checkout/page.tsx:93` — `/checkout` is in the `proxy.ts` matcher *and* the
  page does its own `getServerSession` + `redirect('/login')`
- `components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:139` — `/profile` is in the same matcher

There is no unauthenticated seat map, so gating costs no funnel.

## Why the check is still needed

A server action is its own HTTP endpoint. The matcher guards page navigations; Next
dispatches actions by header. The route's protection was never this function's —
which is exactly why the other fifteen carry their own check, and what AGENTS.md
already says about staff mutations.

Any signed-in traveller may ask about any flight. Scoping it to flights the caller
has booked would refuse checkout, which needs occupancy *before* there is a booking
to check against.

## Also aligned

Checkout guarded on `session?.user` while the action guards on `session?.user?.id`.
A session with a user but no id would have cleared the redirect and thrown inside
the action — a 500 where a trip back to sign-in belongs. Not reachable today, since
`token.id` is always set, but a gratuitous mismatch between a page and the action it
calls.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (580 unit + 21 database), `npm run
build`, plus `booking.spec.ts`, `multi-passenger.spec.ts` and
`booking-authority.spec.ts` against a freshly seeded database — 11 passed, re-run
clean with no order dependence.

The verifier ran the four new tests against the previous `actions.ts`: exactly the
two unauthenticated cases fail, the two characterization cases pass either way. It
also audited all 18 actions and confirmed no third gap, and confirmed no caller I had
missed — `__tests__/components/ProfileClient.test.tsx` mocks the action wholesale, so
it never touches this path.

## One regression, filed rather than fixed

**#175** — `ProfileClient` wraps this call in `.catch(() => [])`, so a failure
renders the seat map with **every seat free**. That `catch` predates this change and
already swallowed database and validation errors; the session check gives it one more
trigger.

I framed the trigger as session expiry, and the verifier corrected me: there is no
`maxAge`, so the NextAuth default is 30 days and that path is unrealistic. The real
one is `token.invalidated` — a password reset, a deleted user, or an admin whose
staff MFA is older than the 8-hour `STAFF_MFA_SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS`. Sign in at 9am,
leave the profile open, open the seat modal at 5pm.

Severity is bounded and I want to be precise about it: **no wrong seat can be
written.** `changeBookingSeatsAction` carries the same gate, so in exactly the state
that produces the blank map the save is refused before touching the database, with
the in-transaction check under `lockFlightForUpdate` and the
`@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])` constraint behind that. It changes how confusing
the failure is, not what anyone can accomplish. The fix belongs in `ProfileClient`'s
error handling and needs its own review.

## On the UI review

I recorded it as not applicable because no reachable state renders differently. The
verifier's pushback is fair: #175 *is* a differing render, it just requires an
already-invalidated session. The accurate record is that the only differing render
requires an invalidated session and is tracked separately.

## A correction on #173

I claimed there that e2e bookings are never cleared between runs. They are —
`booking.spec.ts` and `multi-passenger.spec.ts` both delete their own in
`test.afterAll`. Only an interrupted run strands seats. I have corrected the issue.

pull_requests.body:
The logo was **Google's Gemini wordmark** — another company's trademark serving as
this product's identity. The home hero was a photograph of an aircraft with "Gemini
Airways" painted along the fuselage. The tab icon was the Vercel triangle
`create-next-app` leaves behind. A shared link showed nothing at all.

This issue was parked because inventing a logo is design work rather than a code
change. Here is the design work.

## The mark

An **M drawn as one continuous path, split at its valley into two strokes** —
outbound saturated, return quieter. The monogram and a two-leg itinerary are the
same shape, and a leg is the object this application is built around.

Two decisions worth the words:

- **Square, and no wordmark.** The old asset was 344x127 requested at 20x20 and
  32x32, so Tailwind's `height: auto` painted it as a 7px sliver. Both call sites
  already name the airline in text beside the mark, so a wordmark in the asset would
  only repeat it — which is also why the header `alt` is now empty. It was reading
  "Mona Airways Mona Airways".
- **The legs differ by saturation, not brightness.** My first version dimmed the
  return leg with opacity. The reviewer measured that this inverts with the
  background: a paler stroke is the weaker one on black and the *stronger* one on
  white. Colour carries the hierarchy instead, so it survives the change of ground.

## The hero

A photograph cannot be redrawn, and a stock aircraft would say nothing about this
product, so the hero is **routes between places** — arcs, node dots, two glows.

Two bugs the review caught in my own work:

- **`.home` is the whole search page, not the hero.** Under `background-size: cover`
  the art grew with the results list, so a 16:9 canvas was blown up to twice the
  page width and its arcs ran across the filters and the result cards. It is bounded
  to one viewport now; below that the page is flat.
- **The node dots were landing inside the form controls.** A filled circle the size
  of a radio button was sitting in the FROM combobox on the value baseline. A line
  crossing a translucent card reads as atmosphere; a dot reads as a control. They
  are out of the band the centred card occupies.

On a phone the arcs magnify until they cross the search fields, so narrow screens
get the same light as CSS gradients and **do not fetch the artwork at all** —
verified: no request for `hero-routes.svg` at 390, 768 or 900, and it appears again
at 901.

## Icons and the social card

`app/icon.svg` puts the M on a gradient badge, because a tab strip is light in one
theme and dark in another. At 16px the two-tone split closed the counters and the
quiet leg smeared, so the badge glyph is solid white and larger — a 16px mark
carries one idea.

`app/favicon.ico` is hand-packed, and **I got it wrong the first time**: the
embedded PNG was RGB, Next's decoder requires RGBA, and it failed the build. There
is now a test asserting the ICO header bytes and the PNG colour type, because
`existsSync` is happy with a text file named `favicon.ico`.

The card renders **per request from the home page, not the root layout**.
`metadataBase` resolves when a page renders, and the auth routes are prerendered, so
a card declared at the root baked the build machine's address into every one of them
— `http://localhost:3000/img/og-image.jpg` in any container image, on exactly the
pages people paste into chat. Verified on a production server built with one URL and
started with another: `/` emits `https://mona.example.com/img/og-image.jpg`, and
`/login` emits no card and zero `localhost` references.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (575 unit + 21 database), `npm run
build`, a production server, the standalone server the Dockerfile actually runs, and
the full Playwright suite (28/28 on a clean database).

The verifier confirmed the ICO parses byte by byte — header, directory entry, PNG
signature, IHDR, and all four chunk CRCs — and swept 22 routes on production for the
global 500 my first attempt caused. It also corrected me: a bad ICO *does* fail
`npm run build`; I only saw it at request time because dev compiles that route
lazily.

New tests pin the parts that would otherwise rot silently: the hero CSS pointing at
the artwork, the phone variant, and the social card living on a dynamic route rather
than the layout.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#173** — three e2e specs hard-code seat 11A and `global-setup.ts` never clears
  bookings, so once a local run books that seat those specs fail on that database
  permanently. Same family as #155, but between runs rather than within one.

## Still open under other issues

Both deleted binaries remain in git history, which no `git rm` changes — worth
knowing if the trademark concern is more than cosmetic.
