pull_requests.body:
The boarding pass on checkout step 4 — the e-ticket a customer keeps and shows at
an airport — hardcoded `GEMINI AIRWAYS` with an `alt="Gemini"` logo, long after #72
and #138 consolidated the product identity everywhere else.

The guard that existed to prevent exactly this matched `/Gemini Airways/`, so a
shouted spelling and a bare `alt` both walked straight past it. It passed while the
string shipped.

## The fix

The span renders `BRAND.name.toUpperCase()`. The guard now matches `/gemini/i`.

**It also scans `.prisma` now.** `prisma` was already in the directory list, but the
extension list was `.ts`/`.tsx`, so the whole directory contributed exactly one file
— `seed.ts`. `schema.prisma` is shipped source that can carry the name in a
`@default`, where nothing else would ever see it. The verifier found this after I
had convinced myself the scan's scope was fine.

Both halves are directionally tested rather than assumed:

- The pattern, against the pre-change component: fails with exactly one offender,
  the boarding pass. The old pattern passes against the same bug.
- The extension, against a temporarily mutated `schema.prisma`: caught.

## A bare pattern can fire on something innocent

`/gemini/i` is blunt, deliberately — requiring "airways" would reintroduce the
`alt="Gemini"` half of the hole. But the word is a constellation, a NASA programme
an Orlando city guide could plausibly mention, and a model family. Someone enriching
`CityGuideData.ts` would hit a test named *"carries no carrier name other than the
product"* and see a bare filename.

So the failure message now says what to do:

```
Old carrier name found in: <files>. If this is the product identity leaking,
use BRAND from lib/brand.ts. If the match is legitimate, add the file to
ALLOWED at the top of this test.
```

`ALLOWED` is a named list — previously the `lib/brand.ts` exemption was an inline
filter with no obvious home for a second entry.

## alt=""

The carrier is named in full immediately beside the image, so alt text could only
duplicate it — announcing the airline twice per pass, per leg, per passenger.
`ui-review` confirmed against the live accessibility tree that the card still
conveys the carrier.

Worth stating plainly, because this fix makes it *silent* rather than fixed:
`public/img/logo.svg` still draws "Gemini" as vector paths, so a sighted customer
still sees that mark beside the words MONA AIRWAYS. That is #140, blocked on design
work, and out of scope here — but a screen reader now says the right thing while the
picture does not, so no text-based check will ever flag it again.

I looked at the assets while I was there and added two findings to #140: the site
background `public/img/gemini-background.jpg` is a photograph with **"Gemini
Airways" painted along the aircraft fuselage**, so renaming the file would satisfy a
filename check while leaving the wordmark on screen; and the logo is recognisably a
third party's brand mark, which raises that issue above cosmetic.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (564 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`. `ui-review` exercised a complete round-trip booking to the
confirmation step at phone, tablet and desktop in both `ECONOMY` and
`PREMIUM_ECONOMY` (the widest badge) — no defects, and the shorter name actually
improves the phone layout by 9px of clearance.

Playwright was judged unwarranted by both sub-agents and by me: no e2e spec
references the carrier name, and the two specs that reach the boarding passes assert
on flight numbers and seats.

## One fixture changed

`BookingCheckoutWizard.test.tsx` used `airline: 'Gemini Airways'` as flight data.
Harmless today — the pass does not render the operator — but the new negative
assertion would fail on that fixture the moment a boarding pass starts showing the
operating carrier, and it would read as a brand regression rather than test data.
It is `'Test Air'` now.

The remaining `'Gemini Airways'` fixtures across the suite stay: the verifier
checked each assertion site and they exercise the `airline` *column*, not product
identity. One of them is an airline filter checkbox, which needs a carrier that is
not the product for the test to mean anything.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#169** — the boarding pass prints the raw enum `PREMIUM_ECONOMY`, underscore and
  all, on a customer's e-ticket; at 390px that badge takes 141px of a 274px banner
  and butts against the carrier name with a 0px gap
- Added the `titlebar.tsx` duplicate-announcement case to **#80** — it does the
  opposite of this change, `alt={BRAND.name}` beside a visible name

pull_requests.body:
`/flights` ran `findMany` with no `where` and no `take`, serialising every row into
the RSC payload on every request — **1420 rows, 404 KB**, spanning May 2026 to
August 2027, on a page that answers "is my flight on time". Ascending order meant
the top of the board was the oldest departure in the database.

Now: a window of the last 2 hours through the next 7 days, `take: 200`, and a
`select` of only the eight columns the board renders. **30 rows, 5.5 KB — 73×
smaller.** Measured before and after, and confirmed independently by the verifier.

## Choosing the history window

Two hours rather than a day, because nothing advances `Flight.status` when a flight
leaves. Every row of history is therefore a row asserting "On Time" about a
departure that has already gone — worse than being absent, since absent reads as
ambiguous and "On Time" reads as answered.

```
history= 2h -> 28 rows,  1 departed and badged On Time
history= 6h -> 30 rows,  3
history=24h -> 32 rows,  5
```

Two keeps the case worth having — "did my flight actually leave?" — at one
misleading row until #84 marks a departed flight as departed. The 7-day horizon
holds: one day is 7 rows, two weeks is 57 and starts reaching back toward the
timetable.

## A board holding a window has to say so

Otherwise a search for a flight next month returns nothing and reads as "your flight
is missing". Two `ui-review` passes found the copy was the hard part:

- **The empty state blamed causes the user hadn't created.** One string told a
  customer who had only touched the status dropdown to "try searching for a
  different destination". This is not a corner case: with the window applied, the
  only DELAYED and CANCELLED rows in the whole table fall outside it, so **two of
  the four dropdown options were guaranteed to hit that copy**. It now answers the
  actual cause — search, status filter, both, or an empty window.
- **The both-inputs case needed to know which input was to blame.** A search for
  "London" with Cancelled set was answered "no flights match London" — while London
  *was* on the board and the filter had removed it. It now checks whether the query
  matches ignoring the filter, and raises the window only when the query is genuinely
  the reason.
- **Dates were the wrong unit.** I stated an absolute range first; the reviewer
  measured that the rows format client-side in the viewer's timezone while a
  server-formatted range does not, so an Auckland reader saw "covers to Aug 12"
  above a row dated 13/08 — plus a hydration error and dates silently changing on
  first keystroke. Correct timezone display needs the airport reference #84
  introduces, so the range is a duration: same sentence in every timezone.
- Contrast on that line measured **4.31:1 → 7.20:1**, a visually-hidden
  `role="status"` announces the result count, "No flights found" is an `<h2>` with
  the emoji in an `aria-hidden` span, and the way out is a real link.
- The subtitle no longer claims "Real-time" or "arrivals" — there is no feed and no
  arrivals column, and the new coverage line refuted both one line later. Now pinned
  by a test, which the verifier noticed it wasn't.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (564 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`, and the full Playwright suite — 28 passed, workers:1, no retries,
so every pass is first-attempt.

The verifier ran the new tests against the previous page and component: **13 of 18
fail**. It also flagged that `reads the soonest departures first` passes against the
old code — the old page already ordered ascending, so that one is a characterization
test, not coverage of this fix. Worth knowing rather than counting.

It caught one thing worth repeating: `e2e/admin.spec.ts:239` asserts a newly-delayed
flight appears on `/flights`, which now depends on `HORIZON_DAYS`. It passes because
that spec ticks all seven weekdays, but shortening the horizon below ~2 days would
break it.

`departureWindow()` exists because `Date.now()` in a component body trips
`react-hooks/purity` — a real lint error I introduced. No disable comment; the
window still moves per request, verified by calling the page twice 1.1s apart.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#167** — `Flight.departureDate` has no index, so this is a seq scan
  (`Rows Removed by Filter: 1390`). Harmless at 1.6ms today, but the whole
  justification for `take: 200` is that a real timetable is denser, and at that
  density the cap protects the payload while the scan stays unbounded.
- Concrete call sites added to **#79** (phone: Departure, Status and Price columns
  are entirely off-screen with no scroll affordance) and **#80** (table has no
  accessible name or `th` scope; the status `<select>` has no accessible name at
  all).

pull_requests.body:
`seatAssignmentCoverage` asserts a whole-table orphan count, so it counted the
passenger `seatAssignments` deliberately leaves unseated while asserting that seat
is refused. Roughly one full-suite run in four failed on another file's fixture.

## The fix

Jest now has two projects: `unit` runs in parallel, `database` runs `--runInBand`.
Nine files waiting on one shared Postgres gain nothing from running beside each
other, and serialising them leaves every assertion exactly as written.

The tempting fix — scoping the scan to rows the test created, the #150 pattern —
would have been wrong. The test says so at line 12: *"against the whole table, not
just rows this test creates (#137)"*. Scoped, it becomes a restatement of the test
below it in the same file.

## What the investigation turned up

I added a "scans the rows it claims to scan" guard, and **it failed**.

Seeding creates 1420 flights and 78 users but **zero** bookings, passengers,
itinerary legs and seat assignments. `Passenger JOIN ItineraryLeg` was empty, so the
orphan count has been counting nothing for its entire life. It was vacuous whenever
it passed and counting another file's rows whenever it failed — it has never once
verified its invariant.

Serialising alone would have made it reliably green and still worthless. So the
booking moves into `beforeAll` to give the scan a population, and the guard pins
that it has one. Checked: this was the only global count scan left in the suite;
#150 converted the other.

## Verification

The verifier reproduced the flake against the pre-change config (3 runs, 1 failed,
`Received: 2` matching the two orphan passengers the other file holds open), then
could not provoke it under the new arrangement across 6 full runs plus 18 targeted
ones. `npm test` ran clean 6 consecutive times.

It also confirmed mechanically:

- **The split is exhaustive and disjoint** — `--listTests` per project, `comm`'d
  against every file on disk: 59 + 9 = 68, empty diff both directions, empty
  intersection.
- **`next/jest` nests correctly in `projects`** — `--showConfig` diffed against the
  baseline: `transform`, `moduleNameMapper`, `setupFilesAfterEnv`, `testEnvironment`
  byte-identical, so nothing passes for the wrong reason.
- **The guard is load-bearing** — mutation-tested with an empty `beforeAll`, fails
  `Expected >= 4, Received 0`.
- **Exit codes propagate both ways**, so CI cannot read a failure as success.
- **No row leakage** across ~40 runs: flights back to 1420, users to 78, everything
  else zero.

## Corrections from that pass

My timing claim was wrong and is fixed in the comment: serialising those 9 files
costs about **3s**, not the 0.4s I first measured — my figure came from a cold-cache
run. The suite goes 21s → 31s. The decision stands; the evidence in the comment now
matches reality.

Three gaps it found, all closed here:

- The guard could itself pass on leftover rows from any source. Now scoped to the
  booking `beforeAll` created, expecting exactly 4.
- A `.database.test.tsx` would have landed in the parallel project silently,
  reintroducing #155 with no signal. Both patterns now cover `[jt]sx?`.
- My comment claimed another file's fixture "is never in the table at this moment".
  True of Jest files only — a dev server or a crashed test can still strand rows.
  Reworded: that is a true report about the database, and the fix is to clear the
  leftovers rather than narrow the scan.

## Documentation

AGENTS.md gains the two new scripts and a Gotcha, including that `npm test` no
longer forwards flags — pass them to `test:unit` or `test:database` directly.

## Filed rather than fixed

- #165 — two database test files never `$disconnect` (harmless at 5 of 100
  connections, but in-band execution is what makes it worth watching), and the haste
  collision warning printed on every run

pull_requests.body:
Prisma's `error` log level is enabled outside development, and a Postgres error
embeds the row that caused it. A customer's email address was observed reaching
stdout in production through that path.

## The fix

Warnings and errors are handed to an event emitter rather than written by Prisma.
The handler writes a record built from named fields — `code`, `relation`,
`constraint`, `fields`, `target`, `timestamp` — and never the message itself.
Development keeps stdout logging unchanged, where the visibility is the point and
the data is seeded.

The message is cut at the first row-data marker (`Failing row contains`, `DETAIL:`,
`detail: Some(`, `Key (`) before any pattern reads it. That matters more than it
looks: a NOT NULL or foreign-key violation formats the *entire* message as the
failing row, and a row can contain the literal text a schema pattern is looking for.

Verified live on a standalone production server — three concurrent registrations of
the same address produced:

```
{ level: 'error', timestamp: …, target: 'verificationToken.create',
  code: 'P2002', relation: null, constraint: null, fields: [ 'identifier' ] }
```

`grep -c` for the address across the whole server log: **0**.

## Two things I got wrong, and what the evidence said

**The first redaction leaked.** The patterns ran over the whole message, so a
crafted NOT NULL violation yielded `relation: "LEAKED_USER_SECRET"` read straight
out of the failing row — and the test asserting that couldn't happen passed
vacuously, because its one payload had a genuine `relation "User"` earlier in the
string. `beforeRowData` and a test built on the actual leaking payload fix that.

**Then I over-corrected.** I anchored the patterns to Postgres's sentence templates
and claimed that made them a whitelist. It did not: a caller who can plant
`relation "x"` in their own input can equally plant `new row for relation "x"
violates`. Lengthening the phrase only lengthens the payload — demonstrated on three
live channels, including parameterised `$queryRaw` and pure ORM with no raw SQL
anywhere. Meanwhile it silently dropped the `42P01` / `42P07` / `42704` schema-drift
diagnostics, which are the ones worth most when a deploy meets an unmigrated
database.

So the anchoring is reverted, those three cases are pinned as fixtures captured from
a live client, and the comments now claim only what is demonstrated: `beforeRowData`
is a mitigation, not a boundary, and `identifiers()` filters shape rather than
provenance. What remains is a **forgery** risk, not disclosure — filed as #163 with
the real fix (check extracted names against the schema, not against their shape).

## Diagnostics that were missing and now work

Both confirmed against a live Prisma 5.22 client:

- Raw-query failures spell it `` Code: `23514` `` — capital C, backticks — which the
  original pattern never matched. The repo runs raw SQL in the auth rate-limit,
  token and flight-lock paths, so this was most of the errors an operator sees.
- `Unique constraint failed on the fields: (\`email\`)` carries no SQLSTATE,
  relation or constraint at all, and previously redacted to an entirely empty
  record. It now reports `P2002` plus the column list.
- Foreign-key violations: Prisma 5 says `Foreign key constraint violated:`, not
  `failed on the field:`. The regex was written for wording no live client emits.

## Blast radius worth knowing about

Subscribing at construction means importing `lib/prisma` now **throws** in a browser
context instead of sitting inert. That surfaced two suites testing server-side
concerns under jsdom, where `@prisma/client` resolves to the browser build —
`instrumentation.test.ts` and `lib/env.test.ts`. Both were passing only because
nothing had touched a client member at import time; both now declare
`/** @jest-environment node */`, which AGENTS.md's Gotchas already required.

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` imported `PassengerInput` from a
non-server module as a value. SWC elided it, so client bundles were clean — but
`import type` makes that a guarantee rather than an optimisation. Confirmed: 0
references to `PrismaClient` across all client chunks.

Fixes the defect #143 recorded as the most-reported finding of the roadmap
investigation — raised independently by 8 of 12 areas, never reproduced until now.

## The defect

Step 3 of checkout read `flights[activeLegIndex]`, whichever leg the seat map was
last showing, so a round trip showed **one flight card** on the last screen before
payment. The return leg was not on it. Seats compounded it: a traveller's seats were
joined into `Seats: 11A, 12C` with nothing saying which seat belonged to which
flight.

The confirmation step was fixed for exactly this during the round-trip work and
carries the reasoning in a comment; review was the half that was missed.

## The fix

One card per leg in itinerary order, each carrying that leg's flight details and each
traveller's seat **on that leg**.

Moving seats into the leg cards left the fare rows repeating a name already given
once per leg — and for a lone traveller, a "breakdown" of one row identical to the
total directly beneath it. That case now states the cabin and stops.

## From the `ui-review` pass

It exercised one-way, round-trip, 2-, 3- and 9-passenger bookings at 390/768/1440,
plus the submitting state and a real concurrent seat conflict. Two blocking defects
in the new markup, both fixed:

- **A long name pushed the seat outside the card and the page into horizontal
  scroll** at 390px — measured, the seat landed 93px past the card edge, so the one
  traveller with a long name saw no seat at all. `lib/validation.ts` allows
  100-character names, so this was reachable input, not a contrived fixture.
- **A hyphenated name broke the name↔seat pairing**: the seat wrapped to two lines
  and ended up adjacent to the *next* traveller's name — the same class of confusion
  this change exists to remove.

Also applied: `role="list"` on both lists and an accessible name on the per-leg list
(WebKit strips list semantics from `list-style: none`), an "Itinerary" heading so
heading navigation no longer skips the legs, and a contrast lift on the direction
eyebrow, which was the dimmest text on the card despite being the discriminator that
matters.

It confirmed the fix reports the seat actually held rather than the seat clicked —
the group auto-allocator had reassigned one, and review followed the assignment.

## The e2e assertion that never could have caught this

`e2e/booking.spec.ts` asserted `text=Seats: 11A, 12C` on the review step and passed
throughout the defect's life: a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats
are paired with the right legs. Both it and `e2e/multi-passenger.spec.ts` now assert
seat against traveller, row by row.

The verifier caught that both legs of that spec were picking `11A` — identical empty
layouts, `.first()` on each — which would have made the new assertions
near-tautologies. The inbound leg now takes a different seat so the check
discriminates.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (555 passing, twice), the three changed
e2e specs, and `npm run build` — all clean. The verifier also ran the new tests
against the **pre-change** component in a detached worktree: all eight touched tests
fail there, each for its intended reason, so none of them pass vacuously.

## Filed rather than fixed here

- #158 — the boarding pass still says `GEMINI AIRWAYS`, and `productIdentity.test.ts`
  misses it because its regex is case-sensitive
- #159 — a seat-conflict rejection is invisible on phone, drops focus to `<body>`,
  and leaves the refused seat showing in success green
- #160 — `ProfileClient` keeps a third copy of the direction label and will disagree
  with checkout about a middle leg once #131 lands

Also noted the review step as a call site on #84, which owns timezone-aware
departure display — the leg cards show a date but no time.

Adds a workflow rule: findings that fall outside the current slice get filed as
GitHub issues rather than absorbed into the slice or left in a chat reply.

Two hunks, documentation only.

**Development Workflow step 3** gains one sentence, so the rule appears where slice
scope is being decided.

**Issue Tracking** gains the substance — file before moving on, search for an
existing issue first, and state where the problem is, what was observed, and whether
it was verified against running code or only read in the source.

The third bullet is a guard rather than a restatement of the request: filing is not
a substitute for finishing, and a finding that makes the slice wrong or unsafe to
ship means stopping and saying so, not filing around it. Without it the rule is a
way to ship known-broken work with a ticket attached.

## Why step 3 and not a step 12

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md` and `.claude/agents/verifier.md` cite "AGENTS.md step
6" and "step 7" by number in their frontmatter. A new step in the middle would
silently invalidate both, and nothing tests that coupling — filed as #156.

## Verification

`__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts` passes (it is the test that governs these
files). `npm run lint` and `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. Step numbering confirmed
unchanged against `main`: 11 steps before and after, identical text and order, only
line offsets moved. Playwright and `npm run build` were judged not warranted — the
diff touches no route, component, action, schema or config, and AGENTS.md cannot
reach the build output.

Rendered UI review is not applicable: no UI impact.

## Filed rather than fixed here

Practising the rule the change is adding. None of these are regressions from this
diff:

- #155 — `seatAssignmentCoverage` flakes against parallel database test files.
  Reproduced: one full-suite run in four. Another test file's intentional fixture is
  counted by a whole-table scan. **Expect this to redden CI on this PR
  occasionally; it is not this change.**
- #156 — files that reference AGENTS.md drift without anything failing.

Also filed from the same session's reading, unrelated to this diff: #152, #153, #154.

pull_requests.body:
Refs #121.

## What this changes

`waitForStableTotpWindow` now reports what it consumed, on every run, including when it waits for nothing. That is the third option the issue suggested, and the only part still missing — the bound it also asked for already existed implicitly, so this writes it down: the wait triggers only in the last 6 seconds of a 30-second window and settles 1 second into the next, costing at most 7 seconds and nothing for the other 80% of the clock.

No behaviour change.

## The budget question, measured

Taken on a machine at load average **369 on 24 cores**, so these are pessimistic:

| Test | Used | Budget | Headroom |
|---|---|---|---|
| Admin MFA journey | **35.5s** | 90s (`test.slow()`) | 54.5s |
| Non-admin blocked | 7.8s | 30s | 22.2s |

Worst case with the wait firing is 42.5s against 90s. The journey would have to more than double before the budget mattered.

I did not split the test (the issue's second option). At 35.5s of 90s there is nothing to relieve, and splitting a working journey purely on suspicion is churn.

## Why #121 is probably already closed by other work

Worth stating plainly, because it is the reason this issue outlived its fixes — the two halves were addressed by two different PRs and nobody checked the pair:

- The **titled** mechanism (the TOTP wait exhausting a 30s budget) was mitigated by `test.slow()` in #139, which is where the budget became 90s. The measurements above confirm it holds.
- The **reopen** was triggered by `admin.spec.ts:43`, the non-admin test, which contains no TOTP wait at all. That was the first-sign-in route compile, fixed in #148.

So the recommendation is to close #121 on the strength of #139 + #148 + the observability here, rather than claiming a third fix for something already fixed. Leaving that call to a human, given this issue's history of premature closure.

## Verification

- `e2e/admin.spec.ts` run 6 times: 5 passed, 1 failed on `EMFILE: too many open files` — the dev server could not start its file watcher, machine resource exhaustion from ~400 unrelated chrome processes, not this change
- `tsc` clean, lint 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- Rendered UI review: not applicable, the change is one test helper

None of the 6 runs happened to land in the 20% of the clock that triggers the wait, so every run logged `0ms`. The wait's arithmetic is verifiable by inspection; the log line exists precisely so the next occurrence does not need inspection.

Closes #149.

## The problem

`__tests__/lib/passengerDataProtection.database.test.ts` asserted that `purgeExpiredPassengerData` returned `>= 1`. That return value is a count across the **whole table**, which makes the assertion wrong in both directions:

- **Fragile** — anything else sweeping concurrently claims this row first, and the count comes back 0
- **Weak** — an unrelated expired row would satisfy it while this passenger stayed intact

## Reproduced, not inferred

My first report on #149 attributed the observed failures to `instrumentation.ts` sweeping on dev-server boot, and I could not support that — one occurrence happened with nothing running. So I reproduced it directly instead, by running a second sweep immediately before the assertion:

```
✕ stores only ciphertext, returns only safe fields, and purges on expiry
  Expected: >= 1
  Received:    0
```

That is the reported failure exactly. Mechanism confirmed; the trigger in the wild is still unidentified, but the fix does not depend on knowing it.

## The fix

Drop the count assertion. The assertion immediately after it already checks the behaviour under test — this passenger's ciphertext nulled and `sensitiveDataDeletedAt` set — and is scoped by id, so the count contributed no coverage.

Verified the remaining assertion still has teeth by inverting the purge's filter (`lte` → `gt`): the test fails on the surviving ciphertext.

## Verification

- The simulated race that reproduced the failure now passes
- The changed test: 10/10 runs
- `tsc` clean, lint 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- Rendered UI review: not applicable, the change is one test file

**Note on the full local suite:** two runs failed on *unrelated* jsdom component tests (`ProfileClient`, `UserAuthForm`), both 5s per-test timeouts, different tests each time. This machine is at load average 303 on 24 cores from other workloads — 566 chrome and 137 node processes not from this suite. Those failures are CPU starvation, not this change; CI is the clean arbiter.

pull_requests.body:
Refs #121. Does **not** close it — see below.

## The mechanism

The dev server compiles a route the first time something asks for it, and `app/api/auth/[...nextauth]` costs more than the default budget of the assertion waiting for a sign-in to land. Whichever test signed in first against a server that had not yet compiled it paid that bill and could fail on it.

`e2e/global-setup.ts` already ran before the suite to clear rate limits, so the compile is paid there now. One GET of the NextAuth handler builds the whole route module.

The sign-in assertion goes back to Playwright's **default 5s** timeout. The 30s value it carried was padding for exactly this compile — a fix that still needs the workaround is not a fix.

## Correcting the record on #121

The issue says the failure "only fails as part of the full suite, never alone, which points at cross-spec interference." That is not what governs it. What varies is whether the server in use has already compiled the route:

- `admin.spec.ts` sorts first, so in a full-suite run it is *also* the first sign-in
- `reuseExistingServer: !CI` means re-running a failure against the still-warm server passes — so a re-run proved nothing in either direction

Established by A/B against a cold cache, flipping only the warm-up: **2/2 fail without it, 3/3 pass with it**, plus a cold full suite at `--retries=0`. Server timings pin it — without the warm-up the NextAuth route compiles *inside* the assertion window (~2.5s); with it, the in-test calls drop to ~30-130ms.

`retries: 2` on CI (`playwright.config.ts:10`, `0` locally) is why CI never surfaced this.

## Why this does not close #121

The issue's *titled* mechanism — `waitForStableTotpWindow` eating the admin journey's budget (`e2e/admin.spec.ts:8`) — is untouched here, and mitigated only by the `test.slow()` already on main. This PR addresses the reopening comment's hypothesis, not the original one.

## Dropped from this PR

An earlier draft also made `createVerifiedAccount` upsert, on the issue's suspicion that leftover rows from an interrupted run collide. Verification showed that cannot happen: every caller uniquifies its email, so `create` never collides and the update branch is unreachable. Removed rather than ship code justified by a rationale that does not hold.

## Verification

- Cold full suite at `--retries=0`: passing; A/B as above
- `tsc` clean, lint 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings), `npm run build` succeeds
- Rendered UI review: not applicable, the diff is confined to `e2e/` test infrastructure

## Unrelated flake found while verifying

`__tests__/lib/passengerDataProtection.database.test.ts:95` asserts a **global** purge count `>= 1` on its own back-dated row, while `instrumentation.ts:28` runs an unfiltered `purgeExpiredPassengerData()` on every dev-server boot. Boot the app during Jest and the sweep claims the row first. Reproduced independently. Different subsystem, so it is filed separately rather than folded in here.

Closes #137.

The contract step left over from #69. Every reader moved to `SeatAssignment` in #127 and the last fallbacks went in #146; these columns were still written but no longer authoritative. `Passenger` fused a traveller with a seat on one flight — a traveller is one person per booking, a seat is one per leg — and every reader that had to be told which was authoritative was a chance to get it wrong.

## What this does

- Stops writing `seatNumber`, `cabinClass` and `flightId`, and drops them
- Drops `Passenger`'s unique seat index with them, leaving `SeatAssignment`'s `@@unique([flightId, seatNumber])` as the sole guard against two customers acquiring the same seat — the intended end state, stated explicitly in the migration
- Moves the booking result onto per-leg `seatNumbers`, and the cabin onto the assignment

#137b and #137c could not be split: the columns are `NOT NULL`, so code that stops writing them cannot run against the old schema. The intermediate state is not verifiable, so they land together.

## Two defects fixed on the way

**The round-trip e-ticket.** The boarding pass printed one seat for a whole itinerary — the outbound seat, labelled as the seat for the trip. Dropping the column forced the confirmation onto per-leg seats.

That exposed a second layer: the card was still *one card per traveller*, naming whichever flight the leg switcher was last left on, so the fix at first just printed both seats onto a card belonging to one flight. A two-leg trip now renders one pass per leg, each with its own flight, route, date and seat.

## Verification

- Jest 548/548, Playwright 28/28 from a cold cache, `tsc` and `lint` clean, `npm run build` succeeds
- Migrations apply to an empty database
- The migration refuses to run if any traveller-leg has no `SeatAssignment`. That guard was exercised both ways — it raises on a seeded orphan and passes once the assignment exists — rather than assumed

## Notes for review

- `__tests__/lib/seatAssignments.database.test.ts` came back. The WIP commit deleted it entirely, but only its backfill case was genuinely obsolete (that statement reads a dropped column). The other four cover live constraints, including the double-sell guard this PR makes load-bearing.
- `e2e/helpers/auth.ts` gets a longer sign-in timeout. Pre-existing flake, unrelated to this change: the dev server compiles the NextAuth callback on the first request that reaches it, so whichever test signed in first failed. It moved between tests as ordering changed, which is what gave it away.

First of the #137 contract steps.

## The fallbacks

Three read paths fell back to `Passenger.seatNumber` when a leg had no assignment: `passengersSeatedOnLeg` (the admin manifest), the profile's booking rows, and the seat-change modal's seeding. They existed for bookings taken before #118 backfilled `SeatAssignment`.

That column describes the **outbound** leg. As a fallback it was therefore the wrong answer for every leg but the first — the same shape as the four defects #126 and #127 fixed. A traveller with no assignment on the return leg was shown, and had the modal seeded with, their outbound seat.

They are gone. An absent assignment now reads as "Not assigned", which is what it is: a defect to notice rather than a shape to paper over.

## Proving it was safe first

Removing a fallback is only safe if the invariant it covers actually holds, so `seatAssignmentCoverage.database.test.ts` asserts it against **the whole table** rather than just rows the test creates:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM "Passenger" p
JOIN "ItineraryLeg" l ON l."bookingId" = p."bookingId"
LEFT JOIN "SeatAssignment" sa ON sa."passengerId" = p.id AND sa."legId" = l.id
WHERE sa.id IS NULL
```

Zero on the working database. A second test books a two-leg trip for two travellers and asserts four assignments, so a regression in the write path fails here too rather than being absorbed by a fallback that no longer exists.

That test runs before the fallbacks are removed, and stays as the guard afterwards.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- `npm test` — 548 passed
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed

Two tests asserted the fallback behaviour and are rewritten to assert the replacement rather than deleted, since the case they cover — a leg with no assignment — is still reachable in principle and should read correctly when it happens.

## Next

The columns are still written. #137b stops writing them and reshapes `safePassengerSelect`; #137c drops them, which also removes `Passenger`'s unique seat index and leaves `SeatAssignment`'s as the sole guard against selling a seat twice.

Closes #135. The contract step for the fare, completing the sequence #134 → #144 → this.

## What goes

`Flight.price` and `FlightSchedule.price`. `priceCents` has been authoritative since #134, and #144 moved the last readers — the ones that display money — onto it. The strings were retained and still written so a rollback kept a displayable value. Nothing reads them.

`priceCents` is **NOT NULL** now, so a flight without a fare cannot exist.

## What the migration does with unreadable rows

It fills anything the original backfill could not parse before enforcing NOT NULL. A row readable in neither form is **priced at zero and left visible**, not deleted — a fare of nothing is wrong in a way somebody reports, and a missing flight is wrong in a way nobody sees. There were no such rows on the working database (1,459 of 1,459 flights, 9 of 9 schedules), so this is a guard for environments that were behind.

## Two fallbacks go with the columns

`flightFareCents` no longer parses a string, and the search form no longer needs an infinity sentinel to sort a fare it could not read — there is no such fare. **The tests guarding those paths are deleted rather than contorted**, because the schema now prevents what they described rather than the code handling it.

## Two things the pre-push review caught

**`tsc` could not.** `flightsForCabin` still constructed `price: formatPrice(...)` on its result. Excess properties are not checked on object spreads, so the build was clean while the last emitter of the string survived — re-introducing the dual write this PR removes. Its `catch` had also become unreachable, since reading a field cannot throw.

**A latent bug in the edit form.** It seeds the price input from `formatPrice`, which emits thousands separators, and the validator's pattern rejected them — so a schedule with a four-figure fare could not be re-saved without editing the price. Unreachable today because the form is rendered without `initialSchedule`, but it would have bitten the moment editing was wired up. The validator accepts its own output now, with a test.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- `npm test` — 546 passed
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed
- Migrate + seed against an **empty** database: 1,416 flights, minimum fare 35000, no `price` column

## Note

An administrator still types a fare, and it is still parsed and validated. Only storage changed — the string is no longer kept beside the number.

First of the #135 contract steps, and the one #143 flagged as a blocker for four separate areas.

## The gap #134 left

#134 added `priceCents` and moved the reads that *compute* money onto it. The reads that *display* money still printed the retained string — so the number a customer saw came from formatted text while every calculation came from the column. Two sources of truth for the same fare.

## What moved

Search result cards, the flight status board, the admin occurrence table, the profile's total fallback, and the checkout projection — which now carries `priceCents` through so `BookingCheckoutWizard` totals an itinerary from fares rather than parsed labels.

`parsePriceToCents` is no longer imported by either the search form or the checkout wizard. String parsing has left the components entirely, which is what makes the eventual column drop a schema-only change.

## A bug the pre-push review caught

My first version piped the search form's `fareCents` into `formatPrice`. That helper deliberately returns `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` for a fare that is neither stored nor parseable, so the row sorts last — a sentinel meant only for comparators. Formatting it renders **`$∞`** on the result card, and it also made the itinerary total's "give up and hide" path unreachable, since `Infinity + Infinity` formats rather than throwing.

Display and comparison now use different helpers on purpose. A card falls back to the catalogue string; the total keeps its path.

There is a test for it, and I confirmed it fails against the version the reviewer flagged.

## The other test that matters

Every existing test passed unchanged after this change, which proves nothing — both paths render `"$350"`. So there is one where they **disagree**: a result whose string says `$999` and whose `priceCents` says `35000` renders `$350`, and `$999` appears nowhere.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings)
- `npm test` — 549 passed
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed

`e2e/admin.spec.ts:43` failed again in an earlier full run here, on top of the `toHaveURL` fix I claimed had addressed it — then passed in isolation, as before. That fix removed a real defect but was **not** the cause of the flake. I have reopened #121 and said so. I noted in #139 that four passing runs could not prove absence; they did not, and I should not have written that PR as though the mechanism settled it.

Addresses most of #78. You asked for a redesign rather than a minimal repair.

## What was actually wrong

The page rendered a **full detail panel for every city at once** — title, description, highlights, reviews and a review form each — and every one of them carried `.sticky-sidebar`, which is `position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0`. Ten panels stacked at the same coordinates and sat on top of the city list. That was the overlap.

One panel exists now, for the selected city, in normal flow.

## The review form went with it

A single pair of state values (`reviewContent`, `reviewRating`) drove all ten mounted forms. A draft typed against one city was the draft for every other one, and a rating chosen for one applied to all. Selecting a city now resets the form that belongs to it, and there is a test for it.

## Keyboard and assistive technology

- The city name was an `<h3>` with a click handler; it is a button
- Map markers answered only to a mouse, which made the whole map a decoration for anyone not using one. They take focus and respond to Enter and Space
- Favourite controls carry labels instead of leaving a reader to announce "🤍"
- Selection is conveyed with `aria-pressed`, not colour alone
- The guide's controls bring their own `:focus-visible` ring, because this app defines none (#80)

## States that did not exist

Failures were reported through `window.alert`. They are announced in the page now, in a live region. There are empty states for no guides at all and no city selected, and a map-failure state — the list works without the map, so it says so rather than leaving a blank rectangle.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 547 passed
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed

Reviewed rendered at 390/768/1440. My first capture showed the map stuck on "Loading map…" — that was my screenshot racing hydration, not a defect; confirmed by waiting for the SVG and by checking `/map.json` returns 200 for both GET and HEAD.

Component tests were rewritten for the new interaction model rather than patched: one region at a time, draft resets with the city, keyboard selection, and the empty state.

## Left for the rest of #78

The remaining acceptance criterion is responsive behaviour at mobile widths, which belongs with #79's breakpoint work — the sidebar is still a fixed 472px absolute panel, which is a layout contract shared with other views.

#140 — `public/img/logo.svg` still renders the wordmark "Gemini", so the header reads "Gemini Mona Airways". It is vector paths rather than text, so it needs the mark redrawn; #72's source scan cannot see an image.

Closes #121, which I filed after this spec failed during #125 and then again during #128, #133 and #134.

## Two causes, and the one I first suspected was wrong

I originally guessed the TOTP window wait was consuming the whole 30s budget. It is not — `waitForStableTotpWindow` sleeps at most 7 seconds. And that theory never explained why `:43` also flaked, since it does not call that function.

**The non-admin test had a non-retrying assertion:**

```ts
await expect(page.url()).toContain('/login');
```

`page.url()` is a string read the instant `goto()` resolves. `expect` on a string cannot retry, and the `await` in front of it does nothing — there is no promise to wait on. So the test failed whenever the middleware redirect had not settled yet. It uses `toHaveURL` now, which retries.

**The admin journey is genuinely long.** It enrols MFA, creates a schedule, generates occurrences, checks a passenger manifest and changes live status — several tests' worth of work, with up to 7 seconds spent before any of it starts. It is marked `test.slow()` rather than having the shared timeout raised for every spec.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm test` — 544 passed
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed
- `e2e/admin.spec.ts` run four times in a row: 2 passed each time

I cannot prove absence of a flake by running it four times, so the argument here rests on the mechanism: the assertion could not retry, and now it can.

## Note

This is the fifth PR in which this spec failed and then passed on re-run, which is what makes the non-retrying assertion the likely explanation rather than load.

Closes the tasks on #72.

## The conflict

The site called itself **Mona Airways** while every flight it had ever created was operated by **"Gemini Airways"** — the application and its own inventory disagreed about who the customer was buying from. `AGENTS.md` names the product, so that is the name; the other was demo residue. I did not invent a third name, since choosing one would contradict the repo's own statement of what this is.

## One source

`lib/brand.ts` holds the name, the two-letter designator, the tagline and the support details. Everything a customer reads about the airline comes from there, so they cannot drift apart again. Seeded flight numbers are built from the designator (`MA101`), so the airline code is not decorative — there is a test for that.

A migration renames the carrier on rows created before this. **Flight numbers are deliberately left alone**: they identify a flight on bookings already taken, so renumbering existing inventory would change what someone was told they were travelling on.

## Metadata

Every public route now has its own title and description. Two had titled themselves "Authentication".

The root layout supplies the name through a template — and the home page spells it out, because Next applies a template to *child* segments only. I caught that because the rendered check showed `/` returning a bare "Book flights" while every other route was correct; there is now a test for it.

`app/flightrecord/page.tsx` was a client component, which cannot export metadata at all. The chart moved into its own client component so the route can be a server component and carry a title.

## The footer

It listed Contact Us, FAQ, About us, Agencies, Groups, Corporate, Partners and a newsletter. **None were links** — list items styled to look navigable, leading nowhere, promising sections this application does not have. That is the same defect as a control pointing at `#` (#132), so they are gone rather than pointed at placeholder pages.

What remains is what the product can stand behind. The example contact details are **marked as examples** rather than dressed up as a support desk that does not exist — printing a number that reaches a real stranger would be worse than an obvious placeholder.

While there I found `.footer-columns` had no rule in the stylesheet at all, so the footer had always rendered as a single stacked column flush to the viewport edge despite the class name. It is a responsive grid now.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 544 passed, 66 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed
- Migrate + seed against an **empty** database: one carrier, `MA`-prefixed numbers

`__tests__/docs/productIdentity.test.ts` scans the source for any other carrier name and for routes missing metadata, and guards itself against a broken directory walk passing everything silently.

## Two things the checks caught

**The seed broke.** `ts-node` does not resolve the `@/*` alias, and the seed reaches `lib/data/FlightData.ts`, so my import took the seed down on a fresh database. Found by running migrate + seed against an empty database, not by the unit tests.

**The build broke.** Prepending imports put them above `"use client"`, which must be the first expression. Two files affected.

## Not done here

The README still opens with "Fly with the Octocat!". That is repository framing rather than product surface, and I would rather not rewrite a project's own README voice without asking.

Slice 4 of #70, and its last remaining task.

## The problem

Sorting and the price filter recovered numbers by stripping characters out of the price label the server had just formatted:

```ts
const parsePrice = (priceStr?: string) =>
    parseFloat(priceStr.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, '')) || 0;
```

The ordering depended on how a fare happened to be rendered, and the filter slider was denominated in whatever that parse produced. `"$1,200"` becomes `1200` only because the comma is stripped; a formatter change would silently reorder results.

Both now read `priceCents` — the value the database stores, added in #134. `parsePrice` is gone entirely.

## A hazard this exposed

`flightsForCabin` adjusted the display string for the searched cabin but left `priceCents` at the base fare. Sorting a Business search would have ordered by economy fares, and the filter bounds would have described prices that were not on screen. **Both forms of the fare now change together**, with a test asserting it.

I found this by checking the cabin path before switching the sort over, not after.

## Two judgement calls

**The slider works in minor units** and labels itself with `formatPrice` — the same formatter the result cards use. The control and the cards can no longer disagree about what a number means.

**A fare that can be read neither from the column nor the string sorts last, and the price filter leaves it alone.** It cannot be compared, and the slider starts at the highest known fare — so excluding it would make that flight vanish by default. That is inventory disappearing because of a data defect rather than a customer's choice, which is the same failure mode as hiding cabins in #133.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 539 passed, 65 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 28 passed

New coverage: three component tests (ordering by stored fare where the labels sort the wrong way as text, the slider labelled by the shared formatter, an unreadable fare kept rather than dropped), one action test asserting the integer follows the cabin fare, and an e2e that asserts both sort directions actually produce sorted fares against real seeded data and that the slider's max equals the highest fare on screen.

The ordering test uses `"$1,200"` and `"$900"` deliberately — that pair sorts the wrong way as text and is exactly what the old parser had to special-case.

Slice 3 of #70 — the enabler for server-authoritative sorting and filtering.

## The problem

`Flight.price` and `FlightSchedule.price` are formatted strings (`"$350"`). Every consumer parses text the application itself formatted. That round trip breaks the moment formatting changes, and a formatted string cannot be compared, summed or sorted in the database — which is precisely why sorting and filtering search results happens in the browser today, on numbers recovered from display text.

This is the same correction #107 made for the booking total, in the same shape.

## What changed

- `priceCents` added to `Flight` and `FlightSchedule`, backfilled by the same pattern the application could have written
- Money-computing reads move onto it: search pricing, the itinerary total, the booking service
- `calculateItineraryTotal` now takes minor units instead of strings, so a booking total is never derived from display text
- `flightFareCents` is the single accessor — prefers the integer, falls back to parsing the string for any row the backfill could not read

The fallback lives in one place so it disappears in one place when the string column goes. A stored zero is a fare, not a missing value, and there is a test for that.

## Expand only

The string columns are deliberately retained and still written, matching how #107 → #125 sequenced the booking total: reads move first, the drop follows once the backfill has been observed in a deployed environment. Filed the contract step as a follow-up rather than folding it in.

Slice 2 of #70, and the one control I recommended building rather than removing.

## Why this one, not removal

The cabin select was set by its own markup and read by nothing. Unlike the controls removed in #132, this one **actively misled**: a customer shopping Business saw economy prices in the results and then met a different number at checkout. A dead control does nothing; this quoted a fare nobody would honour.

## What changed

- `searchFlightsSchema` takes `cabinClass`, defaulting to `ECONOMY`
- Results are priced at that cabin's fare using the existing `CABIN_FARE_PERCENT`
- The choice travels in the shared URL as `cabin=`, and is restored from it
- Checkout opens on the cabin that was shopped, so the price quoted is the one offered

## Marked, not hidden

A flight without the searched cabin stays in the results with a badge. On a London→New York First search, one flight has no First cabin and one does — priced $850 and $2,550. Hiding the first would report fewer flights on a route that has seats, which reads as "we do not fly there" rather than "not in that cabin". Those flights carry the fare they can actually be booked at.

## A bug the pre-push review caught, and my test did not

Changing the cabin left populated results on screen while `cabinParam` switched immediately — so clicking Book Now sent the **new** cabin to checkout against a card showing the **old** cabin's fare. That recreated the exact defect this PR removes.

The existing `clearEmptySearchState` only discards an already-empty list, because it was written for route/date edits where the search is re-armed or re-run; nothing re-runs it on a cabin change. Cabin changes now clear the results outright.

**My regression test could not have caught it** — I had seeded it with `searchSuccess([])`, an empty list, which is the one input the old helper did clear. It passed vacuously. It now seeds real results, and I confirmed it fails against the unfixed code.

## Two deliberate asymmetries

**Economy passes through untouched** rather than recomputed. The stored price is already the economy fare, so the default search returns exactly what it did before — recomputing would have reformatted `$1200` to `$1,200` as a side effect.

**An unknown cabin is rejected in search and in the URL parser, but ignored at checkout.** In search, falling back to economy would silently show a different trip from the one the link described. At checkout the itinerary is still valid, so a bad cabin parameter must not turn a live booking link into a 404.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 532 passed, 65 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 27 passed

New coverage: four action tests, four URL tests, four component tests, and two e2e — one asserting the Business fare is exactly twice the economy fare against real seeded data and survives a refresh, one asserting the flight count does not drop when shopping a cabin some flights lack.

For the rendered review I had to clear one seeded flight's First rows to make the badge appear at all, then restored it — every seeded flight currently operates every cabin.

## Process note

Two `Bash` tool outages during this work silently dropped an edit I had already applied. I caught it because tests reported `parsePriceToCents` receiving `undefined`, and re-checked the file rather than trusting the earlier success message.

Slice 1 of #70. Four controls promised something the app cannot do; each is removed rather than left as a promise it cannot keep.

## What went, and why removal rather than wiring

**Search reward flights** — an uncontrolled checkbox: no state, no handler, no effect. Wiring it up was never an option. `PointsActivityService` records status points *earned* and reversed; there is no spendable balance, no award chart, no redemption ledger, no fare priced in points. That is a pricing and loyalty model, not a control fix. Filed as #130.

**Multicity** — a link to `#`. Worth knowing the booking side is closer than it looks: a `Booking` is already an ordered sequence of `ItineraryLeg` rows, `bookFlight` takes `flightIds[]`, the wizard renders `flights[]` with a tab per leg, pricing sums per leg, and the profile renders one row per leg. None of that assumes two. What blocks it is **search** — one origin, one destination, up to two dates — plus `MAX_ITINERARY_LEGS = 2`. Filed as #131.

**Check-In** — a link to `#` in the primary navigation. The task list in #70 does not mention it; its acceptance criteria do ("No primary navigation or booking control points to `#`"). It returns when check-in exists (#77). Its `/checkin` entry in the page-title map went with it — no such route was ever added.

**The travel guide's back control** — `<a href="#">` with `preventDefault`. Not dead, but an anchor doing a button's job: it announced itself as a link to assistive technology, and without JavaScript would have jumped to the top of the page. It is a `<button>` now, styled to read as the inline link it replaced.

## A guard, not just a fix

`__tests__/components/deadControls.test.ts` scans `app/` and `components/` for `href="#"` in each quoting form, so this cannot creep back into a view no test renders. It also guards itself: a broken directory walk would otherwise pass everything silently, so it asserts it found the files it claims to scan.

Closes the last remaining task on #68 — the one blocked until #69 gave search two legs that could fail independently.

## The problem

A round trip is two searches. They ran in sequence and shared a fate: a failure on the return threw away a perfectly good set of outbound results and showed a total failure instead.

## What changed

Both legs now run **together and fail apart**, via `Promise.allSettled`:

- **The outbound is the trip.** If it fails there is nothing to show, and the error stands as before. A return leg on its own is not something anyone can book.
- **The return is a second dependency.** Losing it degrades the result: the outbound results stay, and the return says it could not be loaded, with a retry.

The action's `inbound` becomes a discriminated union — `{ status: 'ok', … }`, `{ status: 'unavailable' }`, or `null` for one-way.

## "Unavailable" is not "none"

That state is deliberately distinct from a return date that genuinely has no flights. One means there is nothing to book; the other means we do not know. Telling a customer the first when the second is true is a lie about inventory, so they get different messages, and a test asserts the empty-list message does *not* appear in the degraded case.

With no return to choose, the outbound falls back to booking one leg at a time — the same thing an empty return list already does.

## Two things the rendered review turned up

I forced an inbound failure locally to see the real component at 390/768/1440 (reverted before committing; the diff on `app/actions.ts` is only the intended change).

- **The panel was translucent over a photographic background**, so the warning's contrast depended on the photo behind it. It is opaque now — the same fix as the round-trip CTA in #120.
- **The retry button had no visible focus ring at all.** Probing with real keyboard navigation showed `outline-style: none`. This app sets no focus style of its own, so a control that relies on the browser default gets nothing. I gave this control its own `:focus-visible` ring rather than leave it unreachable-looking; the wider gap is #80's, and I have not tried to fix it here.

Also confirmed by probe: the retry target is 46px tall and reachable by Tab.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 514 passed, 64 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

New coverage: two action tests (the return failing leaves the outbound intact; the outbound failing still throws) and four component tests (outbound survives with the right message, one-leg booking still offered, the warning clears when a retry succeeds, and the panel is announced as a live region). I confirmed the component tests are load-bearing by suppressing the degraded flag — all four fail.

## Not covered end to end

There is no Playwright case: the failure happens inside a server action, and forcing only the inbound query to fail from a browser is not something the test can reach without a seam that exists only for testing. The action tests cover the split, and the component tests cover the rendering.

Closes #124. The last place the app implied a return you could not actually get.

## Why it had to go

`FlightSchedule.returnTime` existed for one purpose: computing `Flight.returnDate` as departure + 7 days. That column went in #125, leaving this one collected from administrators, validated, stored, and shown on the schedule list as `Departs: 08:00 | Returns: 18:00` — while driving nothing.

Merely unused would have been harmless. This *invited a mistake*: an administrator filling it in reasonably expects return inventory, and gets none. Since #113 a route operates in both directions by having its own schedule each way, which is where a return's departure time actually lives.

## Nothing is lost

The seed already pairs each outbound schedule with a reverse-direction one departing at exactly the time `returnTime` named — CA101 carried `returnTime: '18:00'` and CA102 departs at `18:00`. The data this column held is already recorded as a real flight's departure time, which is the point: it was duplicating the reverse schedule, badly.

## A deleted test

`FlightScheduleService.test.ts` had a test I added in #125 asserting that a schedule carrying a return time produces a flight with no return date. With both columns gone it cannot express anything — there is no return time to carry — so it is deleted rather than adapted. The type system now prevents what it guarded.

- `npx prisma migrate deploy` + `npx prisma db seed` against an **empty** database (the check I got wrong in #125, where the seed's `findFirst` guard meant the failing path never ran): 9 schedules created, column absent
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

## Rendered evidence

I tried to screenshot the admin schedule page and spent too long fighting MFA enrolment for it. The better evidence — and a permanent one — is in `e2e/admin.spec.ts`, which already fills this form and renders this list in a real browser:

- the form offers no `#returnTime` input

The prerequisite #123 named: move the remaining readers off `Passenger.seatNumber` / `cabinClass` / `flightId`. It turned out to be three more live defects of the same family as #126, not a tidiness exercise.

## What was wrong

Those columns describe the **outbound** leg. Every reader that asked them about some other flight got the wrong answer.

**1. `getOccupiedSeatsAction` returned the outbound seat whichever flight it was asked about.** On a round trip the return leg's seat map showed a free seat as taken and the taken one as free — in the checkout wizard *and* the seat-change modal, both of which call it once per leg. A database test books `['11A', '17F']` and asserts the inbound answers `17F`; before this change it answered `11A`.

**2. `updateFlightSeatingLayout` could strand an occupied seat.** Its guard read `Flight.passengers`, which is `Passenger.flightId` and points at the outbound. Seats held on a flight as somebody's *return* leg were invisible to it, so shrinking that cabin was allowed. The new test shrinks economy under a held `25F` and, before this change, the update succeeds.

**3. The admin manifest listed outbound seat numbers on an inbound occurrence's manifest.**

All three now read `SeatAssignment`, which records a seat, a cabin and a flight together. `changeBookingSeatsAction` takes the cabin from the assignment on the leg being changed, for the same reason.

## Also removed

The occurrence generator included `passengers: { select: { seatNumber } }` on a flight lookup and never used it — only `.id` is read, and `updateFlightSeatingLayout` does that check itself.

## Compatibility

Each reader falls back to the passenger row when a leg has no assignment, so bookings taken before #118 still render. The columns are still written, matching how #107→#125 sequenced their contract steps: readers move first, the drop is a separate step once the change has been observed deployed.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 508 passed, 64 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

Two new `*.database.test.ts` files exercise the real code against real Postgres, and both fail against the previous behaviour — that is how defects 1 and 2 were found rather than assumed. The manifest shaping was extracted into `passengersSeatedOnLeg` so it could be unit-tested, including that one traveller's assignment never describes another.

## Scope of the rendered review

The admin manifest is the only rendered change, and its component is untouched — only the data feeding it moved. That is covered by the helper's unit tests plus the existing admin e2e, which renders the manifest. I did not add a round-trip case to `e2e/admin.spec.ts`: that spec is the one flaking in #121, and I would rather not load it further. The inbound-manifest case is therefore covered by unit tests, not a browser journey.

## Next

The columns are now unread except as fallbacks. Dropping them needs the dual writes in `changeBookingSeatsAction`, `cancelBookingAction` and `FlightBookingService` removed first, plus `safePassengerSelect` narrowed — then the migration.

pull_requests.body:
Closes #123. What I found while implementing it is worse than the issue described.

## A live data-corruption bug

`changeBookingSeatsAction` applied changes with:

```ts
await tx.seatAssignment.updateMany({
    where: { passengerId: change.passengerId },
    data: { seatNumber: change.seatNumber }
});
```

A traveller on a round trip has **one assignment per leg**, so that `where` matched both. Changing the outbound seat silently overwrote the seat they still held on the return with the outbound's new number. No unique index caught it, because the two rows are on different flights. Any round trip booked since #119 was exposed.

Occupancy had the same shape of fault: it was read from `Passenger.seatNumber`, which describes the outbound, so the return leg's seat map was validated against the wrong flight's seats entirely.

I reproduced both against a real database before changing anything, and confirmed the new tests fail if the `legId` scope is removed.

## The fix

A seat belongs to a flight, so a change names its leg:

- **Legs are resolved from the booking**, not trusted from the request — a leg id belonging to someone else's booking would otherwise move their seat.
- **Flights are locked in ascending id**, matching `FlightBookingService`, so two requests touching the same pair cannot deadlock.
- **Occupancy comes from `SeatAssignment`**, keyed by flight *and* seat together, excluding this booking's own rows.
- **Updates are scoped to `{ passengerId, legId }`.**

`Passenger.seatNumber` still describes the outbound while the column is written, so only an outbound change updates it.

## Validation moved with it

Both uniqueness rules were wrong for a multi-leg request: one traveller holds one seat *per leg*, so the same passenger legitimately appears once per leg; and two legs are two flights, so the same seat number on each is not a clash. Both are now keyed by leg, and the request cap rises from nine to nine per leg.

## The modal

It gains the leg switcher the checkout wizard already has, with each leg's own occupancy, cabin layout, and seat choice — so the return seat is changeable rather than merely visible (#122 made it visible).

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 501 passed, 62 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

New coverage: a `*.database.test.ts` exercising the real action against real Postgres (the named leg moves, the other survives, and the vacated seat is genuinely retakeable by another booking under the unique index), a component test that the modal shows and submits a different seat per leg, and four validation cases including "the same seat on two legs must be accepted".

The round-trip e2e now continues past booking into the modal, switches to the return leg, changes that seat, and asserts in the database that the outbound seat is untouched.

## One process note

I committed this to `main` by mistake — I went straight from merging #125 into this work without branching. Caught it before pushing: the commit is on `fix/change-seats-per-leg` and local `main` is reset to `origin/main`. Nothing was pushed to `main`.

## Still outstanding

`Passenger.seatNumber` / `cabinClass` / `flightId` are written but no longer authoritative. #123 noted contracting them would remove the ambiguity about which column this action should write, and it still would — the dual write above is the last thing keeping them alive. Slice 3c-ii of #69, and the contract step for the round-trip model.

## What the column was

`Flight.returnDate` never described a return someone could hold. Every flight the application generates wrote it as **exactly seven days after departure** whenever the schedule carried a `returnTime` — a fixed offset, not an inbound flight, and nothing a customer chose could change it.

A round trip is now two flights: #112 searches the return direction on its own route and date, #113 gave those routes inventory, #118/#119 book both legs as one itinerary. The return someone holds is a row in `ItineraryLeg`.

#122 removed the last reader. This removes the three writers — two schedule occurrence generators in `app/actions.ts`, one in `FlightScheduleService` — plus the field in the static seed data, and drops the column.

## The branch that invented the date was never tested

The one generator test that created a flight used a **one-way** schedule (`returnTime: null`), so the code computing departure + 7 days ran in no test at all. A schedule carrying a return time is now asserted to produce a flight with no return date. I confirmed that test fails if the write is reinstated.

## Two things the pre-push review caught that I had missed

Recording these because both were real and my own verification had not found them:

1. **`lib/data/FlightData.ts` still carried `returnDate`**, and the seed spreads that object straight into `prisma.flight.create`. My "the seed still runs" check was worthless: the seed guards each static flight with a `findFirst`, and those five rows already existed in my database, so the failing `create` never executed. Verified properly this time against a **fresh** database, where that path does run — all five static flights are created and the column is absent.

2. **My migration comment claimed every value was reproducible as departure + 7 days.** That is true of generated inventory but false for the hand-written seed rows, whose gaps are 7, 10, 10 and 14 days, with one NULL. The comment now records what is actually lost rather than implying nothing is.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean — it found a third writer my grep had missed (`FlightScheduleService`, whose own comment named #69 as the gap)
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 498 passed, 61 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx prisma migrate deploy` + `npx prisma db seed` against an empty database
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

Note on method: `git stash` does not revert an applied migration, so on this branch it cannot be used to check whether a failure predates the change. I did not rely on it here.

## Left in place

`FlightSchedule.returnTime` now drives nothing, but is still collected, validated, stored, and displayed on the admin schedule list as `Departs: 08:00 | Returns: 18:00`. An administrator filling it in reasonably expects return inventory; they get none. That is the same fiction one level up, and removing it touches the admin form, its validation, and another migration — so it is #124 rather than bundled here.

Slice 3c-i of #69. A round trip could be searched (#120), booked (#119), and stored as two legs (#118) — but the profile still showed it as one flight.

## The gap

Every read went through `outboundFlight()`, and the seat came from `Passenger.seatNumber`, which only ever described the outbound. The return leg and the seat held on it were invisible to the person who booked them.

## One row per leg

Each leg is now its own `<tr>`, with price, status and actions spanning them via `rowSpan`, and one `<tbody>` per booking grouping the legs.

I first rendered three parallel lists inside a single row, one per column. That looked correct at 1440px and fell apart at 390px: the route text wraps to three lines while the flight text wraps to two, so a leg no longer lined up with its own route and date. Letting the table do the alignment is what actually fixes it — matched line heights were never going to hold.

Seats come from each leg's own `SeatAssignment`, falling back to `Passenger.seatNumber` so bookings taken before per-leg seats still render. A cancelled seat's `CANCELLED-*` placeholder exists to satisfy the unique index — it now reads as "Released" instead of being printed at the customer.

## `Flight.returnDate` is no longer rendered

The outbound card showed it as the arrival-side date. It was a fixed seven days after departure, described no real return, and — since #120 — sat directly above the actual return flight's card showing that same date. The arrival side now shows just the destination, matching the return card.

That was the column's **last reader**. `ProfileClient` and `FlightStatusBoard` only mention it in an interface; nothing else reads it. Dropping the column is now a schema-only slice.

## Two stylesheet bugs this exposed

- `.profile td` set `padding: 16px 0`. That rule outranks a utility class, so the `pr-6` I first reached for did nothing and columns ran together (`Paris, France8/3/2026`, `$1,900Confirmed`). The gutter belongs in the stylesheet that claimed the property.
- Its top border drew between the legs of a single booking, making one itinerary look like two bookings. Continuation rows now suppress it, so the rule falls between bookings.

Both are visible in the before/after screenshots I took at 390/768/1440 against a real round trip booked through the UI.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings in untouched files)
- `npm test` — 497 passed, 61 suites
- `npm run build` clean
- `npx playwright test` — 25 passed

New coverage: five component tests (every leg in order, the seat per leg, the round-trip/one-way label, the pre-per-leg fallback, and the released-seat marker), one asserting the outbound card carries no return date, and the round-trip e2e now continues to the profile and checks both flight numbers, both routes, and the seat held on each leg.

I verified the per-leg seat lookup is load-bearing by reverting it to `Passenger.seatNumber`: exactly the two tests that cover it fail.

## Not in this slice

**Change Seats still edits the outbound only.** It opens `outboundFlight(booking)` and seeds from `Passenger.seatNumber`, so on a round trip you can change your departing seat and not your returning one. This PR is display; making that mutation per-leg is its own slice and I did not want to bundle a seat-changing behaviour change into it. Filed as #123.

Dropping the `Flight.returnDate` column (expand/contract migration) is 3c-ii.
