issues.title: Prisma error logs can put customer data on stdout in production
issues.body:
Found during the roadmap investigation and **verified against observed output**.

## The problem

`lib/prisma.ts` configures stdout logging:

```ts
const logLevels: Prisma.LogLevel[] =
    process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'
        ? ['query', 'warn', 'error']
        : ['warn', 'error'];
```

The comment correctly reasons that `query` carries bind parameters and excludes it outside development. But **`error` also carries customer data**, because Postgres error details embed the offending row.

## Evidence

Observed in this repository's own e2e output:

```
ConnectorError(... message: "new row for relation \"User\" violates check constraint
\"User_email_canonical_check\"", detail: Some("Failing row contains
(cmscbchtn0006sizjhse9nkks, Mixed Case, Mixed-1785706161200-9a21e78b2e76b@Example.com,
null, null, not-used, USER, 0, null, null, null)")
```

That is an email address on stdout, from a log level that is enabled in production.

`SECURITY.md` requires raw tokens stay out of logs. The same reasoning applies to email addresses and to any encrypted-column ciphertext that appears in a failing row.

## Fix

Move to event-based logging so the payload can be shaped before it is emitted:

```ts
new PrismaClient({ log: [{ emit: 'event', level: 'warn' }, { emit: 'event', level: 'error' }] })
```

then subscribe and log a redacted record — error code, model, and operation, without `detail`. Keep stdout `query` in development as today.

## Test

A unit test asserting the client is constructed with `emit: 'event'` for error, plus one asserting the handler drops `detail`, would hold this in place. `__tests__/security/` is the established home for this kind of check.
issues.display_title: Prisma error logs can put customer data on stdout in production

issues.title: Jest: passenger retention test races the app's boot-time purge sweep
issues.body:
`__tests__/lib/passengerDataProtection.database.test.ts` fails intermittently when Jest runs alongside anything that boots the app (a dev server, a Playwright run):

```
✕ stores only ciphertext, returns only safe fields, and purges on expiry
  expect(received).resolves.toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(expected)
  Expected: >= 1
  Received:    0
```

## Why

The test back-dates its own passenger to `2026-01-01` and then asserts that its own call purged at least one row:

```ts
await expect(purgeExpiredPassengerData(new Date('2026-01-02T00:00:00.000Z')))
    .resolves.toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
```

`instrumentation.ts:28` runs `purgeExpiredPassengerData()` on **every** dev-server boot, and that sweep is unfiltered — a global `updateMany` over every passenger whose `sensitiveDataExpiresAt` has passed. Whichever runs first claims the row, so the loser counts zero.

The assertion is a global count, which makes it wrong in both directions: fragile (an unrelated sweep can steal its row) and weak (an unrelated expired row would satisfy it).

## Observed

Twice during work on #147/#148, both times on the first `npm test` immediately following a Playwright suite; passed on every re-run. Reproduced deliberately by running the boot sweep's SQL in a loop against the test — 1 of 3 attempts failed.

The other `*.database.test.ts` files are not exposed: they scope their deletes by id, and `authTokens.database.test.ts` uses a future expiry plus a `TEMP TABLE` probe.

## Suggested fix

Scope the assertion to the test's own passenger id rather than a global count — that fixes the fragility and the weakness together.

## Note

Distinct from #121, which is a Playwright timing issue.
issues.display_title: Jest: passenger retention test races the app's boot-time purge sweep

issues.title: Round-trip checkout review shows one leg and unlabelled seats
issues.body:
Found while picking up the roadmap plan in #143, which reports this defect as the most-reported finding of the investigation (8 of 12 areas raised it independently). **Verification status:** confirmed by reading the source. Not yet reproduced by hand in a browser — the runtime confirmation is the first step of the fix. ## Where `components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1163` — step 3, "Review Booking". ## What happens The wizard tracks the itinerary as `flights` and the seat step walks it one leg at a time (`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:74`): ```ts const flight = flights[activeLegIndex]; ``` Step 3 then renders the trip summary from that single `flight`: ```tsx
{flight.airline} {flight.flightNumber}
{flight.from} → {flight.to}
Departure: {new Date(flight.departureDate).toLocaleDateString()}
``` So on a round trip the review page shows **one flight card**, for whichever leg was last active, rather than the itinerary the customer is about to buy. The passenger rows below it have the matching problem: ```tsx Seat{p.seatNumbers.length > 1 ? 's' : ''}: {p.seatNumbers.join(', ')} ``` `seatNumbers` spans every leg, joined into one comma list with nothing saying which seat belongs to which flight. A customer reviewing a Seattle→Tokyo→Seattle booking sees one leg and two unlabelled seat numbers. ## Why it matters This is the last screen before money is committed, on the primary revenue path. The customer cannot check the return leg or confirm which seat they hold on it. ## The fix already exists one step away The confirmation step was fixed for this during the round-trip work and carries the reasoning in a comment at `components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1244`: a seat belongs to a leg, so a card naming one flight can only carry that flight's seat. Review was missed. The fix is to apply the same per-leg card treatment to step 3. ## Timing #143 flags this as worth fixing before #81 splits the checkout wizard into modules, or the defect gets baked into two files instead of one. ## Test A Playwright assertion on the review step of a round-trip booking — both flight numbers present, each seat rendered against its own leg — would hold it in place. `components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` already has round-trip journey coverage to extend.
issues.display_title: Round-trip checkout review shows one leg and unlabelled seats

issues.title: /flights loads every flight row into the RSC payload
issues.body:
Found while picking up the roadmap plan in #143.

**Verification status:** confirmed by reading the source. The row count below is
#143's estimate and has not been measured against a seeded database.

## Where

`app/flights/page.tsx:14`

## What happens

```ts
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

export default async function FlightsPage() {
    const flights = await prisma.flight.findMany({
        orderBy: { departureDate: 'asc' }
    });

    return <FlightStatusBoard flights={flights} />;
}
```

No `where`, no `take`. Every row in `Flight` is loaded and serialized into the RSC
payload on every request — the page is `force-dynamic`, so nothing caches it either.
#143 estimates roughly 1,459 rows against the current seed, and that number grows
with every schedule occurrence generated.

## Why it matters

A flight *status* board is a question about now: what is departing today, what is
delayed, what is cancelled. Shipping the entire historical and future table to the
browser is both a payload problem that scales with the data and the wrong answer to
the user's question — departed flights from weeks ago sort to the top.

## Fix

Bound the query to the window the board actually shows — a date range around now —
and add a `take` as a backstop. The board's own presentation of what window it is
showing should match whatever bound is chosen.

Worth confirming against `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx` what window the
component already assumes before picking one.

## Test

An integration test asserting the query is bounded — that a flight far outside the
window is not returned — would keep the bound from being dropped later.
issues.display_title: /flights loads every flight row into the RSC payload

issues.title: Should getOccupiedSeatsAction require a session?
issues.body:
Found while picking up the roadmap plan in #143, which lists it as an unverified
finding. **This is a question before it is a bug** — the answer is a product
decision, and the code may well be correct as written.

**Verification status:** the missing session check is confirmed by reading the
source. Whether it is a defect is exactly what this issue is asking.

## Where

`app/actions.ts:318`

## What it does

```ts
export async function getOccupiedSeatsAction(flightId: number) {
    flightId = parseInput(numericIdSchema, flightId);
    const assignments = await prisma.seatAssignment.findMany({
        where: {
            flightId,
            leg: { booking: { status: { not: "CANCELLED" } } }
        },
        select: { seatNumber: true }
    });
    return assignments.map(seat => seat.seatNumber);
}
```

Unlike its neighbours in the same file — `toggleFavoriteCityGuideAction` at
`app/actions.ts:335` is the adjacent example — it calls no `getServerSession` and
performs no authorization. Any caller who can reach the server action endpoint can
enumerate seat occupancy for any `flightId`.

## What it discloses

Seat numbers only. It selects `seatNumber` and nothing else: no passenger name, no
booking reference, no user identity. The disclosure is "seat 14C on flight 812 is
taken" — load factor and occupancy patterns per flight, and nothing that identifies
a person.

## The decision

Adding a session check is a one-line change, but it is **not** a free hardening fix:
the seat map needs occupancy to render, so gating this action means an unauthenticated
visitor cannot see a seat map before signing in. That is a funnel change on the
booking path, not a security cleanup.

Three defensible outcomes:

1. **Leave it public and document it.** Occupancy is arguably public-facing product
   data, the way a cinema seat map is. Add a comment at the call site saying the
   omission is deliberate so the next reader does not "fix" it.
2. **Gate it.** Accept that seat maps require a session, and confirm nothing in the
   pre-auth journey renders one.
3. **Rate-limit rather than gate.** Keeps the funnel and blunts bulk enumeration.

## Why it needs an answer either way

Right now the omission is indistinguishable from an oversight. Whichever way it
goes, the outcome should be visible in the code — a check or a comment explaining
its absence — so this does not get re-raised by every future review.
issues.display_title: Should getOccupiedSeatsAction require a session?

issues.title: Aborting a navigation logs a failed notifications fetch
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for #73 step 2a. **Pre-existing** — present on pre-change `HEAD` too.

## What was observed

`Failed to load notifications: TypeError: Failed to fetch` (and `network error`) in the browser console when a navigation aborts the notifications server action while it is in flight. No React warnings, no `pageerror`, and no hydration mismatch accompanied it on any journey.

## Why it matters

Minor on its own, but it is an aborted request being reported as a failure. It trains anyone reading the console to ignore that line, and once real error reporting exists (#87) it becomes a stream of alerts for users navigating normally. The fix is to distinguish an abort from a failure and stay quiet on the former.
issues.display_title: Aborting a navigation logs a failed notifications fetch

issues.title: Playwright silently reuses a stale dev server and reports a false failure
issues.body:
Cost real time during #73 step 2a, and produced a **false regression signal** — verified against running code.

## Where

`playwright.config.ts:36-42`:

```ts
webServer: {
  command: 'npm run dev',
  url: 'http://localhost:3000',
  reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  ...
}
```

## What was observed

`e2e/admin.spec.ts:75` failed 3 runs out of 3 at line 244 — the flight was on the board but its status was never `Delayed`. The same spec passed on `HEAD`. That looks exactly like a regression in the branch, and I started bisecting the diff on that basis.

It was not a regression. A dev server left running from an earlier full-suite run was being reused, and it was serving stale output. After `pkill -f "next dev"`, the unchanged branch passed the spec 3 runs out of 3 and the full suite passed 28/28.

The bisect was worthless for a second reason that follows from the same line: because `webServer` runs `npm run dev`, `npm run build` before a Playwright run changes nothing about what is served. Reverting a file and rebuilding appeared to fix the failure when all it did was restart the server.

## Why it matters

Two failure modes, and the second is the dangerous one:

- A stale server makes a healthy branch look broken, which is where the time goes.
- A stale server can equally make a **broken branch look healthy** — the suite reports a pass against code that is not the code under test. `reuseExistingServer` is off in CI, so this is local-only, but local is where the pre-push decision gets made.

## Suggested fix

Either set `reuseExistingServer: false` outright, or keep the reuse and have the config assert the server is the current one — the runbook note alone is not enough, because nothing surfaces at the point of confusion. Related: #173, where the same line came up alongside e2e cleanup.
issues.display_title: Playwright silently reuses a stale dev server and reports a false failure

issues.title: Notification drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone
issues.body:
Found during the `ui-review` for the test-infrastructure cleanup. **Pre-existing**, measured against running code at 390x844.

## Where

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx:201-311` renders the drawer `position: absolute` inside `header nav ul li`. At `max-width: 600px`, `app/globals.css:887-891` sets `header nav { overflow-x: auto }` — and per spec that forces `overflow-y: auto` too, so the drawer is clipped by the 56px-tall nav.

## What was observed

```
nav:    clientHeight 56, scrollHeight 429, overflowX auto, overflowY auto
drawer: height 389 (top 96, bottom 485)
visible drawer height: 16px
```

`document.elementFromPoint` at the drawer's centre returns the hero `H1`, not the drawer. A signed-in user with 5 unread taps the bell and sees a bare sliver — no notification text, no "Mark all read", no empty state. Same on the admin header.

## Why it matters

The clicks still land (the badge counted down when they were forced), so this is a paint/clip failure rather than a dead control — which is worse, because a user cannot see what they are tapping. The whole feature is unusable on a phone.

Belongs to #79 (P3.2 responsive layouts).
issues.display_title: Notification drawer is clipped to 16 visible pixels on phone

issues.title: A dead dev server now makes the notification poll fail in silence
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` while checking #195's fix. **Introduced by that fix**, and recorded rather than widened into it.

## Where

`components/ui/titlebar.tsx:37-50`. The poll suppresses `console.error` when the rejection's message is one a browser produces for a torn-down request.

## Why the set is not enough

Those strings are correctly identified, but they are not exclusive to navigation. Verified in real Chromium, none of these involving a navigation:

| Scenario | Message |
|---|---|
| server unreachable | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| connection reset before response | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| server dies mid-body | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` |
| response stream fails mid-read (how React's Flight client consumes a server action) | `TypeError: network error` |

So a crashed, killed or restarting dev server now produces **no console output at all**, where it previously printed every 3 seconds.

## Why it matters

#195 was about not crying wolf. This is the opposite failure, and it is the case where a developer most wants the noise — the server they are running is gone and nothing says so.

## The fix

The message cannot carry the signal; whether *this* poll was torn down can. An `AbortController` aborted in the `useEffect` cleanup at `titlebar.tsx:95-99`, or an unmounted flag checked in the `catch`, makes the suppression precise and lets the closed string set go entirely.

Related: #209 (the drawer claims "You're all caught up!" when loading has failed) — together they mean a failed poll is invisible in both the console and the UI.
issues.display_title: A dead dev server now makes the notification poll fail in silence

issues.title: travelguide e2e leaks a user, review and favorite on every run
issues.body:
Found by the `verifier` during the run-isolation cleanup. Same class as #173, which the cleanup did not cover.

## What was observed

After the cleanup, bookings are clean (0) and flights are clean (1412, all seed). But the development database holds **37 `User`, 14 `Review` and 14 `UserFavorite` rows**, all `guidetest-*`.

`e2e/travelguide.spec.ts` has no `afterAll`, so each run adds another set. `booking.spec.ts` and its neighbours do clean up after themselves.

## Why it matters

The suite passes at this accumulation — two full green runs prove it, which does substantiate the "leftover accounts are harmless" reasoning in `e2e/global-setup.ts`. But it grows without bound, and it is the same rot #173 described: a database that quietly diverges from a fresh one until something starts failing for a reason nobody connects to it.

`global-setup` deliberately does not delete users, because it cannot tell a run's account from a developer's. A spec deleting the account it created itself has no such problem — which is what the other specs already do.
issues.display_title: travelguide e2e leaks a user, review and favorite on every run

issues.title: Database test serialisation depends on how Jest is invoked, not on the config
issues.body:
Found while addressing Codex review on #214 — by tripping over it repeatedly.

## Where

`package.json:15` — `"test:database": "npx jest --selectProjects database --runInBand"`.

`jest.config.js` splits the projects and documents at length why the database files must not run beside each other, but the config itself does not enforce it. `--runInBand` in the npm script is the only thing that serialises them.

## What was observed

Running `npx jest --selectProjects database` directly — which looks equivalent, and which the config's own comment does not warn against — runs those files in parallel. That reproduces exactly the interference #155 was filed for:

```
● the route a page renders › comes from the airports on the admin dashboard
  Expected substring: "RTE-66f9eabc"
```

`runIsolation.database.test.ts` calls `clearPreviousRunBookings()`, which deletes every booking by design, while `routeRenderSources.database.test.ts` is holding a fixture booking open. Intermittent: it passed on the immediately following run.

Verified: `npm run test:database` passes 3 runs of 3.

## Why it matters

The split exists so a whole-table assertion cannot count another file's fixtures. That guarantee currently holds only if you type the right command — and the wrong command is the shorter, more obvious one. It cost me several confusing failures in one session, each of which looked like a real regression in the code under review.

`jest` does not support a per-project `maxWorkers`, so the fix is not a one-liner. Options worth weighing: a `globalSetup` for the database project that refuses to run when it detects parallelism; a top-level `maxWorkers: 1` (correct but slows the 64-suite unit project); or a `testSequencer`/wrapper that makes the direct invocation fail loudly with a pointer to the script.

Related: #155 (the original collisions), and the note in `AGENTS.md` under Gotchas that already tells agents to use the scripts.

issues.title: Profile bookings table at phone width hides the status, and the seat cell fails AA
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` while checking the seat-release change (#76 slice 2). All three are
pre-existing and none is caused by that change, which is why they are here rather than
in the pull request. Verified against the rendered application at 390x844, 768x1024 and
1440x900.

## The Status column is scrolled out of view at phone width

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:319` wraps the bookings table in `overflow-x-auto`. At
390x844 the wrapper is 316px holding 490px of content, and the Status cell sits at
x 376–462 — entirely past the visible right edge at 353.

Two bookings for the same flight then look identical except that one seat cell reads
`Alan (11A)` and the other `Grace (Released)`. There is no visible "Cancelled", and the
absence of the Change Seats / Cancel buttons is not visible either. At tablet and
desktop the word "Cancelled" is present and the non-colour indication is fine.

The wrapper has no `tabindex` and no `role`, so a keyboard-only user cannot scroll it to
reach the status at all — WCAG 2.1.1 for scrollable regions.

## The seat cell fails AA contrast

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:359` — `color: rgba(255,255,255,0.4)` at `0.75rem`.
Measured in page, `Grace (Released)` composites to **3.80:1** against `rgb(13,12,20)`;
AA needs 4.5:1 at that size. `Ada (11A)` is the same.

This matters more than it did: after #76 slice 2 the word "Released" is the only thing
distinguishing a released seat from a live one, and at phone width (above) it is the
only thing on the row that does. Roughly `0.62` alpha, or `#9ca3af`, clears AA.

## "Released" is not conveyed as seat information

The accessible name of the row is
`One way Mona Airways MA405 Grace (Released) Paris, France → Chicago, USA …` — the word
"Seat" appears nowhere, visible or accessible, and the happy path reads `Ada (11A)` with
the same problem. A screen reader user gets no signal that the parenthetical is a seat.

`ProfileClient.tsx:361` builds it as `${p.firstName} (${seatFor(...)})`. The pattern to
copy is the visually-hidden caption `CAPTION_FOR_SCREEN_READERS` in
`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx`.

## Related

Same family as #200 (admin tables squeezed at phone width) and #199 (e-ticket caption
contrast), but a different screen; not a duplicate of either.

issues.title: At phone width the disruption notice and its action are unreachable without scrolling sideways
issues.body:
Follow-on from the #229/#208 fix, and deliberately not fixed there. Measured by
`ui-review` and confirmed by the `verifier` at 390x844 on a DISRUPTED booking.

## What was observed

The fix made the *status* visible at phone width — it now renders beside the flight
number, so a disrupted booking is no longer pixel-identical to a confirmed one. What did
not move is everything the customer needs in order to act:

```
status cell        left 368 / right 458   (viewport 390 — a 22px sliver)
"Your seat is held. Cancel for a full refund, with no cancellation fee."  — inside that cell
Cancel button      left 563 / right 619
region scrollWidth 582 / clientWidth 316
```

So the phone user learns the airline cancelled their flight and cannot take the refund
without discovering a horizontal scroll. There is no visible affordance for it:
`offsetHeight === clientHeight`, so no scrollbar gutter, and where a scrollbar is drawn
`app/globals.css:1146` paints the thumb `#2b2640` on a `#0d0c14` track — roughly 1.4:1.

Keyboard users can reach it: the region is focusable now and arrow keys scroll it.

## Why it was not fixed in that slice

It is a pre-existing layout constraint, not a regression — before the fix the customer
could not see the status either, so nothing that worked has been removed. The verifier's
judgement was the same: a strict improvement, file rather than widen.

## What would fix it

The bookings table wants a card layout below `sm`, the way the rest of Phase 3 (#79)
handles narrow widths — flight, route, status and actions stacked, no horizontal scroll
at all. Patching the current table would mean choosing which of route, price and actions
to sacrifice.

Related: #200 (admin tables at phone width), #193 (checkout scrolls horizontally at
390px) — same shape, same phase.

issues.title: Seat buttons have no usable accessible name
issues.body:
Found by `ui-review` during #74 slice 1. Pre-existing, but that slice makes it
matter more.

## What was observed

Aria snapshot of a seat button on the checkout seat map:

```
- button "A" [disabled]     (occupied)
- button "A"                (free)
```

The `title="Seat 11A Occupied"` never becomes the accessible name: text content
wins under accname, and the button's text is the single seat letter. A screen
reader user hears "A, button, unavailable" — no row, no seat number, no reason.

## Why it matters more now

#74 added an error that says "Seat 11A is being held by another customer while
they check out. Please choose a different one." That message is announced
correctly via `role="alert"`. So the one group of users who reliably *receive*
the instruction is the group that cannot then locate 11A on the map, because no
seat announces its number.

Before this change the seat map was merely hard to use with a screen reader.
Now a recoverable error depends on it.

## What would fix it

`aria-label` on the seat button carrying row, letter and state — "Seat 11A,
available" / "Seat 11A, occupied" — since `title` cannot win against text
content. Worth checking the same pattern in the profile seat-change modal,
which renders seats the same way.

Verified against the running application with a Chromium aria snapshot.

## Status: steps 1 and 2 are complete, and the prerequisite is done

Recording this against the repo so the plan does not drift from it. This plan was written at `110cf2d`; `main` is now `ff2730d`.

### Step 1 — contract steps

Both closed before this run: #135 (drop the flight and schedule price strings) in #145, #137 (drop `Passenger.seatNumber`, `cabinClass`, `flightId`) in #147.

### Step 2 — cheap correctness fixes: **empty**

| Issue | Delivered |
|---|---|
| #142 Prisma error logs leak customer data | #164 |
| #140 logo asset carries the old identity | #174 |
| #152 round-trip review shows one leg | #161 |
| #153 `/flights` loads every flight row | #168 |
| #154 `getOccupiedSeatsAction` has no session check | #176 |
| #155 `seatAssignmentCoverage` flake | #166 |
| #158 boarding pass says GEMINI AIRWAYS | #170 |
| #160 third copy of the leg direction label | #172 |
| #169 raw cabin enum on the e-ticket | #179 |

Everything named in the "most-reported defect" and "other unverified findings" sections is now either fixed or filed. The round-trip review defect was real, and the e2e assertion covering it (`text=Seats: 11A, 12C`) had passed throughout its life — a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats are paired with the right legs.

The one finding from this plan still unverified is **itineraries whose legs are out of order or do not connect**. Nobody has looked at it, so it is deliberately not filed.

### The prerequisite this plan named — done

> Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines in four files into one function.

Done in #180. One correction: it is **four** sites, not five. `searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled *flights* out of search results, which reads almost identically and answers a different question — a cancelled flight is not a released seat.

It landed as a function rather than an object to spread, because a caller's own `leg` key written after a spread compiles cleanly and silently removes the booking filter from the SQL. Applied last, the rule cannot be dropped by accident.

## #73 is much smaller than it reads

Five of its seven tasks are already delivered by work since this plan was written:

| Task | State |
|---|---|
| Airports with IATA code, country, IANA timezone | **Done** — `model Airport`, `lib/airports.ts` |
| Schedules separate from dated instances | **Done** — `FlightSchedule` + `Flight` |
| Itinerary and itinerary-leg models | **Done** — `ItineraryLeg` (#118) |
| Money as integer minor units | **Done** — `priceCents`, `totalPriceCents` (#134, #144, #145) |
| Traveler and seat-assignment records | **Done** — `Passenger`, `SeatAssignment` |
| **Typed cabin, fare, currency, booking, payment, flight, notification statuses** | **Not started** |
| Migration plan, rollback, recovery | Ongoing discipline |

`Booking.status`, `Flight.status`, `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` and `currency` are all bare `String`. `Role` is the only real enum in the schema. That is not abstract cleanup: verification during #169 established that `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no check constraint and no Postgres enum**, so the four-cabin guarantee is Zod at the booking boundary and nothing else.

## A correction to the ownership table's neighbourhood

I was about to recommend "typed statuses" as the next slice under #73. That would have walked into exactly the collision this plan exists to prevent — the table above assigns **`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**, with #73 and #75 as consumers.

So the split is:

- **#76 owns** `Booking.status` typing. Leave it.
- **#73 owns** `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK. That one needs the decision below.
- **Nobody owns** `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` or `Flight.status` typing. Those are free to take now, and `cabinClass` has the evidence behind it.

## Decisions: take them just in time

Six are listed here, belonging to four different slices. Deciding all of them now means committing months ahead of the code, and this plan's own premises have already drifted in a fortnight. Only one is needed to start #73:

> must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?

The cancellation policy table and staff-cancel behaviour belong to #76, hold TTL and timing to #74, authorize-vs-capture to #75, and document attestation to #77. Each is better answered by whoever opens that slice.

## Not in this plan, and worth adding to it

The test infrastructure is not ready for the volume. Four distinct shared-resource failures surfaced in one run: #155 (a parallel Jest flake which turned out to be a **vacuous** assertion — the scan it performed had been counting zero rows for its entire life), #173 (e2e seats stranded by an interrupted run), #178 (`booking.spec.ts:267` has ~12s of headroom and times out on a cold run), plus #165.

Phase 3 alone is ~40 PRs. Every one pays that tax, and every red run for an unrelated reason erodes the signal that tells you a real regression happened. Worth clearing before the volume rather than during.

## Filed along the way

Not part of any phase, all found by verification rather than by looking for them: #156, #159, #162, #163, #165, #167, #171, #173, #175, #177, #178.

| #152 round-trip review shows one leg | #161 |
| #153 `/flights` loads every flight row | #168 |
| #154 `getOccupiedSeatsAction` has no session check | #176 |
| #155 `seatAssignmentCoverage` flake | #166 |
| #158 boarding pass says GEMINI AIRWAYS | #170 |
| #160 third copy of the leg direction label | #172 |
| #169 raw cabin enum on the e-ticket | #179 |

Everything named in the "most-reported defect" and "other unverified findings" sections is now either fixed or filed. The round-trip review defect was real, and the e2e assertion covering it (`text=Seats: 11A, 12C`) had passed throughout its life — a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats are paired with the right legs.

The one finding from this plan still unverified is **itineraries whose legs are out of order or do not connect**. Nobody has looked at it, so it is deliberately not filed.

### The prerequisite this plan named — done

> Extracting them into one `lib/seatOccupancy.ts` predicate first turns twelve lines in four files into one function.

Done in #180. One correction: it is **four** sites, not five. `searchFlightsAction` filters cancelled *flights* out of search results, which reads almost identically and answers a different question — a cancelled flight is not a released seat.

It landed as a function rather than an object to spread, because a caller's own `leg` key written after a spread compiles cleanly and silently removes the booking filter from the SQL. Applied last, the rule cannot be dropped by accident.

## #73 is much smaller than it reads

Five of its seven tasks are already delivered by work since this plan was written:

| Task | State |
|---|---|
| Airports with IATA code, country, IANA timezone | **Done** — `model Airport`, `lib/airports.ts` |
| Schedules separate from dated instances | **Done** — `FlightSchedule` + `Flight` |
| Itinerary and itinerary-leg models | **Done** — `ItineraryLeg` (#118) |
| Money as integer minor units | **Done** — `priceCents`, `totalPriceCents` (#134, #144, #145) |
| Traveler and seat-assignment records | **Done** — `Passenger`, `SeatAssignment` |
| **Typed cabin, fare, currency, booking, payment, flight, notification statuses** | **Not started** |
| Migration plan, rollback, recovery | Ongoing discipline |

`Booking.status`, `Flight.status`, `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` and `currency` are all bare `String`. `Role` is the only real enum in the schema. That is not abstract cleanup: verification during #169 established that `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with **no check constraint and no Postgres enum**, so the four-cabin guarantee is Zod at the booking boundary and nothing else.

## A correction to the ownership table's neighbourhood

I was about to recommend "typed statuses" as the next slice under #73. That would have walked into exactly the collision this plan exists to prevent — the table above assigns **`Booking.status` typing + status history to #76**, with #73 and #75 as consumers.

So the split is:

- **#76 owns** `Booking.status` typing. Leave it.
- **#73 owns** `Flight.from/to` → `Airport` FK. That one needs the decision below.
- **Nobody owns** `SeatAssignment.cabinClass` or `Flight.status` typing. Those are free to take now, and `cabinClass` has the evidence behind it.

## Decisions: take them just in time

Six are listed here, belonging to four different slices. Deciding all of them now means committing months ahead of the code, and this plan's own premises have already drifted in a fortnight. Only one is needed to start #73:

> must already-shared search URLs (`?from=Seattle%2C+USA`) keep working after the switch to IATA codes, or may they 404?

The cancellation policy table and staff-cancel behaviour belong to #76, hold TTL and timing to #74, authorize-vs-capture to #75, and document attestation to #77. Each is better answered by whoever opens that slice.

## Not in this plan, and worth adding to it

The test infrastructure is not ready for the volume. Four distinct shared-resource failures surfaced in one run: #155 (a parallel Jest flake which turned out to be a **vacuous** assertion — the scan it performed had been counting zero rows for its entire life), #173 (e2e seats stranded by an interrupted run), #178 (`booking.spec.ts:267` has ~12s of headroom and times out on a cold run), plus #165.

Phase 3 alone is ~40 PRs. Every one pays that tax, and every red run for an unrelated reason erodes the signal that tells you a real regression happened. Worth clearing before the volume rather than during.

## Filed along the way

Not part of any phase, all found by verification rather than by looking for them: #156, #159, #162, #163, #165, #167, #171, #173, #175, #177, #178.

comments.body:
## Decisions, and what is already here

Recording the two answers this issue was waiting on, plus what reading the code first
turned up — because this is not greenfield.

### What already ships

`app/actions.ts:428` cancels a booking transactionally today: it locks the flights in
ascending order, releases the seats, sets the status and notifies. What it has no
concept of is **eligibility**. So two of this issue's tasks are live defects rather
than missing features:

- A customer can cancel **after the flight departed** — releasing a seat on a flown
  flight and deducting status points for a trip they took.
- Staff can set a flight to `CANCELLED` (`app/actions.ts:986`) and the bookings **stay
  `CONFIRMED`, still holding their seats**. The only consequence is a notification, so
  the customer keeps a boarding pass for a flight that is not operating.

Both read from the source; neither is confirmed against a running app yet.

Also relevant to the tasks above: `Booking.status` is a bare `String` with no enum and
no check constraint (`lib/seatOccupancy.ts:27` says so, and that literal is the whole
definition), and seats are released by renaming them to `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` to
dodge the unique index — which is why `lib/bookingItinerary.ts:82` has to translate the
placeholder back into the word "Released" for display.

### Cancellation policy

| Cabin | Before 24h | Inside 24h | After departure |
|---|---|---|---|
| First, Business | Full refund | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Premium Economy, Economy | Refund minus 20% | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Any, flight `DISRUPTED` | Full refund, no fee, no cut-off | | |

- **Percentage, not flat.** `Booking.currency` already exists, so a flat fee is wrong
  the moment a booking is not in USD and needs FX to stay right. A percentage of
  `totalPriceCents` needs neither. Rounding is floor, in minor units, stated here so
  tests pin it rather than inheriting whatever the implementation did first.
- **Cancellation stays allowed inside the cut-off, at zero refund.** Refusing strands
  the customer with a booking they cannot act on and keeps a seat held that could be
  resold.
- **Refused after departure** — an integrity rule more than a policy one. Cancelling a
  flown flight rewrites history, corrupts the points ledger and frees a seat that was
  used.
- Every cabin stays refundable. A non-refundable Economy would mean the most common
  path never exercises the refund calculation, leaving the e2e coverage thinnest where
  the traffic is heaviest.

### A staff-cancelled flight moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED`

Not `CANCELLED`. Auto-cancelling forecloses the rebooking this issue's own acceptance
criteria ask for, releases seats that may be wanted for that rebooking, deducts status
points for something the customer did not do, and is a one-way door — a misclick then
reversed leaves bookings destroyed and seats resold.

Keeping the paths distinct is also what buys the rule that matters: **an involuntary
cancellation refunds in full, bypassing the fare rules and the cut-off**, because the
airline caused it. That is not expressible if both paths converge on one status.

If one leg of a round trip is cancelled, the whole booking goes `DISRUPTED`. Half an
itinerary is not a usable trip.

### Money

#75 (real payments) lands after this issue, so this one **calculates and records** the
refund — an amount plus an immutable status-history row — and does not attempt a money
movement. That keeps this shippable standalone and gives #75 a recorded figure to
refund against.

### Slices

1. Type `Booking.status` as an enum and add the status-history table. Behaviour-neutral; #74 and #75 are both waiting on it.
2. Replace the `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` rename with `releasedAt` and a partial unique index — "release seats without rewriting seat identifiers", which also deletes the display hack.
3. Eligibility and refund calculation.
4. Staff cancel to `DISRUPTED`, and the customer's refund-or-rebook choice.
5. End-to-end coverage for the self-service and staff-assisted paths.

comments.body:
Two findings from slice 1's verification that belong to later slices rather than to it.

## Two changes in one transaction share a timestamp, with no tiebreaker

`record_booking_status_change` stamps `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which is transaction start
time, so three status changes in one transaction all carry the same instant:

```
 from      | to        | createdAt
           | CONFIRMED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 CONFIRMED | DISRUPTED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 DISRUPTED | CANCELLED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
```

`@@index([bookingId, createdAt])` cannot order those, and `id` is a random uuid, so
"the latest status change" is not answerable by `ORDER BY`. The order is recoverable
only by chaining `from` to `to`.

Nothing does two status changes in one transaction today, so this is harmless now.
**Slice 3 records a refund against a history row and slice 5 shows a timeline** — both
will want a monotonic column. Adding one is a small migration; noting it here so it is
a decision rather than a rediscovery. Verified against running code.

## The backfill is only exercised by a database that predates the migration

`prisma/seed.ts` creates no bookings, and dev and CI databases are built from empty by
`migrate deploy` or `migrate reset`. So when the "has an entry for every booking"
assertion runs, the only bookings present are ones the trigger already covered:
deleting the backfill `INSERT` from the migration leaves the suite green everywhere it
normally runs.

The verifier did exercise it by hand — a pre-migration database holding two bookings,
migrated over, produced exactly one history row each with `from` null and the booking's
own `createdAt`, zero orphans — and the guard was confirmed in the same way, rejecting
`'REFUNDED'` and `'pending'` and rolling back whole.

The assertion is kept because the invariant it protects is real going forward. The gap
is that the only database where the backfill matters is a deployed one, which nothing
tests against. Worth remembering for any later migration in this issue that backfills.

comments.body:
## What slice 4 covers, and what is left of this issue's task list

Slice 4 delivers the staff side and the refund half of the customer's choice: a staff
flight cancellation moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED`, the seat stays held, the customer
can take a full refund, and reinstating the flight puts them back.

**Rebooking is not in it, and should be its own slice.** "Offer rebooking, refund, or
credit for disrupted itineraries" needs a flight search constrained to the same route and
a comparable date, seat reselection on the new flight, a fare difference to resolve, and
a decision about what happens to the original booking's history — none of which is a
small addition to the profile row. Building a fraction of it alongside the refund would
have made both worse.

Credit is also untouched: there is no credit balance anywhere in the schema, and #75
owns money.

So what remains on this issue after slice 5 (end-to-end coverage):

- Rebooking a disrupted itinerary onto another flight.
- Credit as an alternative to a refund, if it is wanted at all once #75 lands.

Both are worth their own issues rather than lingering here; happy to file them when the
slices are done, or fold rebooking into a Phase 4 customer-support item, whichever you
prefer.

## One deliberate gap in the disruption path

`lib/PointsActivityService.ts` keys every branch off `=== 'CANCELLED'`, so a `DISRUPTED`
booking still earns status points and still shows as an ordinary credit. That is the
right behaviour — the customer has not cancelled and may yet fly a rebooked itinerary —
but nothing tests it, and it will need revisiting when rebooking lands.

| Slice | PR | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | #228 | `Booking.status` typed as an enum; an append-only status history that writes itself |
| 2 | #230 | Seats released by saying so, not by overwriting the seat number |
| 3 | #231 | The cancellation policy: eligibility, fees, refunds recorded |
| 4 | #232 | A staff flight cancellation disrupts its bookings, and can be undone |
| 5 | #233 | Browser journeys for the self-service and staff-assisted paths |

Against this issue's original task list:

- **Cancellation eligibility by fare and departure time** — done. Refused once departed;
  First and Business refund in full before the 24-hour cut-off, Premium Economy and
  Economy less a fifth; inside the cut-off cancellation is still allowed at nothing back.
- **Release seats without rewriting seat identifiers** — done. A partial unique index
  covers held seats only, so a released row keeps the seat the traveller actually sat in.
- **Calculate and record refunds** — done, on the history row, via a transaction-local
  channel. No money moves: #75 owns that and will have a figure to refund against.
- **Handle airline-initiated cancellations** — done, as `DISRUPTED`, reversibly.
- **Preserve immutable booking and status history** — done, enforced by a trigger rather
  than by convention.
- **Offer rebooking, refund or credit** — the refund only. Rebooking is now #234; credit
  is folded in there and probably depends on #75.

Acceptance criteria: the changes are transactional and auditable, customer, inventory and
notification states stay consistent, and the two journeys are covered end to end.

## Worth knowing before this is called finished

**#84 undercuts the departure guard.** `Flight.departureDate` is local wall-clock time
labelled UTC, so east of UTC a departed flight stays cancellable for the length of the
origin's offset — the exact case slice 3 closes. The policy is exact against the value it
is given; the value is not. Recorded on #84.

**#229 and #208 together hide this feature on a phone.** The Status column is scrolled out
of the visible area and the notification drawer renders behind the page, so a disrupted
booking looks identical to a confirmed one and the fallback channel is unreadable.
Neither is caused by this work; both are now load-bearing for it.

Leaving this open rather than closing it, since #234 came out of it and the milestone is
yours to call.

","state":"open","user":{"login":"scottdensmore","name":"scottdensmore","email":null,"avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/125055?v=4","id":125055},"assignees":null,"labels":[{"name":"roadmap","color":"5319e7","description":"Product hardening work migrated from REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md"}],"milestone":3,"state_reason":null,"comments":4,"created_at":"2026-07-27T05:10:00Z","updated_at":"2026-08-10T20:09:40Z","closed_at":null,"display_url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76","display_title":"P2.4 Implement cancellation, disruption, and refund rules"},"comments":[{"url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235526479","body":"## Decisions, and what is already here

Recording the two answers this issue was waiting on, plus what reading the code first
turned up — because this is not greenfield.

### What already ships

`app/actions.ts:428` cancels a booking transactionally today: it locks the flights in
ascending order, releases the seats, sets the status and notifies. What it has no
concept of is **eligibility**. So two of this issue's tasks are live defects rather
than missing features:

- A customer can cancel **after the flight departed** — releasing a seat on a flown
  flight and deducting status points for a trip they took.
- Staff can set a flight to `CANCELLED` (`app/actions.ts:986`) and the bookings **stay
  `CONFIRMED`, still holding their seats**. The only consequence is a notification, so
  the customer keeps a boarding pass for a flight that is not operating.

Both read from the source; neither is confirmed against a running app yet.

Also relevant to the tasks above: `Booking.status` is a bare `String` with no enum and
no check constraint (`lib/seatOccupancy.ts:27` says so, and that literal is the whole
definition), and seats are released by renaming them to `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` to
dodge the unique index — which is why `lib/bookingItinerary.ts:82` has to translate the
placeholder back into the word "Released" for display.

### Cancellation policy

| Cabin | Before 24h | Inside 24h | After departure |
|---|---|---|---|
| First, Business | Full refund | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Premium Economy, Economy | Refund minus 20% | Cancel, no refund | Refused |
| Any, flight `DISRUPTED` | Full refund, no fee, no cut-off | | |

- **Percentage, not flat.** `Booking.currency` already exists, so a flat fee is wrong
  the moment a booking is not in USD and needs FX to stay right. A percentage of
  `totalPriceCents` needs neither. Rounding is floor, in minor units, stated here so
  tests pin it rather than inheriting whatever the implementation did first.
- **Cancellation stays allowed inside the cut-off, at zero refund.** Refusing strands
  the customer with a booking they cannot act on and keeps a seat held that could be
  resold.
- **Refused after departure** — an integrity rule more than a policy one. Cancelling a
  flown flight rewrites history, corrupts the points ledger and frees a seat that was
  used.
- Every cabin stays refundable. A non-refundable Economy would mean the most common
  path never exercises the refund calculation, leaving the e2e coverage thinnest where
  the traffic is heaviest.

### A staff-cancelled flight moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED`

Not `CANCELLED`. Auto-cancelling forecloses the rebooking this issue's own acceptance
criteria ask for, releases seats that may be wanted for that rebooking, deducts status
points for something the customer did not do, and is a one-way door — a misclick then
reversed leaves bookings destroyed and seats resold.

Keeping the paths distinct is also what buys the rule that matters: **an involuntary
cancellation refunds in full, bypassing the fare rules and the cut-off**, because the
airline caused it. That is not expressible if both paths converge on one status.

If one leg of a round trip is cancelled, the whole booking goes `DISRUPTED`. Half an
itinerary is not a usable trip.

### Money

#75 (real payments) lands after this issue, so this one **calculates and records** the
refund — an amount plus an immutable status-history row — and does not attempt a money
movement. That keeps this shippable standalone and gives #75 a recorded figure to
refund against.

### Slices

1. Type `Booking.status` as an enum and add the status-history table. Behaviour-neutral; #74 and #75 are both waiting on it.
2. Replace the `CANCELLED-<passengerId>` rename with `releasedAt` and a partial unique index — "release seats without rewriting seat identifiers", which also deletes the display hack.
3. Eligibility and refund calculation.
4. Staff cancel to `DISRUPTED`, and the customer's refund-or-rebook choice.
5. End-to-end coverage for the self-service and staff-assisted paths."},{"url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5235702982","body":"Two findings from slice 1's verification that belong to later slices rather than to it.

## Two changes in one transaction share a timestamp, with no tiebreaker

`record_booking_status_change` stamps `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which is transaction start
time, so three status changes in one transaction all carry the same instant:

```
 from      | to        | createdAt
           | CONFIRMED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 CONFIRMED | DISRUPTED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
 DISRUPTED | CANCELLED | 2026-08-10 03:53:34.791
```

`@@index([bookingId, createdAt])` cannot order those, and `id` is a random uuid, so
"the latest status change" is not answerable by `ORDER BY`. The order is recoverable
only by chaining `from` to `to`.

Nothing does two status changes in one transaction today, so this is harmless now.
**Slice 3 records a refund against a history row and slice 5 shows a timeline** — both
will want a monotonic column. Adding one is a small migration; noting it here so it is
a decision rather than a rediscovery. Verified against running code.

## The backfill is only exercised by a database that predates the migration

`prisma/seed.ts` creates no bookings, and dev and CI databases are built from empty by
`migrate deploy` or `migrate reset`. So when the "has an entry for every booking"
assertion runs, the only bookings present are ones the trigger already covered:
deleting the backfill `INSERT` from the migration leaves the suite green everywhere it
normally runs.

The verifier did exercise it by hand — a pre-migration database holding two bookings,
migrated over, produced exactly one history row each with `from` null and the booking's
own `createdAt`, zero orphans — and the guard was confirmed in the same way, rejecting
`'REFUNDED'` and `'pending'` and rolling back whole.

The assertion is kept because the invariant it protects is real going forward. The gap
is that the only database where the backfill matters is a deployed one, which nothing
tests against. Worth remembering for any later migration in this issue that backfills."},{"url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5244346371","body":"## What slice 4 covers, and what is left of this issue's task list

Slice 4 delivers the staff side and the refund half of the customer's choice: a staff
flight cancellation moves its bookings to `DISRUPTED`, the seat stays held, the customer
can take a full refund, and reinstating the flight puts them back.

**Rebooking is not in it, and should be its own slice.** "Offer rebooking, refund, or
credit for disrupted itineraries" needs a flight search constrained to the same route and
a comparable date, seat reselection on the new flight, a fare difference to resolve, and
a decision about what happens to the original booking's history — none of which is a
small addition to the profile row. Building a fraction of it alongside the refund would
have made both worse.

Credit is also untouched: there is no credit balance anywhere in the schema, and #75
owns money.

So what remains on this issue after slice 5 (end-to-end coverage):

- Rebooking a disrupted itinerary onto another flight.
- Credit as an alternative to a refund, if it is wanted at all once #75 lands.

Both are worth their own issues rather than lingering here; happy to file them when the
slices are done, or fold rebooking into a Phase 4 customer-support item, whichever you
prefer.

## One deliberate gap in the disruption path

`lib/PointsActivityService.ts` keys every branch off `=== 'CANCELLED'`, so a `DISRUPTED`
booking still earns status points and still shows as an ordinary credit. That is the
right behaviour — the customer has not cancelled and may yet fly a rebooked itinerary —
but nothing tests it, and it will need revisiting when rebooking lands."},{"url":"https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/76#issuecomment-5245398004","body":"## All five slices are merged

| Slice | PR | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | #228 | `Booking.status` typed as an enum; an append-only status history that writes itself |
| 2 | #230 | Seats released by saying so, not by overwriting the seat number |
| 3 | #231 | The cancellation policy: eligibility, fees, refunds recorded |
| 4 | #232 | A staff flight cancellation disrupts its bookings, and can be undone |
| 5 | #233 | Browser journeys for the self-service and staff-assisted paths |

Against this issue's original task list:

- **Cancellation eligibility by fare and departure time** — done. Refused once departed;
  First and Business refund in full before the 24-hour cut-off, Premium Economy and
  Economy less a fifth; inside the cut-off cancellation is still allowed at nothing back.
- **Release seats without rewriting seat identifiers** — done. A partial unique index
  covers held seats only, so a released row keeps the seat the traveller actually sat in.
- **Calculate and record refunds** — done, on the history row, via a transaction-local
  channel. No money moves: #75 owns that and will have a figure to refund against.
- **Handle airline-initiated cancellations** — done, as `DISRUPTED`, reversibly.
- **Preserve immutable booking and status history** — done, enforced by a trigger rather
  than by convention.
- **Offer rebooking, refund or credit** — the refund only. Rebooking is now #234; credit
  is folded in there and probably depends on #75.

Acceptance criteria: the changes are transactional and auditable, customer, inventory and
notification states stay consistent, and the two journeys are covered end to end.

## Worth knowing before this is called finished

**#84 undercuts the departure guard.** `Flight.departureDate` is local wall-clock time
labelled UTC, so east of UTC a departed flight stays cancellable for the length of the
origin's offset — the exact case slice 3 closes. The policy is exact against the value it
is given; the value is not. Recorded on #84.

**#229 and #208 together hide this feature on a phone.** The Status column is scrolled out
of the visible area and the notification drawer renders behind the page, so a disrupted
booking looks identical to a confirmed one and the fallback channel is unreadable.
Neither is caused by this work; both are now load-bearing for it.

Leaving this open rather than closing it, since #234 came out of it and the milestone is
yours to call."}]}]

The next PR should be:

**`fix(checkout): isolate seat holds per checkout`**, referencing [roadmap issue #74](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/74).

### Roadmap status

PR [#91](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/91) moved the roadmap from `REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md` into GitHub issues and phase milestones. The repository now explicitly treats those issues as the source of truth ([AGENTS.md](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/AGENTS.md:703)).

| Roadmap area | Current state |
|---|---|
| Phase 0, #63–#67 | Complete |
| Phase 1, #68–#72 | Complete |
| P2.1, #73 | Complete |
| P2.2, #74 | Partially complete |
| P2.3, #75 | Waiting behind #74 |
| P2.4, #76 | Five main slices merged; rebooking split to #234 |
| P2.5, #77 | Not started |
| Phases 3–5 | Later work |

There are currently **no open PRs**, and local `main` is clean and synchronized at [`55f25db`](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/commit/55f25db413683aa2faa8e0ea53b0639a4117f712).

### Why this PR is next

PR [#257](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/257) delivered the first #74 slice: expiring holds and automatic abandonment/release behavior. Its follow-up comment records a verified defect: `holderKey` is currently the user ID, so two checkout tabs belonging to the same user can release or refresh each other’s seats.

The current code confirms that:

- Hold claims and releases use `session.user.id` ([actions.ts](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/actions.ts:423)).
- `SeatClaim` anticipates a future checkout-scoped identity but does not have one yet ([seatHolds.ts](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/lib/seatHolds.ts:23)).
- The wizard does not create its request identifier until booking submission, after seats were held ([BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:696)).

The PR should:

- Establish a validated checkout identifier before the first hold.
- Scope claim, refresh, visibility, and release operations to that checkout.
- Ensure two tabs for one account cannot interfere with each other.
- Add database concurrency, component, and browser coverage.
- Leave atomic hold-to-booking conversion and the visible expiry/recovery countdown for subsequent #74 slices.

That is the smallest independently shippable slice and removes a prerequisite blocker before the more delicate transaction work.

issues.title: feat(checkout): hold a seat while the customer is choosing it
issues.body:
First slice of #74. Converting the hold at booking and showing the customer a
countdown are later slices; this one stops two customers being invited to buy
the same seat.

## The problem

A seat only became unavailable once a booking existed. Between picking 12A and
paying for it, the seat stayed on every other customer's map. The partial unique
index on `SeatAssignment` already made it impossible for two people to *own*
12A — but nothing stopped them both being invited to try, and the loser found
out at the payment step.

## Three decisions worth review

**A hold is not an assignment.** An assignment is a seat somebody owns and part
of a booking's history; a hold is a claim with a deadline belonging to nobody's
itinerary. Putting unpaid rows in `SeatAssignment` would make all four queries
behind `heldSeats()` learn the difference.

**The unique index is unconditional** — the opposite of the partial one chosen
for `SeatAssignment` in `20260810050000`. An expired hold is *taken over in
place* by `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, never deleted, so a second row for a seat
should never exist, dead or alive. Claiming is one statement for the same
reason: read-then-write loses to the interleaving where both customers read
first, while a conflict is decided inside the row's own lock.

The verifier attacked this directly rather than trusting the `Promise.all`
test — two genuinely overlapping transactions, B's statement issued while A was
open and confirmed blocked for 400ms:

| isolation | case | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| READ COMMITTED | empty seat | one winner, one row, loser gets `false` |
| READ COMMITTED | expired row | one winner, one row |
| SERIALIZABLE | either | loser gets `40001` |

Every call is autocommit, so READ COMMITTED is what runs. Deadlock is not
possible as written: no transaction ever holds two seat locks at once. Both
properties are now stated in the docstring, because making the loop
transactional would buy an ordering-dependent deadlock.

**Every timestamp is the database's**, in `TIMESTAMPTZ`. `now()` decides the
expiry and the liveness test, so no clock skew can make a hold read live to one
party and dead to another. The zone-aware column matters for the same reason:
the verifier measured one hold, written under UTC, reading as *430 minutes
remaining* in Los Angeles and *530 minutes expired* in Tokyo. `Flight.departureDate`
is `TIMESTAMPTZ` from #84 for exactly this.

**Nothing sweeps expired rows**, which is what satisfies "abandoned checkout
does not permanently reduce inventory" — no cleanup job whose failure could
quietly lose seats.

## What review caught

`ui-review` found four blocking defects and the `verifier` a fifth. All fixed:

- **The refusal blamed the wrong leg.** A round trip carries 16A twice, so the
  client marked whichever leg it found first — telling a customer the outbound
  seat they had just been *granted* was gone, drawn red and disabled, while the
  leg that really failed sat on a tab they weren't looking at.
- **The error rendered off-screen** — 598px above the viewport at 390, 207px at
  1280. Announced to screen readers, so the only people who learned the request
  failed were the ones not looking at the button.
- **The refused seat stayed selected**, so the passenger list said it was theirs
  while the map drew it occupied, and pressing the button re-failed forever.
- **A thrown action was silent** — an expired session gave an unhandled
  rejection and a dead button.
- **Nothing released a hold on the success path.** A bought seat stayed held for
  ten more minutes and outlived the account that took it, since `holderKey` is
  not a foreign key. That failed two Playwright specs *deterministically*, and
  the #213 leak detector missed it because it did not track `SeatHold`. It does
  now, and the full suite leaves zero holds behind.

## Mutation testing

Two mutants survived and drove changes:

- Deleting the read-side integration entirely — another customer's hold no
  longer greying out the seat — was **green across the whole suite**. The hold
  would have decided races invisibly. Two database tests now kill it.
- Asserting the claims payload on a *single-leg* flight is equivalent to the bug:
  `flights[0].id` is the right answer by accident. Only a round trip
  distinguishes "the leg this seat belongs to" from "the first leg".

One reported count was wrong: I claimed "advancing no longer holds seats → 2
red" when the current source gives 4, because I ran it before two round-trip
tests existed. The verifier caught that the number wasn't auditable.

## Verification

794 unit, 111 database, **38/38 Playwright**, build, tsc, lint 0 errors.
Migration applied to a fresh *and* a populated database with no drift; the
`expiresAt > createdAt` check exercised in both directions including the exact
boundary, plus the unique index and the foreign key.

Filed rather than fixed: #255 (seat buttons announce as just "A", so the group
that hears the error can't locate the seat), #256 (seat map scrolls horizontally
at 390px).

Note on #252: it did not reproduce in this run — all 38 passed — so that
failure is less deterministic than reported, and the stranded holds may have
been contributing to it.

issue.title: P2.2 Add inventory holds
issue.body:
Migrated from `REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md`.

## Tasks

- [ ] Create expiring seat/fare holds during checkout.
- [ ] Release abandoned holds automatically.
- [ ] Convert holds atomically when booking completes.
- [ ] Display expiry and recovery behavior to the customer.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two customers cannot purchase the same seat.
- Abandoned checkout does not permanently reduce inventory.
- Hold expiry and conversion are covered by concurrency tests.

comments.body:
Slice 1 delivered in #257 (`8f8e4e8`). Left open — two of the four tasks remain.

**Done**

- [x] Create expiring seat/fare holds during checkout. `SeatHold`, claimed when
  the customer leaves the seat map, expiring after 10 minutes.
- [x] Release abandoned holds automatically. By expiry rather than by a sweeper,
  which is what makes "abandoned checkout does not permanently reduce inventory"
  true without depending on a job that could fail. `releaseHoldsExcept` also
  drops a seat the customer swaps away from, and a completed booking releases
  what it bought.

**Remaining**

- [ ] **Convert holds atomically when booking completes.** Today the release
  happens *after* `bookFlight` returns, deliberately — a hold is an optimisation
  and failing to tidy one up must never undo a purchase. But it is not a
  conversion: between the assignment being written and the hold being deleted
  there is a window where both exist, and if the release fails the seat stays
  "held" by its own buyer until it expires. Doing it inside the booking
  transaction is the real acceptance criterion and needs the deadlock question
  below answered first.
- [ ] **Display expiry and recovery behaviour to the customer.** Nothing tells
  them a seat is being held at all, and nothing shows the countdown. A customer
  can sit on the review step past ten minutes and have the confirmation succeed
  or fail on a race they were never told about.

**Two things the review turned up that the next slice has to answer**

`holderKey` is the user id, not a checkout session. Two tabs on the same flight
therefore stomp each other: advancing in the second releases the first tab's
seat, and another customer can take it. Verified. A per-checkout key fixes it
and is a prerequisite for guests booking at all.

`holdSeat` returns `false` for "someone else has it" only at READ COMMITTED,
which is what every call uses today because each is autocommit. Wrapping the
claim loop in a transaction — the obvious way to make conversion atomic — makes
the loser raise `40001` instead, and introduces an ordering-dependent deadlock
between two customers claiming the same pair of seats in opposite order. Both
are noted in `lib/seatHolds.ts`; neither is a problem until the next slice
starts.

Filed while working on this: #255 (seat buttons announce as just "A"), #256
(seat map scrolls horizontally at 390px).

test(suite): keep tests to product code and the run harness (#266)

Six suites had the repository as their subject rather than the product: they
asserted on package.json, .dockerignore, the set of git-tracked files, where
test files may live, and the Jest and CI harnesses. A test like that pins a
property nobody asked the product for, and goes red on a refactor that broke
nothing.

Remove five, and write the rule down so the next one is not written:

- __tests__/docs/databaseTestHygiene.test.ts
- __tests__/security/committedSecrets.test.ts
- __tests__/security/containerSecrets.test.ts
- __tests__/security/dependencyPolicy.test.ts
- __tests__/security/scanImageLayers.test.ts

The rule is in AGENTS.md under Testing Expectations: tests are written against
code or assets that ship, or that produce what ships. Subject decides it, not
technique — a recursive scan of app/components/lib qualifies, reading
package.json does not, however it is written.

One exception, because a rule without it deletes the wrong things: the harness
deciding whether a Jest or Playwright run can be believed. e2e/global-setup.ts,
the leak snapshotter and jest.database-setup.js ship nothing, but a silent
failure in any of them invalidates every other test rather than failing
honestly — which is how three specs leaked data for months (#213), how a
parallel database run counted another file's fixtures (#155, #215), and how a
stale server made a healthy branch look broken (#196). A CI check sits outside
it: a green CI job is not a test result.

Two files move rather than go. databaseSerialisation.test.ts and
productIdentity.test.ts are restored byte-identical under __tests__/harness/
and __tests__/app/ — the first is covered by the exception, the second was
never in scope, its subject being app/globals.css, app/layout.tsx,
lib/data/FlightData.ts and the shipped assets. __tests__/docs/ is gone; it was
the wrong home for both.

Removing a guard silently is how the property gets lost, so each one is filed
before it goes: #263 for the CI gates, the layer scanner and $disconnect()
hygiene, #265 for the dependency pins and the committed-secret scan. SECURITY.md
no longer claims a recurrence control that no longer exists.

Verified: lint 0 errors/8 warnings, tsc clean, unit 720/720, database 111/111,
the parallel-run guard still aborting. Baseline on main was 773 unit tests; the
drop of 53 is the five deletions exactly, both restorations contributing zero.

One older assertion now fails for a legitimate reason: the generic occupancy endpoint has no checkout identifier, so it can no longer treat every hold owned by the same user as “mine.” That old behavior is exactly what allowed a profile seat change—or another checkout tab—to ignore an active hold. I’m tightening that assertion to require both live holds.
